Colorado State.title: A defensive disaster: CSU gets embarrassed on Homecoming, Tyson Summers is out
Colorado State.summary:
What should have been a celebration turned into another nightmare for CSU football. A record 41,000 fans packed Canvas Stadium for Homecoming and the Rams’ first Pac-12 conference game, only to watch Oregon State roll up 650 yards without punting once in a 56-26 rout. Joel and Mike break down another historically bad defensive performance before diving into the biggest story of the weekend: Jim Mora stripping defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of play-calling duties mid-game, Summers leaving the sideline, and his subsequent dismissal from the program. Was the change overdue? And, why did Mora allow the defense to reach this point in the first place? The guys examine Summers’ surprising retention from the previous staff, Mora’s own responsibility for CSU’s three-game collapse, and whether new play-caller Kenny McClendon can use the bye week to finally make this defense remotely competent.

Gonzaga.title: No. 12 Arkansas Holds Off No. 15 Gonzaga in Exhibition
Gonzaga.summary: FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – In an exhibition matchup between Top 15 teams, No. 12 Arkansas rallied to defeat No. 15 Gonzaga, 76-72, Saturday inside Bud Walton Arena.

Gonzaga.title: Despite loss, No. 15 Gonzaga finds value in 'high-level' exhibition meeting with No. 12 Arkansas | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark . – Two hours before tipoff, a line of students started to form outside Bud Walton Arena, snaking through a grass courtyard and stretching out to a block of academic buildings 30 to 40 yards away.

Later on, a security guard led Arkansas’ iconic “Woo Pig Suie” chant, drawing a positive response from the few hundred students waiting to get in the door.

With an announced attendance of 16,436, Saturday’s meeting between No. 12 Arkansas and No. 15 Gonzaga was an exhibition in name only. If that wasn’t evident beforehand, it became clear once the ball was tipped, with six lead changes, physical play at both ends and a brief dustup between Gonzaga’s Massamba Diop and Arkansas’ Miika Muurinen that resulted in double technical fouls.

Arkansas won 76-72, but Gonzaga didn’t come away empty-handed from the experience.

“This was a great experience for us and great to see what Cal’s built here,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said of longtime friend and Arkansas counterpart John Calipari. “It was great seeing Fayetteville. Really, really impressed with the whole area and all that, so we’ll take what we can and we’ll learn from this. All in all, I’m pretty happy for everything.”

Our first exhibition rewind of the 2026-27 season takes a deeper look at the relationship between the Naismith Hall of Fame coaches, eligibility news Gonzaga received roughly 24 hours before tipoff in Fayetteville and the Bulldogs’ point guard situation.

Mad respect

The Few-Calipari relationship can be traced back to the early 2000s, when both coaches were trying to get quality games on their nonconference schedules while at Gonzaga and Memphis.

“You may say, how did you two get together?” Calipari said. “Both of our programs needed each other. I was at Memphis, he was at Gonzaga just getting it going and we needed each other. When we started playing, I wouldn’t play him at the pound (Kennel) because it’s 8,000, 9,000 and it’s crazy students. So I said I’ll play you in Spokane. It was huge television, it helped both programs and he and I have stayed close since then.”

Calipari regrettably agreed to a six-year nonconference series with Gonzaga, traveling to Numerica Veterans Arena in 2022-23 and hosting Few’s team at Rupp Arena the following season. Gonzaga won the first meeting convincingly, 88-72, and squeaked by Kentucky the following season, 90-89, for an important resume-boosting win that put Few’s team on the right side of the NCAA bubble.

“And me being goofy, I’m at Kentucky now, let’s play,” Calipari said. “We go to his place, they beat us by like 20 – I think they were up by 30 at halftime. Then they come to our place, how hard is it to win in that building? Well, they won and they won by about 30 last year and I think they canceled the series. But Mark’s terrific and you notice they never gave up.”

Saturday’s exhibition can be mutually beneficial for Gonzaga and Arkansas teams that boast preseason top-15 rankings and both have Final Four aspirations. The coaches plan to debrief in the coming days to share thoughts and notes about their teams, hoping to gather valuable intel that can help one week out from the regular season.

“Anytime we get our teams together, it’s always a high-level game,” Few said. “We have teams that can compete for Final Fours and obviously can play deep into the tournament. So it’s fun in that way. In an exhibition game, it’s fun to play against your friends. It’s not playing against your friends in real games, it’s kind of torturous. But yeah, we’ve had quite a year together here.”

Few and Calipari have had more run-ins than usual the last three months.

The Arkansas coach was one of three active Naismith Hall of Famers – along with Grant Hill and John Stockton – to present Few when he received his orange jacket in Springfield, Massachussetts, two months ago.

The coaches met up again at Capitol Hill in Washington , D.C. , last month to advocate for the Protect College Sports Act that would institute sweeping changes across college sports, including a cap on revenue sharing and new transfer regulations.

The bill likely came up in conversation when Few, Calipari and Gonzaga athletic trainer Josh Therrien met for dinner Friday night at Cheers, a Southern comfort restaurant in downtown Fayetteville.

“I just think when you have a bipartisan bill that passed the Senate 78-22, name the last bill that passed the Senate 78-22,” Calipari said. “We’ve got to get it through the house. I’ve made it clear, I’m being selfish. I’ve got a son in this, Mark has a son in this, Tom Izzo has a son in this, Kelvin Sampson has a son in this. We’ve all got sons in this, you want to leave it this way?”

Almansa’s arrival

Gonzaga teammates describe Izan Almansa as stoic and even-keeled – someone who doesn’t express much emotion when he’s on the court and probably even less he’s away from it. But even Almansa couldn’t hide his grin when the Spanish forward learned he was cleared by the NCAA on Friday morning, just before Gonzaga boarded its charter flight to Fayetteville.

“He’s a dude who’s pretty quiet,” Braden Huff said, “but you could see the excitement on his face when he got the news and we were all super excited for him.”

It marked the end of a five-month wait for Almansa, who committed to Gonzaga in May but faced a long, uncertain road to eligibility given his professional experience overseas and tenure in the NBA G League. Almansa most recently played at Real Madrid in the Spanish ACB, but also had yearlong stints with the Perth Wildcats of Australia’s NBL and G League Ignite.

Almansa, who hadn’t been part of Gonzaga’s exhibition plans even 30 hours earlier, was Few’s top contributor off the bench and played valuable minutes spelling Diop when the 7-foot-1 center encountered foul trouble in the first half.

The sophomore was GU’s second-leading scorer behind Huff, totaling 12 points on 6 of 9 from the field and 1 of 2 from the 3-point line. He also had six rebounds and led the Zags with two blocked shots.

“That’s a big get for us, he was huge today,” Huff said. “I expect that from him all season. For him to be eligible is great, he’s going to be really good for us.”

Point of concern?

Even with three point guards in place now, the position group that dominated offseason headlines continues to be something to monitor closely eight days out from the season opener against Purdue.

Xaivian Lee, Nathan De Sousa and Javon Bennett all had stints on the ball Saturday, with De Sousa getting the largest share of minutes (33), followed by Lee (19) and Bennett (16).

Provided he stays eligible through an injunction in his California lawsuit, Lee is expected to handle starting point guard duties, though foul trouble limited his opportunities in Saturday’s exhibition. The Florida transfer navigated early shooting struggles to make two momentum-shifting 3-pointers late in the game and finish with eight points on 3 of 6 shooting and 2 of 4 from distance.

It was a rough go for De Sousa in his first collegiate game. The French native posted horrendous shooting numbers, making 2 of 17 shots from the field and 1 of 8 from the 3-point line, but he had three assists with just one turnover and tied for the team lead with two steals.

“They struggled, they struggled to shoot the ball,” Few said. “But Nate’s got quite the fighting spirit. He’s a tough guy, we knew that. I’d say Xaivian did a nice job of responding there, especially in that second run, we put him in to step up and make shots because he was struggling a bit early and he got the fouls.”

According to Few, Bennett learned he’d be eligible to play in Saturday’s exhibition not long before tipoff. Similar to Lee, the fifth-year senior is currently involved in a 5-in-5 lawsuit and recently got a favorable decision from the Ohio Supreme Court, which issued a stay to temporarily clear player plaintiffs listed in the case.

Few partially attributed Bennett’s offensive struggles on Saturday to . The Dayton transfer was 1 of 8 from the field and 0 of 4 from the 3-point line, scoring only two points.

“Javon will be fine, he knows how to make buckets and get in there,” Few said. “He got the news very, very late today, right before the game that he was going to be eligible to play. I’m not sure as far as preparation may be, I think that may have impacted him a little bit. They definitely have room for improvement after looking at those numbers right there.”

Gonzaga.title: Davis Fogle-less Gonzaga struggles offensively, falls 76-72 to Arkansas in exhibition
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – College basketball exhibition games often come with an extended list of asterisks. The list for Saturday’s preseason matchup between No. 12 Arkansas and No. 15 Gonzaga ran slightly longer than normal.

The Razorbacks prevailed 76-72 over the Zags in a back-and-forth game that featured at least three major momentum swings and saw both teams lead by as many as 10 points.

As for the asterisk, or caveat, even Arkansas coach John Calipari couldn’t avoid pointing out on multiple occasions during a postgame press conference? Davis Fogle was parked at the end of Gonzaga’s bench in street clothes, not stuffing the stat sheet for a team that went through multiple dry spells offensively in both the first and second half and didn’t make a 3-pointer for the first 15 minutes.

“Their best player wasn’t playing,” Calipari told reporters, “so this probably would’ve been a different game.”

If the point wasn’t clear enough, Calipari came back around to it later on in a 14-minute postgame availability, stressing how much of a difference Fogle could’ve made had he been on the floor, not resting an injured left leg at Bud Walton Arena.

“Let me say this, too. That team over there with Fogle, I told Mark (Few) after, I grabbed him I said, ‘You play Fogle, we get beat by 20 today,’” Calipari said. “Because he’s another veteran, shooting 3’s, off the bounce, the kid’s a pro. And he didn’t play today. He’s okay, but (Few) said, ‘He just banged up his knee and I’m going to leave him out, it’s an exhibition game.’ And their first game is a hard game. But they’re good.”

Fogle or no Fogle, the Zags also have plenty of room for growth – a reality for virtually all 365 Division I basketball teams in the country during the final week of October.

Despite missing its first 11 looks from the 3-point line, Gonzaga managed to take an early lead and stayed in front for the majority of the first half, going up by double digits on Braden Huff’s jumper with 2 minutes, 14 seconds to play.

Arkansas responded with an offensive storm that stretched from the final stages of the first half to the opening minutes of the second. All told, it was an 18-0 Razorbacks run – a 9-0 run in the first half followed by an identical 9-0 run in the second – that ultimately helped Calipari’s team go up 50-39 on Cooper Bowser’s dunk with 14 minutes, 21 seconds to play.

The contributing factors to Arkansas’ game-turning run?

“Really bad offense by us,” Few said. “But obviously, it was impacted and caused by great defense by Arkansas. I think that was a major thing and that was a stretch where somehow we ended up on the positive side of the rebounds and second-chance points, but it sure didn’t feel like that. Definitely not during that stretch right there.

“Also those free-throw rebounds, it was crazy. I think they just got eight to 10 points on free throw rebounds and block outs.”

The Zags still weathered the storm and had chances down the stretch to tie the game or go back in front. Huff got a short floater to rattle in with 2 minutes, 17 seconds left, trimming Gonzaga’s deficit to five points, and Xaivian Lee knocked down a pull-up 3-point shot in transition to make it 68-66. After Miika Muurinen’s layup stretched the lead back out to four points, Huff came back down and got another floater to fall.

But Arkansas freshman Davion Thompson responded with a clutch pull-up 3-pointer from the top of the arc and Gonzaga trailed by two possessions for most of the final minute, until Izan Almansa converted a tip-in with four seconds to play.

There were plenty of teaching points for a Gonzaga team that finished 6 of 28 (21.4%) from the 3-point line weeks after making 18 of 33 at Kraziness in the Kennel. The Zags often struggled to defend without fouling and four players finished with four fouls apiece. The Razorbacks went to the charity stripe for 30 free throws, but made just 17.

“That’s what these games are great for,” Few said. “I thought it was an awesome, awesome environment. In the past, we’ve done closed-door scrimmages and stuff and there’s a lot to be gained from that. But this was a great experience for us.”

Huff shrugged off a slow shooting start to finish with game-highs of 19 points and 11 rebounds. Spanish forward Izan Almansa was Gonzaga’s only other double-digit scorer, scoring 14 points and pulling down six rebounds roughly 30 hours after he was deemed eligible by the NCAA.

Billy Richmond III led the Razorbacks with 17 points while Thompson had 12 and both Muurinen and JJ Andrews finished with 10 apiece.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga wing Tyon Grant-Foster selected No. 15 by Sioux Falls Skyforce in G League Draft
Gonzaga.summary:
Tyon Grant-Foster will start his professional basketball career in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, after the former Gonzaga wing was selected No. 15 overall by the Sioux Falls Skyforce – an affiliate of the Miami Heat – in Saturday’s NBA G League Draft.

The 26-year-old Grant-Foster wasn’t selected in the 2026 NBA Draft, but signed an NBA Summer League deal with the San Antonio Spurs, making one appearance at the California Classic and three more at Vegas Summer League.

The well-traveled wing had stops at four colleges before transferring to Gonzaga for his final season of eligibility. The NCAA initially denied Grant-Foster’s eligibility waiver, but the veteran wing filed a lawsuit against the sport’s governing body and secured a preliminary injunction in Spokane County Superior Court, clearing him to suit up for Mark Few’s team in 2025-26.

Grant-Foster played at Indian Hills Community College, Kansas, DePaul and Grand Canyon before transferring to Gonzaga last spring. The wing mostly played a bench role for the Zags, starting in just six of 35 games, but still finished as one of the team’s three double-digit scorers while averaging 11.1 points, 5.0 rebounds and 1.2 assists.

Grant-Foster was one of three first-round picks for Sioux Falls on Saturday. The team used its No. 7 pick on Rhode Island’s Tyler Cochran before taking Central Arkansas’ Masai Olowokere with the 24th pick.

The Texas Legends (Dallas Mavericks) had the first overall pick, selecting former Baylor and San Antonio Spurs forward Jeremy Sochan.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga wing Davis Fogle sidelined for Arkansas exhibition with left leg injury
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – Gonzaga missed one of its top scoring options in today’s preseason exhibition against Arkansas.

Davis Fogle didn’t dress or take part in pregame warmups at Bud Walton Arena as the sophomore wing continues to recover from a minor leg injury he suffered during a recent practice.

A school official said Fogle is day-to-day and pushed to play in Saturday’s exhibition, but Gonzaga chose to take precautions nine days before a highly-anticipated season opener against Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

Fogle still traveled with the team to Fayetteville and wore a black Gonzaga warmup shirt and black sweatpants on the visiting bench Saturday afternoon.

The wing is expected to be one of the breakout players in college basketball and stole the show at Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel showcase on Sept. 26, scoring 30 points in 20 minutes on 11 of 15 shooting from the field, 6 of 7 from the 3-point line and 2 of 2 from the free throw line.

Fogle was a deep reserve for Gonzaga during the early stages of his freshman season, but gradually became one of the team’s top scorers, averaging 10.9 points over the team’s final 16 games. The Anacortes native finished the season averaging 8.6 ppg, 3.1 rpg and 1.3 apg while shooting 51.8% from the field, 35.0% from the 3-point line and 72.3% from the free throw line.

Fogle has a good chance to play in the season opener and could return for Wednesday’s home exhibition against NAIA Lewis-Clark State.

Wing Chauncey Wiggins also didn’t dress as the Florida State transfer continues to pursue an additional year of eligibility through a 5-in-5 lawsuit in his home state of Georgia. Gonzaga’s two other fifth-year transfers, Xaivian Lee (Florida) and Javon Bennett (Dayton), are currently eligible after recent rulings in California and Ohio.

Without Fogle, Gonzaga started three guards against Arkansas – Lee, Nathan De Sousa and Isiah Harwell – alongside forward Braden Huff and center Massamba Diop.

Walk-on Carter Nilson was the third Gonzaga player not to dress as the guard continues to recover from a hand injury.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga Adds Spanish Forward Izan Almansa
Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. – Gonzaga men's basketball head coach Mark Few announced the addition of Izan Almansa, an experienced forward from Spain, for the 2026-27 season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Izan Almansa deemed eligible by NCAA one day before Arkansas exhibition
Gonzaga.summary:
Five months after quietly committing to Gonzaga, Spanish forward Izan Almansa has been cleared by the NCAA and just in the nick of time, with Mark Few’s team visiting Arkansas for Saturday’s marquee exhibition matchup.

The 21-year-old was formally announced by Gonzaga on the school’s social media platforms Friday afternoon, roughly 24 hours before the Bulldogs are set to take on John Calipari’s Arkansas team in a 1 p.m. exhibition at Bud Walton Arena. More importantly, Almansa will now be at Few’s disposal when 15th-ranked Gonzaga travels to Las Vegas in nine days to open the 2026-27 campaign against Purdue in a nationally mtelevised game at T-Mobile Arena.

Almansa, a 6-foot-10 sophomore, will have three years of eligibility under the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model and cements what many believe could be one of the strongest frontcourts in the country this season, providing depth behind all-conference candidates Braden Huff and Massamba Diop.

The Murcia, Spain, native showed glimpses of his offensive game and rebounding during Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel showcase, scoring seven points on 2 of 4 shooting while matching Huff with a scrimmage-high seven rebounds.

With three years of professional basketball under his belt, Almansa took a unique, winding route to American college basketball, recently playing for Real Madrid of the Spanish ACB, where he averaged 4.9 points and 2.2 rebounds in 10.2 minutes per game.

Before that, he spent one season playing for the Perth Wildcats of Australia’s NBL – widely considered to be the most competitive international basketball leagues outside of Europe – averaging 7.6 points and 4.3 rebounds in 17.2 minutes per game.

Almansa spent the 2023-24 season playing for now-defunct G League Ignite, sharing the court with former Gonzaga guards Jeremy Pargo, David Stockton and Admon Gilder. The forward started in all 16 games he played in for Ignite, averaging 8.2 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.3 blocks.

Pargo reacted to Friday’s news on social media, commenting on a post from Gonzaga basketball’s official Instagram account: “Yeahhhhhhhh @izanalmansa_ let’s gooooo”

Almansa entered the 2025 NBA draft and accepted a green room invitation to attend the second round at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York. Despite mock drafts projecting him as a fairly safe second-round pick, Almansa didn’t hear his name called and proceeded to sign an NBA Summer League deal with the Philadelphia 76ers, averaging 3.0 ppg and 1.3 rpg during a four-game stint in Las Vegas. Rather than pursue additional opportunities in the G League, Almansa opted to return to his home country, signing a one-year contract with Real Madrid.

In addition to his professional experience, Almansa has a handful of international caps with Spain’s senior and youth national teams. Most recently, he was on the senior team’s roster for FIBA World Cup European qualifying games, averaging 7.7 ppg and 5.0 rpg in six appearances.

The NCAA gave Almansa a green light despite cracking down on eligibility guidelines for international players this offseason. The regulatory body offered new guidelines, stating international players may not be eligible if they earned above “actual and necessary expenses” from professional teams outside of the United States.

Friday’s development reduces the list of roster concerns for a Gonzaga team that has three other players awaiting legal verdicts in various 5-in-5 eligibility lawsuits. Florida transfer Xaivian Lee and Dayton Javon Bennett are currently eligible to suit up as a result of recent legal decisions in California and Ohio, but Florida State transfer Chauncey Wiggins isn’t expected to play until oral arguments are heard in his Georgia lawsuit.

According to Austin Massey of Scarlet and Black Insider, oral arguments have been scheduled for Jan. 12. At least one player plaintiff, Texas Tech’s Jamichael Stillwell, has withdrawn his name from the Georgia lawsuit, but Wiggins’ intentions remain unclear.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, Arkansas seeking competition and growth from exhibition: 'I want it to be a war'
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – Mark Few and John Calipari recently took a detour from their conversations about the Protect College Sports Act, ongoing 5-in-5 eligibility issues and other pertinent topics that have prompted coaches in their position to advocate for the future of the game.

Few and Calipari had more pressing business to discuss on their latest phone call, namely the upcoming exhibition matchup between their Gonzaga and Arkansas programs, what both programs hope to get from it and how the longtime friends can help one another roughly a week before their teams dive into rigorous nonconference schedules.

So Few and Calipari, two of the four active Naismith Hall of Fame coaches still drawing up plays in 2026-27 – St John’s Rick Pitino and Michigan State’s Tom Izzo being the others – briefly tabled the PCSA and other macro NCAA issues to discuss ball and strategy.

“We’ve got Gonzaga,” Calipari told local media earlier this week. “Mark and I talked the other day. I’ve said, ‘Do you have your zone in yet?’ ‘Nope, I’ve got no zone.’ Great, neither one us are playing zone. I go, ‘Do you want me to press some?’ He said, ‘Yeah, let’s press each other so we can turn it over and have something to teach.’ I told him our out of bounds plays, these are what we have, and he told me his out of bounds plays.”

The 1 p.m. contest between the 15th-ranked Zags and 12th-ranked Razorbacks at Bud Walton Arena will be televised on streaming platform SEC Network+. It’s the first of two exhibition matchups for Gonzaga, which hosts NAIA Lewis-Clark State four days later at McCarthey Athletic Center before opening the season Nov. 2 against Purdue in Las Vegas.

It’s not uncommon for coaches, particularly those with the history and tight-knit friendship of Few and Calipari, to trade thoughts, notes and ideas before exhibition games that have no bearing on regular-season win/loss records, AP Top 25 rankings or NCAA Tournament seeding.

So on Saturday, Gonzaga might provide a specific look to help Arkansas in an area where the Razorbacks have struggled during preseason practices, just as long as Calipari returns the favor later in the game.

“We’re friends, I want it to be a war,” Calipari said. “When you’re playing this type of team, there’s times you’re saying I hope we get beat so I can grab the attention of this team. But I just tell everybody come and enjoy watching these guys. … We should have a roster of 10, 11 being able to play in that game.”

The Hall of Fame coaches go as far back as 2000, when Few’s Gonzaga program visited Calipari’s Memphis team for a nonconference game. The Bulldogs and Tigers played every year from 2006-09, often finding a way to wedge nonconference games into their conference schedules during January and February. Memphis claimed four straight wins against Gonzaga before Calipari left to become the Kentucky coach in the spring of 2010.

Few and Calipari scheduled a six-game nonconference series between their Gonzaga and Kentucky programs in 2022, but Calipari was involved in just two of those matchups – 88-72 and 89-85 wins for Gonzaga – before accepting the Arkansas job in 2024.

The faces on Arkansas’ roster may be new, but the Razorbacks’ makeup should be familiar to anyone who’s monitored Calipari at his previous stops. Arkansas secured the country’s top-rated recruiting class, bringing in three of the top-20 prospects from the 2026 recruiting class, and a heralded international recruit.

The group is led by powerful combo guard Jordan Smith, a candidate to be the No. 1 pick in the 2027 NBA draft, and fellow five-stars Abdou Toure and Davion Thompson. Miika Muurinen, an athletic 7-foot Finnish prospect who played at AZ Compass Prep in 2024-25 with Gonzaga wing Davis Fogle, recently gained eligibility and joins the Razorbacks as a five-star international freshman.

The Zags will trot out some version of the roster they hope will stay on the floor throughout the 2026-27 season, though 5-in-5 eligibility lawsuits continue to complicate things eight days out from the opener. Fifth-year transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida) and Javon Bennett (Dayton) are currently eligible to play Saturday, but Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State) is expected to sit out as he continues to face eligibility hurdles.

Gonzaga coaches have spent the week reminding players Saturday’s opportunity is only an exhibition by name, urging them to approach it the same they would a top-25 showdown during the regular season.

“Just going out there and making sure we play our hardest and first of all, treat it like a real game because we’re trying to prepare for the season and get our bearings rolling,” said Gonzaga guard Isiah Harwell, who scored six points off the bench for Houston in a 94-85 victory over Arkansas last season at the Prudential Center in New Jersey. “Just going out there, making sure we’re playing hard, we’re rebounding, boxing out, making sure we’re doing all the little things right.”

Gonzaga.title: Calling Hogs and Zags: Parker Jefferson's family allegiances add meaning to Gonzaga-Arkansas exhibition
Gonzaga.summary:
Parker Jefferson was indoctrinated into Arkansas fandom years before he could tie his own shoes, dribble a basketball or even put together a coherent sentence.

There wasn’t really a choice for someone whose parents met as college athletes in Fayetteville, Arkansas, outfitted their children in Arkansas apparel – the novelty rubber Razorback hog noses were always a hit – and routinely made the five-hour drive from the Dallas area to their college town to visit family and attend football and basketball games.

Yes, Jefferson could probably perform a perfect rendition of the iconic Arkansas “Woo Pig Sooie” rally cry, but he’ll have to abstain when the sophomore forward and his Gonzaga teammates take the floor for Saturday’s 1 p.m. PT exhibition (SEC Network+) between the Bulldogs and Razorbacks.

“I can remember having them laying on my lap when kids are too young to even move their arms and legs,” mother Carrie Jefferson said Thursday during a phone interview. “Kind of like you’d play peek-a-boo with a kid, I’d raise their arms and go ‘Woooooo Pig Sooie.’ My kids have literally been learning how to ‘Call the Hogs’ since they were infants.”

Saturday’s meeting is nothing more than an exhibition, unless you’re one of the estimated three- to four-dozen family members or friends seated in the Jeffersons’ section at Bud Walton Arena.

On Wednesday, the Gonzaga forward reported the official headcount was 22. The next day, his mother offered a correction: That’s only how many tickets Parker managed to gather from Gonzaga teammates and coaches

willing to offload some of their own. The actual number could be closer to 40, Carrie confirmed, with nearly 20 relatives, former Arkansas women’s basketball teammates and other acquaintances expected to purchase their own seats or use season tickets.

“Man, I had to basically scramble to get as many (tickets) as I could,” Parker said.

It’s an especially meaningful occasion for Carrie, who was born roughly 75 miles south in the small town of Charleston, Arkansas, where Parker’s grandparents still reside. With no professional sports in the state and no major college programs that could compare with Arkansas, Carrie was raised on Razorbacks football and basketball, idolizing Hall of Fame hoops coaches Eddie Sutton (1975-85) and Nolan Richardson (1985-2002).

“I was really little then … I really didn’t understand there was a men’s and women’s. I was just saying, I was going to grow up and play for Nolan Richardson,” Carrie said. “So it was pretty cool to then go there and get to be around Nolan. So when you’re raised in Arkansas, you’re just a Razorback fan. It’s kind of by default.”

Carrie suspects it could be emotional watching her son jog through the tunnel and onto the court Saturday afternoon. She enjoys telling people she “opened” Bud Walton Arena 33 years ago, and it’s not far from the truth. Carrie’s freshman season in ’93 began just weeks after construction finished on the 19,368-seat building that now sits in the heart of campus. She and Arkansas teammates would finish practice at Barnhill Arena, strap on hardhats and wander over to the construction site, where workers were still bolting seats into the ground.

“We got to kind of be involved in the process of designing our locker room and that kind of thing,” said Carrie, who had the opportunity to watch daughter Kaylee play at Bud Walton during her tenure at Sam Houston State. “It’s just such a nostalgic thing. … I can’t even describe it. I literally feel like I can still feel the sweat I poured out there.”

Fayetteville is also where Carrie met Jefferson’s father, Mike, an offensive lineman on the Razorbacks’ football team who hailed from Germany before moving to Louisville, Kentucky. Carrie and Mike met at a popular college bar, where they were introduced by Mike’s football teammate and began dating after an Arkansas Athletes Outreach event. Jefferson’s parents are now separated, but both plan to be in attendance for Saturday’s exhibition.

Parker attended games at Bud Walton as a kid and returned in 2022 as a prospective Arkansas basketball player. Eric Musselman offered a scholarship to the three-star prospect – then rated as one of the top 45 centers in the country – and easily persuaded Jefferson to take an official visit as a high school sophomore.

But any chance of Jefferson following in his parents’ footsteps fizzled when Musselman left for USC. Jefferson passed up on an offer from the Trojans to sign at Minnesota before reopening his recruitment when Gophers coach Ben Johnson was fired. One month later, he was committed to Gonzaga.

“Obviously it was good for the storyline and having parents there,” Jefferson said. “It was a cool thing that I was getting recruited by them, but my parents were never pushing it on me.”

Jefferson and his mother have traded stories about their varying experiences as college athletes.

“We’re so spoiled now, the student-athletes. They were barely even getting a pack of ramen noodles from their coaches,” Parker laughed.

Carrie concurred.

“Every recruiting visit we went on, we’d see the protein shake bar or whatever different places had,” she said. “I would be like, ‘Oh my gosh, I would’ve killed for an extra peanut butter and jelly sandwich sometimes.’ They would just roll their eyes at me and I was like, ‘You guys don’t even understand.’ ”

Carrie and her Arkansas teammates resided in dorms at the top of a large hill and often navigated tricky winter conditions to make practices at Bud Walton, located at the base of the slick and icy slope.

“Coach (Gary) Blair would be like, ‘Well, you ladies figure out a way to get to practice,’ ” she said. “There were great memories of us getting out and sledding down the hill.”

In 1995, Carrie and the Razorbacks qualified for the school’s fifth NCAA Tournament. She played one minute off the bench in a first-round win over San Francisco at Seattle’s Alaska Airlines Arena, but didn’t log any time during a second-round loss to Washington.

Parker, who redshirted in 2025-26, expects a good mix of Gonzaga and Arkansas colors in the Jeffersons’ section on Saturday but hopes to see more navy blue No. 32 jerseys than cardinal red T-shirts. Two of Jefferson’s younger cousins have custom-printed shirts with both logos and hearts underneath. A former Arkansas women’s basketball teammate told Carrie she planned to wear a Gonzaga hat with a Razorback shirt.

“I think they might still be calling the Hogs, who knows, but they’ll probably, definitely, hopefully be in some blue and red,” he said.

Carrie relayed her biggest concern before picking up older son Michael on Thursday and driving to Fayetteville from the family’s home in Waxahachie, Texas.

“Somebody’s just going to have to forgive me if I raise my arms and start calling the Hogs,” she said. “It’s just something you learn as a little kid.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Xaivian Lee, Ines Bettencourt maintain eligibility after injunction in California lawsuit
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga basketball players Xaivian Lee and Ines Bettencourt moved one step closer to competing in 2026-27 after a key ruling in the Glancey vs. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit Tuesday morning.

Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Beth McGowen granted a preliminary injunction to Lee, Bettencourt and more than 70 other player plaintiffs seeking another year of competition through the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model, according to CBS Sports’ Jon Rothstein.

Tuesday’s injunction is the most significant development in the lawsuit so far and means Lee, who transferred from Florida to play for Mark Few and the Gonzaga men, and Bettencourt, who returned to play a fifth season for Lisa Fortier and the Gonzaga women, are both eligible to compete this season.

The NCAA is expected to appeal the decision, according to Rothstein, meaning Lee, Bettencourt and other players named in the lawsuit likely have to overcome one final hurdle before getting clearance to play through the 2026-27 college basketball season.

Until a decision is made on the appeal, Lee and Bettencourt will be eligible to compete in their respective teams’ preseason exhibition games. Lee and the 15th-ranked Gonzaga men open the exhibition slate on the road Saturday against 12th-ranked Arkansas at 1 p.m. (SEC Network+) before returning home to host NAIA Lewis-Clark State on Oct. 28. Bettencourt and the GU women host Division II Westmont College in their only exhibition on Oct. 27.

Eligibility questions persist elsewhere for the Gonzaga men, who picked up commitments from three 5-in-5 transfers in August and added Spanish prospect Izan Almansa, a veteran forward who’s still waiting on the NCAA to approve his international waiver.

Lee and fellow fifth-year guard Javon Bennett are both eligible to play in Saturday’s exhibition after Tuesday’s injunction was granted in California and last week’s stay in the Ohio Supreme Court, temporarily clearing Bennett after the Dayton transfer was previously ruled ineligible. Chauncey Wiggins, Gonzaga’s third 5-in-5 transfer, is currently ineligible after the Georgia Court of Appeals stayed a prior injunction.

A native of Ontario, Canada, Lee spent three seasons at Princeton, averaging 17.0 points his final two years before transferring to Florida in 2025-26 and averaging 11.6 points with 4.2 assists for a Gators team that earned a No. 1 seed at the NCAA Tournament. Provided he remains eligible, Lee is widely expected to take over as GU’s starting point guard months after projected starter Mario Saint-Supery left to sign a contract with Valencia of Spain’s ACB.

Although he never resided or competed for a school in California, Lee opted to join the Glancey vs. NCAA lawsuit, citing the four games he played in San Diego and Sacramento against student-athletes “participating in their fifth seasons of competition,” according to a court declaration.

In the declaration, Lee also stated “Gonzaga University has a roster spot currently available and reserved for me for that purpose, and my taking that roster spot would not result in another playing losing their spot.”

Making his case against class of 2022 high school graduates returning to college for a fifth season, NCAA President Charlie Baker stated on Oct. 16 “allowing them to return for an unexpected fifth season of competition would give them a benefit they never reasonably could have expected, to the detriment of thousands of eligible student-athletes who have been waiting for their opportunity to compete.”

Bettencourt is pursing another season of eligibility after the versatile, two-way guard started in all 33 games for Fortier’s team last season, averaging 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.5 steals. The Portugal native played two years at UConn before transferring to Gonzaga in 2024-25.

LSU’s Donovan Dent, a fifth-year point guard Gonzaga was expected to pursue when Saint-Supery left the program, was also impacted by Tuesday’s injunction. Dent and fellow fifth-year UCLA transfer Skyy Clark, another player named in the lawsuit, could both be on the floor for LSU when the Tigers travel to Spokane for a Nov. 14 matchup against the Zags at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Gonzaga.title: Analyzing the situation for every former Gonzaga and Washington State player in the NBA
Gonzaga.summary:
The NBA’s regular season officially tips off Tuesday with three games taking place throughout the afternoon and evening, followed by a full slate of games the following day.

There will be 10 former Gonzaga players and five from Washington State represented on opening-day rosters. For anyone who requires a refresher, we list and break down the situation for all 15 former Zags and Cougars who could be suiting up as the NBA returns this week.

Graham Ike, Golden State Warriors

Experience: Rookie (signed undrafted two-way contract with Warriors in September)

2025-26 statistics: N/A

The situation: Ike parlayed a championship run with Golden State at NBA Summer League – where he averaged 9.3 points and 7.2 rebounds over eight starts – into a two-way contract with the Western Conference organization. Golden State’s older frontcourt, coupled with ongoing uncertainty around center Kristaps Porzingis and a current injury to forward/center Charles Bassey, could lead to early playing time for Ike, the reigning West Coast Conference Player of the Year.

Ryan Nembhard, Denver Nuggets

Experience: Second season (signed undrafted two-way contract with Dallas Mavericks in 2025)

2025-26 statistics: 6.6 ppg, 5.3 apg, 2.2 rpg in 60 games (27 starts)

The situation: Front office changes in Dallas played a role in Nembhard’s move away from the Mavericks, who relied on the undrafted point guard heavily through long stretches of his rookie season. Nembhard was initially traded to Atlanta and then to Charlotte before finally washing up in Denver on a two-way contract. Gonzaga’s single-season assists leader is expected to compete for backup point guard minutes behind Jamal Murray.

Malachi Smith, Toronto Raptors

Experience: Second season (signed 10-day contract with Brooklyn Nets in 2025)

2025-26 statistics: 8.3 ppg, 3.4 rpg, 3.3 apg in 15 games (4 starts)

The situation: Smith’s success story continues three years after he won WCC Sixth Man of the Year honors at GU. The guard bided his time in the G League for the better part of three seasons before agreeing to a 10-day contract with the Brooklyn Nets in March. Smith shot efficiently from the 3-point line and played well enough in other areas – he registered 19 points, 10 assists and eight rebounds against Milwaukee – to earn a two-way contract from Toronto.

Chet Holmgren, Oklahoma City Thunder

Experience: Fourth season (drafted No. 2 overall by Oklahoma City in 2022)

2025-26 statistics: 17.1 ppg, 8.9 rpg, 1.9 bpg in 69 games (69 starts)

The situation: Oklahoma City fell short of reaching the NBA Finals last season, and Holmgren was largely ineffective matching up against San Antonio phenom Victor Wembanyama in the Western Conference finals. The former Gonzaga one-and-done center still posted career-best scoring and rebounding numbers while earning the first All-Star bid of his young career. Holmgren’s role isn’t expected to change much in year four, but keep an eye on potential double-big lineups featuring the 7-foot-1 All-Star and 7-foot-3 first-round rookie Aday Mara.

Andrew Nembhard, Indiana Pacers

Experience: Fifth season (drafted No. 31 overall by Indiana in 2022)

2025-26 statistics: 16.9 ppg, 7.7 apg, 2.8 rpg in 57 games (57 starts)

The situation: Despite playing the fewest games of his career, Nembhard predictably set career-high point and assist totals with Indiana point guard Tyrese Haliburton sidelined for the season. Nembhard should return to more of an off-ball role with Haliburton back on the floor and the Pacers are expected to be competitive in the Eastern Conference once again after last year’s 19-63 record. Ideally the former Zag can replicate his outside shooting after making a career-high 36% of his 3’s on a career-best 5.2 attempts per game.

Jalen Suggs, Orlando Magic

Experience: Sixth season (drafted No. 5 overall by Orlando Magic in 2021)

2025-26 statistics: 13.8 ppg, 5.5 apg, 3.9 rpg in 57 games (56 starts)

The situation: Suggs almost willed Orlando to a first-round playoff series victory over Detroit, averaging 16.6 points and making nine 3-pointers over the final three games, but the Magic ultimately came up short in their seven-game series. A young Orlando team returns its starting five from last season and should still be a legitimate playoff contender, even in a vastly improved Eastern Conference. Suggs continued to look more comfortable as Orlando’s primary ball-handler, leading the team in assists for the first time in his career.

Corey Kispert, Atlanta Hawks

Experience: Sixth season (drafted No. 15 overall in 2021 by Washington Wizards)

2025-26 statistics: 9.2 ppg, 2.3 rpg, 1.6 apg in 58 games (10 starts)

The situation: A midseason trade saw the Washington Wizards move Kispert and CJ McCollum to the Atlanta Hawks in exchange for Trae Young. It allowed the former Gonzaga sharpshooter to see playoff minutes for the first time in his career, though he struggled during an opening-round series against the New York Knicks, averaging 2.2 ppg off the bench while shooting 18.3% from the field and 8.3% from the 3-point line. Kispert could be Atlanta’s third option at shooting guard this season, behind starter Nickeil Alexander-Walker and newly-acquired Lu Dort.

Rui Hachimura, Los Angeles Clippers

Experience: Eighth season (drafted No. 9 overall by Washington Wizards in 2021)

2025-26 statistics: 11.5 ppg, 3.3 rpg, 0.6 apg in 68 games (41 starts)

The situation: The former Gonzaga forward didn’t have to go far – just 10 miles – to find his new NBA home. Hachimura moves on from the Lakers after four seasons and 36 playoff games, but the eighth-year pro should have no trouble nailing down a starting role with a Clippers team that moved on from Kawhi Leonard this offseason. Hachimura is expected to join a starting unit that could also include Darius Garland, Bradley Beal, Derrick Jones Jr. and Isaiah Jackson.

Zach Collins, Chicago Bulls

Experience: Ninth season (drafted No. 10 overall in 2017 by Portland Trail Blazers)

2025-26 statistics: 9.7 ppg, 5.6 rpg, 1.5 apg in 10 games

The situation: Collins is looking for a bounce-back season in Chicago after missing time due to a left wrist fracture and toe injury – injuries that sidelined him for all but 10 regular-season games. The reserve forward/center missed the Bulls’ entire preseason slate with his toe injury, but is optimistic about his chances to return for the team’s opening game against Toronto. He’s expected to compete for backup center minutes behind projected starter Nic Claxton.

Domantas Sabonis, Sacramento Kings

Experience: 11th season (drafted No. 11 overall in 2016 by Oklahoma City Thunder)

2025-26 statistics: 15.8 ppg, 11.4 rpg, 4.1 apg in 19 games (15 starts)

The situation: One of the most durable players in the NBA the last 11 seasons, Sabonis was limited to a career-low 19 games after partially tearing his meniscus. Despite seeing his name in trade rumors throughout the summer, Sabonis returns to Sacramento for year six seeking a return to the playoffs after the Kings won just 22 games with the former All-Star sidelined most of the year. It could be an uphill battle for a team that already suffered two major injuries, to Maxime Raynaud and Ben Simmons, during the preseason.

Drew Timme, Phoenix Suns

Experience: Third season (signed 10-day contract with Brooklyn Nets in 2024)

2025-26 statistics: 3.4 ppg, 1.2 rpg, 0.9 apg in 27 games (one start)

The situation: Timme was a last-second addition for Phoenix, which signed the forward off waivers on Monday, two days after he was released by the Minnesota Timberwolves. Gonzaga’s career scoring leader took the Suns’ final two-way contract, meaning he’ll split time between the NBA team in Phoenix and G League team in Tempe. Timme’s playing time with the Los Angeles Lakers was sparse last season, but the former Zag was one of the top scorers in the G League, averaging 23.9 points for South Bay.

Washington State

Cedric Coward, Memphis Grizzlies

Experience: Second season (drafted No. 11 overall by Memphis Grizzlies in 2025)

2025-26 statistics: 13.6 ppg, 5.9 rpg, 2.8 apg in 62 games (47 starts)

The situation: The former Washington State/Eastern Washington wing earned NBA All-Rookie honors last year and should take on an expanded role for a Memphis team that traded All-Star point guard Ja Morant in the offseason. Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo indicated Coward could be handling the ball more in Year 2 and the wing was generally solid in four preseason games, recording 11 assists with just two turnovers.

Isaac Jones, Detroit Pistons

Experience: Third season (signed undrafted two-way contract with Sacramento in 2024)

2025-26 statistics: 1.3 ppg, 0.7 rpg, 0.1 bpg in seven games (one start)

The situation: After his move from Sacramento last November, Jones should benefit from having a full offseason in Detroit’s system. The former Washington State and Idaho standout only played in four games for the Pistons, but he excelled with the G League Motor City Cruise, earning All G League First Team honors after averaging 22.2 points, 8.9 rebounds, 2.8 steals and 1.9 blocks. Jones could see more time with the NBA team in Detroit this season, but for now he’s projected to be the Pistons’ third or fourth option at power forward.

Jaylen Wells, Memphis Grizzlies

Experience: Third season (drafted No. 39 overall by Memphis Grizzlies in 2024)

2025-26 statistics: 12.5 ppg, 3.2 rpg, 1.6 apg in 69 games (69 starts)

The situation: Despite moving to the bench during the team’s fourth preseason game, Wells, who’s started in all but five of his 148 career games, is expected to return to the Grizzlies’ starting lineup alongside Coward, point guard Ty Jerome, forward Cameron Boozer and center Zach Edey. The third-year pro was on track to play all 82 games last season before a toe injury kept him off the court for the final three weeks.

Mouhamed Gueye, Atlanta Hawks

Experience: Fourth season (drafted No. 39 overall by Atlanta Hawks in 2023)

2025-26 statistics: 4.4 ppg, 3.6 rpg, 0.9 apg in 77 games (eight starts)

The situation: A left foot fracture will keep Gueye out for the start of the regular season, but the former Coug’s positional versatility should still be valuable for an Atlanta team that likes to deploy him at both power forward and center. Gueye’s production and efficiency have fluctuated but the Senegal native appeared in a career-high 77 games last season – more than twice from the previous year – and the Hawks still see long-term potential in someone who brings length, shooting and athleticism to the frontcourt rotation.

Klay Thompson, Miami Heat

Experience: 14th season (drafted No. 11 overall by Golden State in 2011)

2025-26 statistics: 11.7 ppg, 2.1 rpg, 1.4 apg in 69 games (eight starts)

The situation: For the first time in his accomplished career, Thompson was demoted to a bench role and averaged just over 21 minutes per game for the Dallas Mavericks. The veteran guard shot a career-low 38.3% from the 3-point line and struggled to turn things around during Miami’s preseason, when Thompson made just 3 of his 20 attempts from deep. Despite his cold shooting stretch, Thompson is expected to take a starting spot in Miami, where he’ll play alongside Davion Mitchell, former Golden State teammate Andrew Wiggins, Giannis Antetekounmpo and Bam Adebayo.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga debuts at No. 15 in preseason Associated Press poll
Gonzaga.summary:
Before Monday’s Associated Press poll was released, just five college basketball programs had the claim of being ranked in the preseason Top 25 each of the last 16 years.

The group is now down to four but it still includes Gonzaga after the Bulldogs debuted at No. 15 in Monday’s preseason poll.

Gonzaga, Duke, Kansas and Kentucky all kept their streaks alive at 17 consecutive years. North Carolina, meanwhile, saw its streak end after voters kept the Tar Heels and first-year coach Michael Malone out of Monday’s rankings.

It also marks the 26th straight year the Zags have been ranked in the AP poll. It’s Gonzaga’s highest preseason rating since 2024, when Mark Few’s team opened at No. 6.

Florida was the overwhelming choice at No. 1, picking up 47 of 59 first-place votes. The Gators were followed by No. 2 Duke and No. 3 Illinois, who claimed 10 and two first-place votes, respectively. The Zags will play the Blue Devils in a Feb. 20 nonconference game at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

Reigning national runner-up UConn checked in at No. 4 and Arizona, which enters year No. 5 under former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd, came in at No. 5.

Michigan State, another one of Gonzaga’s nonleague opponents, is ranked No. 6, followed by No. 7 Texas, No. 8 Tennessee, No. 9 Virginia and No. 10 Houston.

Voters may have been split on what to do with a Gonzaga team facing a series of eligibility questions just two weeks out from the season opener. Seven voters ranked Gonzaga inside the top 10, with one placing them as high as No. 7. On the opposite end of the spectrum, 11 voters ranked Few’s team between 20-25 and one kept the Zags outside of the top 25 completely.

As of Monday, two of Gonzaga’s three 5-in-5 transfers – point guards Javon Bennett (Dayton) and Xaivian Lee (Florida) – are eligible to suit up, while another, wing Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State) is not. Spanish forward Izan Almansa is also ineligible at the moment as the NCAA reviews his international waiver.

The Zags are guaranteed to see one other preseason Top 25 team, No. 22 UCLA, during their nonconference schedule but could encounter a few others at the Players Era 16 in Las Vegas. Ranked teams on GU’s side of the bracket include No. 14 Miami, No. 16 Michigan and No. 20 Alabama. The other side features No. 8 Tennessee, No. 11 Louisville, No. 13 St. John’s, No. 18 Iowa State and No. 19 Texas Tech.

Purdue, Gonzaga’s opponent in the Nov. 2 season opener, narrowly missed out on a preseason ranking, but finished third among teams receiving votes. The Arkansas team Gonzaga is set to face in Saturday’s preseason exhibition at Bud Walton Arena came in at No. 12 in the preseason poll.

The only other Pac-12 Conference team to earn Top 25 mention was Utah State, which collected one Top 25 vote and finished 19th among those receiving votes.

Gonzaga came in slightly higher in Monday’s preseason USA Today Coaches Poll, debuting at No. 12. Florida also checked in at No. 1 in the Coaches Poll, followed by No. 2 Duke, No. 3 Illinois, No. 4 Arizona, No. 5 UConn, No. 6 Michigan State, No. 7 Texas, No. 8 Houston, No. 9 Tennessee and No. 10 Virginia.

Gonzaga.title: Denver Nuggets guard, former Gonzaga standout Julian Strawther sidelined indefinitely with knee sprain
Gonzaga.summary:
Denver Nuggets guard Julian Strawther, the former Gonzaga standout, will be sidelined indefinitely after spraining his left knee earlier this week during a preseason game, the team announced Friday night.

Strawther will be re-evaluated in six weeks, the Nuggets said.

The 24-year-old sustained the injury during Wednesday’s game against the Los Angeles Clippers. Strawther was tripped up and fell while attempting to drive, and his leg bent awkwardly as he fell on it. He stayed down on the court for a moment before being helped to the locker room.

Strawther is projected to be a key player off the bench for the Nuggets this season. He started a career-high 14 games last year and made 57 appearances, averaging 7.2 points, two rebounds and 1.1 assists per game.

The 6-foot-6, 205-pound Strawther was selected by Denver with the 29th overall pick of the 2023 NBA draft after starting 68 games for the Zags during the 2021-22 and 2022-23 seasons. He has played in 172 games for the Nuggets.

Gonzaga.title: Ohio Supreme Court decision temporarily reinstates eligibility for Gonzaga's Javon Bennett
Gonzaga.summary:
For the first time in more than a month, Gonzaga received a piece of encouraging news on the 5-in-5 eligibility front.

Point guard Javon Bennett, a Dayton transfer trying to secure a fifth college season through the ongoing Borovicanin v. NCAA lawsuit, temporarily regained eligibility after the Ohio Supreme Court stayed a previous decision by the Ohio Court of Appeals.

For now it means Bennett, who ranked fifth in Atlantic 10 scoring last season while averaging 15.8 points, can suit up for a Gonzaga team that opens its exhibition slate on Oct. 24 against Arkansas at Bud Walton Arena.

Bennett joined a group of player plaintiffs that filed a lawsuit against the NCAA as part of Borovicanin v. NCAA. The veteran guard was cleared to play through a preliminary injunction on July 9 and subsequently committed to Gonzaga on Aug. 6.

Less than two weeks later, Bennett and the other players in Borovicanin v. NCAA encountered an obstacle when the NCAA was granted a stay in the lawsuit, temporarily reversing their eligibility until the case was resolved.

Wednesday’s decision was the latest development in the Ohio 5-in-5 suit, restoring the lower court’s injunction and making the players eligible until more information is collected.

Along with Bennett, other high-profile college basketball players impacted by the decision include Xavier’s Filip Borovicanin, Cincinnati’s MJ Collins Jr. and St. John’s Keyshawn Hall.

The stay motion comes one day after Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed a controversial executive order permitting colleges in the state to determine whether various 5-in-5 candidates could compete this season. The order would only impact athletes currently enrolled at Ohio institutions and therefore not apply to Bennett, who spent the last three seasons at Dayton.

With Bennett back in the fold, Gonzaga could have a full fleet of point guards available for next week’s marquee exhibition. French prospect Nathan De Sousa was recently cleared to compete for the Zags this season and fifth-year Florida transfer Xaivian Lee is currently eligible through a temporary restraining order in the state of California.

Lee’s lawsuit, Glancey v. NCAA, will resume Oct. 20 in Santa Clara, California, although it’s unlikely a final ruling on the case will be made then. Gonzaga women’s player Ines Bettencourt is also one of the plaintiffs listed in the lawsuit.

One other Gonzaga player, wing Chauncey Wiggins, is currently involved in a 5-in-5 lawsuit. Wiggins initially obtained a fifth season of eligibility through a preliminary injunction, but the NCAA applied for a stay motion in that case, temporarily reversing the decision.

Wiggins and Lee both competed in Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel showcase on Oct. 3, but Bennett didn’t participate due to a minor shoulder injury, according to coach Mark Few.

The 5-foot-10 guard is coming off his most productive offensive season, averaging 15.8 points to go with 2.9 assists and 2.2 rebounds while earning All-Atlantic 10 first-team honors. Bennett made 98 starts over three seasons for the Flyers, helping Anthony Grant’s program earn an NCAA Tournament berth in 2023-24.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga learns tipoff times, TV delegations for remaining nonconference and Pac-12 games
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s new television schedule might be a breath of fresh air for devoted fans who’ve been pulling late nights to catch Mark Few’s team the last handful of years.

Tipoff times and television designations for all 31 of Gonzaga’s regular-season games, including the inaugural Pac-12 Conference schedule, were released Wednesday morning.

The announcement came with a few encouraging developments for Gonzaga fans, particularly for those residing in Central and Eastern time zones. All 31 regular-season games will appear on national broadcasts and only a select few will start after 7 p.m., with 10 afternoon tip times mixed in during nonleague and Pac-12 Conference play.

Throughout the year, Gonzaga will appear on eight different television networks with games on ESPN, Fox, TNT and Prime Video. A majority of the team’s Pac-12 games will be broadcast by CBS, USA Network, the CW and CBS Sports Network. Every game televised by the CW and KHQ will also be available to ESPN Unlimited subscribers.

Before the Zags open the regular season, Mark Few’s team will face two exhibition opponents, traveling to Arkansas on Oct. 24 for a 1 p.m. (SEC Network+) tipoff against John Calipari’s Razorbacks. The exhibition season will continue four days later when GU hosts NAIA Lewis-Clark State at 6 p.m. (KHQ) at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga will appear on five different networks during a five-game stretch to start the regular season: Nov. 2 against Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas (4:30 p.m., TNT/truTV/HBO Max), Nov. 7 vs. New Mexico State (2 p.m., KHQ), Nov. 14 vs. LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena (12:30 p.m., USA Network), Nov. 17 vs. Montana State (8 p.m., CBSSN) and Nov. 24 vs. Kansas State at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas (9:30 p.m., ESPN). Gonzaga’s remaining games at Players Era will also air on ESPN networks.

The Zags will close the calendar year with a Dec. 2 home matchup against NAIA Eastern Oregon (7 p.m., CBSSN), a Dec. 5 trip to play UCLA at the Honda Center in Anaheim (8:30 p.m., Fox), a Dec. 9 home contest against Incarnate Word (6 p.m., the CW), a Dec. 12 trip to Creighton (7 p.m. , Fox), a Dec. 19 game against Michigan State at Acrisure Arena in Palm Desert (2 p.m., CBS) and a Dec. 31 home matchup with Cornell (5 p.m., the CW).

With the exception of Gonzaga’s Feb. 20 nonconference clash with Duke at Detroit’s Little Caesars Arena (5 p.m. , Prime Video), the team’s remaining regular-season games will air on CBS, CBSSN, USA Network and the CW, including a Jan. 30 nonleague matchup with Oregon at Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena (11 a.m., CBS).

Tipoff times and TV designations for Gonzaga’s Pac-12 games are as follows: Jan. 6 at Washington State (6 p.m., the CW), Jan. 9 vs. Colorado State (3:30 p.m., USA Network), Jan. 13 at Fresno State (8 p.m., CBSSN), Jan. 16 vs. Boise State (7:30 p.m., CBSSN), Jan. 21 at Utah State (5 p.m. , USA Network), Jan. 27 vs. Fresno State (7 p.m., USA Network), Feb. 4 vs. Texas State (7 p.m., CBSSN), Feb. 6 at San Diego State (3:30 p.m., USA Network), Feb. 10 at Boise State (5 p.m. , the CW), Feb. 13 vs. Utah State (5 p.m., USA Network), Feb. 17 vs. Washington State (7 p.m., CBSSN), Feb. 25 at Texas State (6 p.m. , USA Network), Feb. 27 vs. San Diego State (1 p.m., CBS) and March 3 vs. Oregon State (6 p.m., the CW).

Gonzaga-UCLA tickets on sale this week

Tickets for Gonzaga’s Dec. 5 nonconference matchup against UCLA at the Honda Center in Anaheim will go on sale this week.

A one-day presale will begin at 11 a.m. on Thursday and tickets will go on sale to the general public at 11 a.m. the following day. Fans interested in registering for the presale or purchasing tickets can find more information at WestCoastHoopsShowdown.com.

Gonzaga.title: KenPom, analytic models split on where Gonzaga belongs in preseason college basketball polls
Gonzaga.summary:
Nearly three weeks out from the regular season, Gonzaga’s roster remains unsettled and analytic models ranking college basketball teams seem divided on where to place Mark Few’s team in preseason top 25 polls.

There could be a wide range of outcomes for a team waiting on four starting-level/rotation players to become eligible, with preseason exhibitions and a Nov. 2 opener against Purdue quickly approaching. Other teams, such as the LSU program visiting Spokane for a Nov. 14 nonconference game at Numerica Veterans Arena, face a similar dilemma as court cases around the country determine whether a large swath of fifth-year seniors will be eligible in 2026-27.

Among other things, it’s added another layer of difficulty to the daunting challenge of ranking more than 300 college basketball teams before games officially tip off in November.

On Sunday, well-known college hoops statistician Ken Pomeroy unveiled his always-anticipated preseason rankings. Gonzaga will open the season ranked No. 14 at KenPom.com, boasting what Pomeroy will be the nation’s No. 7 adjusted offense and No. 21 adjusted defense.

Pomeroy detailed his process of ranking teams this season, explaining in a Substack article that he’s compiling rankings based off who’s listed on each roster, even if certain players on those rosters remain in limbo.

“This was the most challenging year to do ratings because of the eligibility uncertainty hanging over so many players,” Pomeroy wrote. “For the initial release, I am assuming that all players listed on a team’s official roster are eligible.”

In Gonzaga’s case, Pomeroy’s rating is based on the assumption all four of Xaivian Lee, Chauncey Wiggins, Javon Bennett and Izan Almansa will be cleared to suit up. Lee, Wiggins and Bennett are fifth-year hopefuls trying to gain eligibility through lawsuits in California, Georgia and Ohio, while Almansa is an international transfer still waiting on the NCAA to approve his eligibility waiver.

Pomeroy’s model also attaches a win percentage probability to every regular-season game. According to that, Gonzaga is favored to win all but two games on its schedule: Dec. 19 versus Michigan State (45%) and Feb. 20 versus Duke in Detroit (29%). Pomeroy’s projected win-loss record for Gonzaga, which doesn’t necessarily equal the sum of individual game predictions, is 22-6 and 13-3 in the Pac-12 Conference.

Even without four players whose eligibility could be decided as early this week or still a few months from now, other analytic models are still bullish on a Gonzaga team that returns forward Braden Huff and wing Davis Fogle, while bringing in a pair of high-caliber transfers in center Massamba Diop (Arizona State) and guard Isiah Harwell (Houston).

Evan Miyakawa, who uses the Bayesian Performance Rating, to rank college basketball teams, believes the Zags have top-10 potential with or without Lee, Wiggins, Bennett and Almansa.

Miyakawa’s updated preseason rankings, which went live on Sept. 18, feature a unique tool that allows users to view rankings based on every player in limbo becoming eligible and another that reflects a rankings if none are eligible.

At Miyakawa’s website, EvanMiya.com, Gonzaga has a relative ranking (all players eligible) of No. 6. Excluding the quartet of players in limbo, the Zags still check in as a top-10 team according to Miyakawa, ranked No. 9 in the country. Huff is the only Gonzaga player ranked inside the top 50 of Miyakawa’s individual player ratings, although Fogle and Lee aren’t far behind, respectively sitting at No. 59 and 60.

BartTorvik.com, another analytics website used by the NCAA Tournament’s Selection Committee to parse through March Madness candidates every year, demonstrates the disparity in how various analytics models view the Zags entering 2026-27. Torvik ranked the Zags at No. 17, also assuming the four players in limbo will be on Few’s roster throughout the regular season.

As the season draws closer, other computer-based rankings such as ESPN’s BPI (Basketball Power Index), and various human polls, including the Associated Press Top 25 and USA Today Coaches Poll, will release preseason rankings.

Gonzaga.title: Freshman center Sam Funches has embraced early challenges at Gonzaga: 'Just waiting for everything to click'
Gonzaga.summary:
Sam Funches figures it could be a long year for Gonzaga’s opponents trying to convert inside against Mark Few’s reconstructed frontcourt.

It was a long summer for the freshman center, who didn’t get much variety during intrasquad scrimmages and individual frontcourt drills, almost exclusively matching up with Massamba Diop at a stage in the offseason when senior forward Braden Huff was recovering from a knee injury and Spanish import Izan Almansa still hadn’t arrived on campus.

Funches, a 7-footer with a 7-foot-5 wingspan, didn’t need much creativity or space to get his shot off playing against high school competition back home in Germantown, Mississippi, but he realized how quickly those same windows can close at the college level not long after he arrived at Gonzaga in June.

During one of his first practices, Funches thought he’d scored a rare victory on Diop, getting the 7-foot-1 Arizona State transfer to bite on a pump-fake. As Funches went to lay the ball in, Diop rebounded back off the hardwood and met his teammate at the rim to reject the shot.

“I made a good move on Massamba, I got this man in the air and as soon as I went up, he was already back in the air,” Funches said. “I thought that man double-jumped. I was like, ain’t no way, this finna be a long year.”

While humbling now, Funches anticipates the daily duels with Diop to be beneficial in the long run. If he can find occasional success against a high-level defender who ranked second in Big 12 blocked shots last season, Funches figures things will come easier when he’s matched up against opposing forwards and centers that don’t possess Diop’s height, athleticism or instincts.

“I’ve got to go against Massamba every day, who’s tall, faster than me and more athletic, stronger than me,” Funches said. “It’s going to get me better regardless.”

Whether Funches is in Gonzaga’s rotation or situated on the bench, the next six to seven months will be pivotal for the freshman center, who arrives after capturing Mr. Basketball honors in Mississippi and averaging a double-double (21.7 points, 11.6 rebounds) during his senior season at Germantown High School.

Funches chose Gonzaga over LSU and multiple SEC schools in his home state with hopes of developing into the program’s next NBA-caliber big man. Outside of a few exceptions, that typically doesn’t happen in a year and Funches could find minutes difficult to come by as a freshman, with Huff, Diop and Almansa expected to fill out a dynamic three-man frontcourt rotation for the Zags. Things could change if Almansa’s international eligibility waiver is denied, hypothetically moving Funches up one position on the depth chart.

“I think as of right now, I’m just competing for playing time,” Funches said this summer. “I’ve got to prove to the coaches that I belong, I’ve got to gain Mark Few’s trust and all that stuff. As of right now, I’m just trying to get used to everything and bond with my teammates. I haven’t really looked that far yet.”

The level of competition is just one adjustment Funches had to make after moving across the country in June. Weight training sessions with strength coach Travis Knight looked significantly different than the ones Funches had grown accustomed to at Germantown.

“It’s a lot of core stuff, a lot of legs, a lot of balancing stuff,” Funches said. “It’s different, like I said, I’m not used to it. Usually, it’s just a lot of bench press I used to do. I didn’t do a lot of one-leg balancing stuff, so it’s different.”

His favorite aspect of living in the Pacific Northwest?

“Being able to walk outside and not getting hit by bugs all the time,” Funches said. “One time I was walking out in Mississippi. I was walking and my teammates were in front of me. … I get hit by a locust in my face. I was just so confused. I just looked at it and it looked right back at me. Then we just went on about our day. I was like, ‘I’ve got to get out of here.’ ”

Before moving across the country, Funches picked up valuable experience participating in Team USA’s U-18 minicamp, held in Colorado Springs, Colorado, to determine which 12 players would represent the country at FIBA AmeriCup in Puerto Rico. Funches didn’t make the final roster, but feels he held up well competing against the top high school players in the country.

“It was still a good experience as far as all the NBA scouts that were there,” he said. “… It was a great experience and it helped. Some of the college coaches there talked to coach (Brian) Michaelson and told them I could probably be pretty good this year.”

For now, Funches’ role on this Gonzaga roster is still undefined. He missed both of his shot attempts and didn’t score during Kraziness in the Kennel, although it’s worth mentioning he was matched up with Diop – an assignment he’ll be glad to hand off to Gonzaga’s exhibition opponents later this month – for the vast majority of his 10 minutes on the floor.

“It’s not all bad. I’m still competing,” he said. “Even if (Diop) is better than me in every single way, I can still come and compete. … But still just waiting for everything to click.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women show off versatility, experience during Fan Fest scrimmage
Gonzaga.summary:
Most Fan Fest’s are a happy-go-lucky time, nothing more than an opportunity to put the jersey on for the first time and take to the court under the lights.

For the Gonzaga women’s basketball team, Saturday was different. The Zags didn’t just want to go through the motions. Ten of them played in the Fan Fest a year ago and they weren’t happy with the product they put on display.

Yes, the Zags were squaring off against their teammates, their friends. But judging by the competitiveness, it meant something to them.

Few will remember the score or which color prevailed come March. But for the record, Blue, led by Lauren Whittaker, Ines Bettencourt and Teryn Gardner, topped White 42-30 in the 20-minute scrimmage at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Equivalent to half a game, Whittaker, the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season had 12 points, five rebounds, two assists and two steals. Bettencourt, who is seeking a fifth year of eligibility and is presently eligible, had 10 points and Gardner, who is vying for a starting position and more playing time this season, had nine points on 3-of-6 shooting from 3-point range.

Gonzaga was the top 3-point shooting team in the nation, and the Zags will likely be among the leaders again this season. Blue and White combined to make 9 of 18 from distance.

But as the scrimmage showed, the Zags can do a number of things. And there’s much room for improvement. Coach Lisa Fortier, who along with dedicated assistants Stacy Clinesmith, Jordan Green and husband, Craig Fortier, begin their 13th season, will watch the Fan Fest video.

“We’ll go back and see all the problem areas,” Fortier said. “Half the time I was talking to my friends (during the scrimmage). So we’ll definitely go back and watch (the video).”

As she always does at Fan Fest, Fortier left the in-game coaching to her assistants.

“I liked how we were trying to push the ball (in transition), get the ball outletted faster, run the floor harder,” Fortier said. “We’ve done it in a little bit different way in the past where we’ve had the point guard really pass it full court. So last year we got bogged down a little bit with too many dribbles in transition. So I thought our team ran hard and looked to (pass) the ball to people. We didn’t always score in transition, but we’re getting those opportunities.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile sat out, her left foot still in a boot recovering from what she called an overuse injury. She said she expects to be back in two to three weeks.

Eleven of 12 Zags scored. Interestingly, the one who didn’t, junior guard Allie Turner, won the 3-point shooting contest. She edged Gardner. Turner and Gardner led the Zags in 3-point shooting last year.

All three new Zags - freshman Abby Lusk and transfers Emmy Roach and Jocelyn Medina - scored. Roach led with six points.

Bettencourt had an interesting passing partner during the 3-point shooting contest - former UConn teammate Azzi Fudd, the No. 1 draft pick by the Dallas Wings in the 2025 WNBA draft.

All five returning starters made cases for securing their starting job. And Gardner is certainly making a case to be a starter.

“There are people who are more likely (to start) based on their tenure here,” Fortier said. “Last year we ended up starting the same lineup (every game). That’s kind of been our style, but we’re always trying to not have that be a thing. You have to earn it every day in practice and even after you’ve gotten it that doesn’t mean you get it forever.”

Bettencourt thought the Zags did a number of things well Saturday.

“I mean, what is there not to like,” Bettencourt said. “We started off strong with our (drill) competitions - what we can do individually and then in the scrimmage. We were just having fun. It’s always better to be playing in front of a crowd instead of a silent gym and the coaches yelling at us constantly. It was just good to be back in front of the fans.”

That’s why they call it Fan Fest.
