Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga star Kevin Pangos reportedly to join Tommy Lloyd's staff at Arizona
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga point guard Kevin Pangos announced his retirement from basketball last weekend, but it appears he’s hardly finished with the sport.

According to a report online, Pangos will join Tommy Lloyd’s staff as an Arizona assistant coach.

Pangos, 33, played four years at Gonzaga while Lloyd was an assistant on the Zags staff, becoming the WCC player of the year as a senior in 2014-15 before beginning a professional career.

Pangos played 10 seasons professionally, spending last season in Turkey, before announcing his retirement via Instagram on Saturday. He played 24 games with the NBA’s Cleveland Cavaliers in 2021-22, and was also a longtime member of the Canadian national program.

“I don’t know if any athlete finishes their career completely content. We always believe we’re capable of more. But I can 1,000% say I gave it everything I had. I never let the circumstances dictate my approach.

“We left it all out there and accomplished everything you always dreamed of. Now it’s time to do the same for the next chapter.”

Pangos appears likely to take the open UA assistant coaching spot vacated when Ken Nakagawa left to become an assistant coach with the G League’s Salt Lake Stars, SB Nation reported last Friday.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with experience, Gonzaga women appear better than ever ahead of annual Fan Fest
Gonzaga.summary:
When it comes to the Gonzaga women’s basketball team’s Fan Fest, it’s less about execution and more about embracing the moment.

More than anything, it’s the first opportunity for the Zags to wear their uniforms and step onto the court at McCarthey Athletic Center in a pseudo-competitive environment. Just because the Bulldogs aren’t playing a real opponent, playing against each other can bring out the competitive spirit.

After all, teammates don’t like to lose to teammates – whether it’s a table-top game, a 3-point shooting contest or an intrasquad scrimmage.

That alone is reason for a crowd to show up Saturday when things tip off at 2 p.m. and fans can get their first look at the 2026-27 lineup.

Junior point guard Allie Turner, who has started nearly all Gonzaga games since her arrival from St. Louis, Missouri, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

Turner hopes the Zags put forward a better showing than a year ago.

“Hopefully we’re way better than last year,” Turner said of Fan Fest. “I remember some people being like ‘(we) should have moved (Fan Fest) back a few weeks last year.’ But hopefully this year we look like a well-oiled machine out there.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier was told that Turner brought up Fan Fest and her expectation of making a better debut this year.

“It’s funny that Allie brought up Fan Fest. I don’t even remember it to be honest with you,” Fortier said.

Fortier won’t be looking at the final statistics. She doesn’t put much stock in who scores what or who has the most rebounds in a scrimmage.

“The big thing is getting them under the lights,” Fortier said. “It’s good to see where everyone is. For me it’s good for my coaches to get to coach. I sit on the side and rib everybody and take notes.”

Ten of the 13 Zags have suited up for a Fan Fest. It’ll be a new experience for freshman forward Abby Lusk, GU’s lone incoming frosh from Pocatello, Idaho; guard Emmy Roach, a junior transfer from Rider University; and guard Jocelyn Medina, a senior transfer from Denver.

A roster is usually needed for Fan Fest. Not this year. Even returning is graduate guard Ines Bettencourt, who gained a fifth year of eligibility this summer late under the new 5-in-5 eligibility format. So her former uniform number (8) had been assigned to Medina. Bettencourt’s new number is 0.

Former Mead standout Teryn Gardner, who transferred from Boise State last year and made an immediate impact coming off the bench, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

“We have basically the same team back so I think we’re all super excited for that,” Gardner said. “It’s going to be a fun time.”

Gardner said the goal for Fan Fest isn’t anything complicated.

“We want to start solidifying our plays,” she said. “We want to help the three new girls get to know everything and how we run the system and whatnot. We want to have fun but we want to make it a good scrimmage.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile will be sitting on the sideline. She’s still wearing a boot on a foot she injured during the summer. The injury is healing and doesn’t appear to be longterm, Fortier said.

Haile was selected as the West Coast Conference Sixth Woman of the Year last season.

Fortier has been cautious with Haile’s recovery.

A deep roster

It stands to figure Gonzaga will be a much more polished team this year.

But there are questions to be answered. Can GU win a championship in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12? Can it win an NCAA Tournament game and go further than any previous GU team? With all five starters back, does coach Fortier just roll out the 2025-26 starting lineup? And with five other returners who got quality playing time, how does Fortier divvy up minutes?

Lots of questions and no hurry to come up with answers.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Fortier has decided to stay away from concrete specified goals with her team this year.

“We’re not even really setting those in the same way,” Fortier said. “Our team goal is to show up every day in practice. We’re not even putting that (goals) to paper. We talk about the process a lot. I think it does them a disservice to (talk about goals). They may or may not have those in the back of their heads, but we’re not gonna verbalize those things. I believe if we show up every day and try to get better then all of the end is going to take care of itself.”

Fortier is right. There will be much conversation about potential by a number of people – right, wrong or indifferent – so the Zags would do themselves favors by veering away from those conversations.

They know, for example, they’ll have a target on their backs. With essentially the whole team back they can’t help but be picked to win the Pac-12 Conference and advance to the NCAA Tournament.

There will also be talk of the potential to be the best team ever under Fortier and best in school history. But it does the Zags no good to get caught up in those expectations.

Gonzaga is going to be good. The Zags know it. The Bulldogs will be out to stack days together. And that could get them to where they want to go.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga forward Kelly Olynyk inks contract with Italian club BC Roma
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga standout Kelly Olynyk will resume his basketball career in Europe after 13 seasons in the NBA.

The 35-year-old forward signed a contract with BC Roma in Italy’s top league, the Lega Basket Serie A (LBA), the team announced on Saturday. One of the club’s co-founders is Los Angeles Lakers All-Star Luke Doncic.

“I am very happy with this opportunity and to become part of the BC Rome project,” Olynyk said after signing. “I can’t wait to arrive in Rome, meet my new teammates, and start working together with the team. I am thrilled with this new experience.”

Olynyk spent time with eight different teams over his 13 seasons in the NBA, most recently playing a deep bench role for the San Antonio Spurs team that lost 4-1 to the New York Knicks in the NBA Finals.

The journeyman forward didn’t make an appearance in the Finals, but logged minutes in four games during San Antonio’s Western Conference Finals win over the Oklahoma City Thunder. Olynyk averaged a career-low 3.2 points and 1.8 rebounds while averaging 8.6 minutes per game last season.

“He understands basketball, can space the floor with his three-point shooting and can pass the ball,” Roma coach Alessandro Magro said. “I’m confident he can fit into our systems quickly and help us right from the start.”

After being selected by the Dallas Mavericks with the 13th overall pick of the 2013 NBA Draft, Olynyk was traded to the Boston Celtics on Draft night. He played four seasons with the Celtics, mostly as a reserve, and helped the team advance to the Eastern Conference Finals.

Olynyk spent four more seasons with the Miami Heat, reaching the NBA Finals in 2020 when Erik Spoelstra’s Heat lost in six games to LeBron James and the Los Angeles Lakers.

The former Zag also had stints with the Houston Rockets (2020-21), Detroit Pistons (2021-22), Utah Jazz (2022-24), Toronto Raptors (2023-25) and New Orleans Pelicans (2024-25) before signing with the Spurs ahead of the 2025-26 season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Davis Fogle caps highlight day with 'pretty incredible' 30-point eruption at Kraziness in the Kennel
Gonzaga.summary:
Braden Huff’s Kraziness in the Kennel scoring record wasn’t on Davis Fogle’s radar when Saturday’s intrasquad scrimmage started at McCarthey Athletic Center, nor did it look like something that would be in jeopardy when Fogle missed his first two shots from the field, leaving the sophomore scoreless through five minutes.

Then Fogle drained a 3-pointer, found his offensive rhythm and continued to pump in shots from virtually every area of the floor, blowing past Huff’s scoring record with 30 points during a 56-45 victory for the White squad.

Fogle showed glimpses of his improved outside shooting, finishing 11 of 15 from the field, 6 of 7 from the 3-point line and 2 of 2 from the free-throw line. Huff previously owned the two highest-scoring scrimmage totals, with 19 points in 2023 and 17 in 2025, but Fogle officially took the record from his teammate with a 3-pointer at the 6-minute, 37-second mark and continued to attack, scoring nine points over the final five minutes.

“Luckily he was on my team, I was a little upset (about the record),” Huff said, seated two chairs down from Fogle during a post-scrimmage press conference. “He could’ve scored at least 20, 21, barely broken it, but just had to score 30. All jokes aside, that was pretty incredible. It was a good performance and we’re excited to see that against someone other than our own guys.”

Fogle, who carved out a role in Mark Few’s rotation during the final two months of his freshman season, scored all 30 of his points during a span of 14 minutes, 12 seconds, and squeezed 11 points into one two minute-stretch.

“I had no idea what the record was, just going out there hooping,” Fogle said. “I was open, they got me open, just made the shots.”

Added Huff: “I wouldn’t have passed you the ball if I would’ve known.”

Fogle, who had an ice pack taped to his left leg when he arrived to the postgame presser, delivered many of the highlights during Saturday’s preseason showcase, and not necessarily just during the 20-minute scrimmage portion.

Earlier on, he picked up a dunk contest crown after leaping over 7-foot-1 Massamba Diop, who stood at the egde of the foul circle as Fogle dribbled into the lane and took off, barely clearing the Arizona State transfer before stuffing the ball into the basket with one hand.

“It was honestly a couple weeks ago in the gym, (SID) Barrett (Henderson) talked to me about doing the dunk contest, I was like this is what I’m going to do,” Fogle said. “Tried it once, pretty easy. (Diop) was cool with it, he trusted me.”

There were other reassuring signs on Saturday for a Gonzaga team facing a litany of eligibility questions less than a month out from the season opener against Purdue.

Harwell, one of the 11 players guaranteed to be on the team’s roster for that game, scored 17 points on 6-of-8 shooting and 4 of 5 from the field in his Kraziness debut.

“It’s been amazing, especially coaches and players, I feel like we’ve all been pushing each other,” said Harwell, a Houston transfer who considered signing with Gonzaga out of high school. “Beginning of the summer, we only had about eight players so just being able to go against each other and have full reps every day and getting back to being myself again.”

Huff, who hadn’t played in front of a full crowd at the Kennel in 268 days since dislocating his kneecap, was the scrimmage’s third double-digit scorer, totaling 11 points on 4-of-11 shooting.

The quartet of Fogle, Huff, Harwell and Diop should give the Zags a solid foundation, even if one or multiple eligibility decisions don’t go their way in the upcoming weeks or months. The outlook for a projected preseason top 10-20 team would obviously be even better if fifth-year transfers Xaivian Lee, Chauncey Wiggins and Javon Bennett, and Spanish forward Izan Almansa are cleared to suit up.

Three of those four participated in Saturday’s scrimmage, with Bennett sitting out due to a minor shoulder injury the point guard suffered earlier this week. Lee started at point guard for the White squad, scoring nine points to go with four assists, while Wiggins had eight points on two made 3’s and Almansa added seven points and seven rebounds for the Blue team.

Lee is currently eligible through a temporary restraining order in California, but Wiggins and Bennett are ineligible after the NCAA was granted a stay motion in their respective state lawsuits. Almansa, meanwhile, is still waiting on the NCAA to approve his eligibility waiver.

“The best expectation would be the NCAA just lets these guys play,” Few said. “It’s really unfortunate they’re taking this stance. Classes before all these guys have gotten five, six, seven years. Now with our new rule, the classes after them. So I’m not sure why we’re sticking to targeting this one specific group.

“But now we’ve started school everywhere and rosters are set, it’s a really, really small number that are out there in these things. Our three guys are wonderful guys, they’re good students working on their Master’s. These are the type of guys we should have in college basketball.”

French point guard Nathan De Sousa, who was recently cleared to play by the NCAA, was solid for the Navy team, tallying seven points and five assists.

Collectively, the Navy and White teams combined to finish 18 of 32 (56%) from the 3-point line during Saturday’s 20-minute scrimmage – another encouraging sign for a team that shot 33.3% last season, never making more than 14 3’s in a single game.

Gonzaga.title: Multiple Zags show promise from behind 3-point arc at Kraziness
Gonzaga.summary:
For the first time in at least a decade, Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel didn’t include a 3-point competition, so the Navy and White teams used an entertaining 20-minute scrimmage to show off their perimeter shooting.

The Zags, coming off the worst 3-point shooting season (33.3%) in program history, had no issues from distance Saturday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

White, which pulled away to win 56-45, canned 11 of 17 behind the arc, paced by sophomore wing Davis Fogle’s 6 of 7. Navy wasn’t far behind, hitting 7 of 15, led by Houston transfer Isiah Harwell’s 4 of 5 on 3s.

The annual Kraziness event served as the public’s first glimpse at the 2026-27 Zags and fans got to see 3-point accuracy that often was missing on last year’s squad.

Making snap judgements from a preseason scrimmage isn’t advisable, but it was a promising sign when five different Zags – Harwell, Fogle, Florida transfer guard Xaivian Lee, Braden Huff and Florida State transfer forward Chauncey Wiggins – connected on 3-pointers in the scrimmage’s first 6 minutes and 8 seconds.

Lee finished 3 of 6 on 3s and the 6-foot-11 Wiggins made 2 of 5.

Gonzaga head coach Mark Few witnessed improved 3-point shooting throughout summer and fall drills from a revamped roster with just two returning players, Fogle and Huff.

“We’ve shot it good,” Few said. “Actually (Dayton transfer guard) Javon (Bennett, who sat out with a shoulder injury) shoots it really good, so we missed that today. But ‘X’ (Lee) has shot it good. It was nice to see Isiah step up and make some and obviously Davis has shot it really well.”

There’s a reason for that. Fogle estimated he put 500-600 shots daily in the offseason, streamlining his form with assistant coach Stephen Gentry.

“Last year I had a pretty good season, but I knew (perimeter shooting) was going to be a big step in my game, not only for college but just for the next level,” Fogle said. “Me and coach Gentry really started from zero right when season ended. We were just (taking) form shots, mid-range shots, really trying to keep (the ball) on my right side and eliminate all the moving parts.

“That, along with me coming back in the gym at night and just repping it out every day, it just became more and more comfortable.”

Fogle actually was one of the team’s better shooters last season at 35% on 3-pointers as a freshman but understood there was room for growth.

“Literally when the season was over, we started a 21-day program totally rebuilding his shot, down to how he catches the ball,” Gentry said. “The big emphasis was it’s tight to his body, it’s right and he’s really driving the ball. He’ll hear me say all the time: ‘Tight, right and drive.’

“To his credit, he totally bought in, totally coachable. He’s got a little shooting routine he goes through every single day as his warmup. He probably knows it better than me at this point.”

The 6-6 Harwell was a five-star recruit on Gonzaga’s radar before he spent his freshman year at Houston. The Cougars didn’t get the best version of Harwell, who lost valuable development time recovering from a torn ACL as a high school senior.

“At the beginning, I was with Gentry and ‘B-Mike’ (assistant Brian Michaelson) and we had just been shooting,” said Harwell, who made 27.1% on 3s while averaging just under 14 minutes per game at Houston. “Being able to have an actual offseason where I’m not in the training room as much and just being on the court and getting everything going again was nice.”

Huff, a 33.3% 3-point shooter last season, made 2 of 3 treys. The 6-10 senior, highly productive and wildly efficient inside the arc the last three seasons, was just 2 of 8 on 2-pointers.

“I took a lot of time working on (3-point shooting),” Huff said. “I just want to first off get more up this year but also make more at a higher clip. It felt good today. I’ve got to get back to making some hooks and floaters. I missed more than I usually do.”

The season opener against Purdue is roughly a month away, but Gentry, like Few, has seen encouraging signs from Gonzaga’s primary shooting threats.

“Xaivian is a way better 3-point shooter than last year’s stats,” Gentry said. “He’s got a good stroke. Javon can really shoot it. There’s nothing we’re doing with his shot. It’s ready to go. (French guard Nathan) De Sousa can shoot it, get a little more arc on his shot. Chauncey obviously can shoot it and get it off, crazy quick. (Izan) Almansa can make open 3s.

“The unique thing is, too, these guys can make 3s off the bounce, which is really important in attacking switching and respecting guys in ball screens. We’ve had some awesome days in practice and today was maybe a little bit higher than usual, but nothing crazy.”

Gonzaga.summary:
From staff reports

The schedule is set for the new-look Pac-12 women’s basketball season.

The Gonzaga and Washington State teams learned the dates of their conference matchups Friday, the Pac-12 announced. The conference is using the same Wednesday/Saturday and Thursday-Sunday schedule as the men’s games, which were announced Wednesday.

There are 16 games for the eight-team conference with each team playing each other home and away.

Gonzaga opens at home against Oregon State on Jan. 6, while Washington State hosts Texas State on Jan. 9. Times and TV information are to be announced.

Conference play concludes on March 6 with Gonzaga hosting WSU at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga holds a 14-7 series lead over WSU and won all four meetings while they played in the West Coast Conference the last two years.

Gonzaga.title: Braden Huff's return and four other things to watch at Gonzaga's Kraziness in the Kennel
Gonzaga.summary:
The exact makeup of Gonzaga’s 2026-27 roster remains unclear one month out from the season opener, but the group of players Mark Few and his staff assembled will take the floor for the first time on Saturday at Kraziness in the Kennel.

The annual preseason showcase, sold out as of Thursday afternoon, will start at 2 p.m. at McCarthey Athletic Center with player introductions followed by hype videos, a 3-point shooting contest, skills contest, intrasquad scrimmage and player/coach speeches. ESPN’s Sean Farnham is emceeing for the third straight year and SWX will carry the live broadcast.

While it’s often difficult to learn much from an abbreviated scrimmage between teammates in the early stages of October, this year’s Kraziness could be more compelling than years past. We break down five of the reasons below.

B-Huff is back

Braden Huff may end up owning a few more Gonzaga scoring and efficiency records by the time his college career ends but he already holds one, posting the top two scoring totals in Kraziness history, with 19 points in 2023 as a true freshman and 17 last season.

Huff’s scoring total won’t necessarily be what fans are focused on when the 6-foot-10 forward takes the floor for the first time since dislocating his kneecap in mid-January, forcing him to miss Gonzaga’s final 17 games in 2025-26.

The real story will be Huff’s strength, mobility and conditioning nine months removed from the injury that prematurely ended his junior season. The crafty forward who led the country in 2-point field goals before his injury has been back on the floor for at least the last two months without any limitations, but the Zags are still slow-playing his return and it’s unclear how many of the 20 minutes he’ll play during Saturday’s scrimmage.

Either way, his return to the floor, and to Gonzaga’s roster, is why many think the Zags will have a chance to play deep into the 2027 NCAA Tournament.

“We’ve been very, very, very conservative with him, especially this summer,” Few told The Spokesman-Review during Naismith Hall of Fame festivities in August. “There’s no need for him to do that. He’s in great shape and looks good.”

Who’s actually available?

This is a question we might be revisiting before both of Gonzaga’s exhibitions, prior to the Nov. 2 opener against Purdue and throughout the early stages of the regular season.

Similar to a handful of schools around the country, Gonzaga continues to wait on eligibility lawsuits and international waiver decisions that will determine whether starters and key rotation players can actually compete this season.

Fifth-year transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida), Javon Bennett (Dayton) and Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State) are currently involved in lawsuits that will determine whether they can suit up, with no real clarity on when verdicts will arrive.

Lee is currently eligible under a temporary restraining order, but still needs a favorable decision from the Superior Court of Santa Clara County on Oct. 20. Bennett and Wiggins earned preliminary injunctions in Ohio and Georgia, but are now ineligible after courts in both states granted an emergency stay motion, revoking the pair’s eligibility until their individual cases are heard.

Spanish forward Izan Almansa is the fourth player in limbo as the Real Madrid product waits on the NCAA to process his international eligibility waiver. Slowly but surely, the sport’s governing body is getting to waivers filed by basketball players and recently approved Gonzaga point guard Nathan De Sousa, a native of France, but Almansa’s wait continues into the first week of October.

All four players are on campus, listed on the web roster Gonzaga published earlier this week and depicted in player posters at the Volkar Center, but Lee, Bennett, Wiggins and Almansa haven’t been formally announced by the school at this point, nor have they been featured in social media photos shared by the basketball program.

Will the quartet of players participate in Kraziness? Outside of Huff’s return, it’s probably the most intriguing storyline leading into this year’s event. For reference, Tyon Grant-Foster obtained a practice waiver that enabled him to take part in Kraziness last year while the NCAA reviewed his eligibility case. When Grant-Foster’s eligibility waiver was denied the following week, his practice waiver became inactive.

Diop’s debut

Between unexpected point guard issues, 5-in-5 court cases and looming uncertainty around international transfers, it’s easy to forget Gonzaga’s offseason started with a bang in the transfer portal.

The Zags won a high-stakes bidding war with Rick Pitino and St. John’s for 7-foot Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop, widely considered to be the top center available during the most recent portal cycle.

Diop is technically listed at 7-1 and 245 pounds on GU’s new roster and Zag fans will have a chance to see the towering sophomore in person for the first time – or at least for the first time since last November, when he had 11 points, four rebounds and two blocks in a 77-65 loss to his new teammates in Tempe, Arizona.

“We haven’t had somebody like him,” Few said. “So big, so athletic, lob-catcher, rim-protector. Maybe (Ronny) Turiaf or somebody would be the closest one we’ve had over the years, I’d have to think about that. Great personality, plays with joy but also kind of work in progress.”

The Zags are hopeful Diop can impact the game on both ends of the floor, but defensive rim protection could be his most valuable asset to this team, considering the offensive firepower they’ll have elsewhere, particularly with Huff and sophomore wing Davis Fogle.

First day of school (and Kraziness)

The impact of Gonzaga’s freshman class could largely hinge on the eligibility of the four players we mentioned earlier, but all three of Luca Foster, Sam Funches and Juwan Ekanga should get significant run Saturday afternoon in a scrimmage setting.

While this may not be considered one of Gonzaga’s best freshman classes, it definitely is not among the worst either. Foster, Funches and Ekanga make up a well-rounded group consisting of two top-50 high school prospects that selected Few’s program over a handful of power conference suitors and an intriguing international prospect who’s already played games in France’s top professional league.

It’s also a good time to remind fans Fogle wasn’t projected to play a high-usage role for the Zags in the lead-up to Kraziness last year, let alone crack the team’s rotation at any point. Injuries and inconsistent play from others at his position eventually made Fogle the team’s sixth man and the freshman wing went on to average double figures the final two months of the season.

If all three 5-in-5 transfers and Almansa are eligible to compete this year, it’s unlikely Gonzaga would have to lean heavily on its freshman class, but last season reaffirmed how quickly things can change.

In any event, Saturday’s scrimmage gives Foster, Funches and Ekanga the chance to show how they’ve developed since arriving on campus and perhaps which of the three would be best-equipped to step into Gonzaga’s rotation if the situation calls for it.

Roebuck returns

The Zags have a solid hit rate when it comes to signing recruits who visit campus during Kraziness weekend.

They picked up a commitment from Funches within a week of last year’s event, signed four-star guard Dusty Stromer months after his visit in 2022 and, most notably, went 4-for-4 with Jalen Suggs, Chet Holmgren, Julian Strawther and Dominick Harris after the group of four- and five-star prospects traveled to Spokane in 2019.

Another important recruiting weekend is in store for the Zags, with four-star guard Gene Roebuck returning to the Kennel for his official visit. Roebuck traveled from La Mirada, California, last year for an unofficial visit that coincided with GU’s opener, but the 45th-ranked player in the class of 2027 is returning to Spokane after taking official visits to California and Washington earlier this fall.

A 6-foot-4, 180-pound combo guard, Roebuck is a consensus four-star prospect according to major recruiting services, the No. 9-ranked guard in the class and No. 4-ranked player in California.

The Zags currently have one player, five-star guard Dooney Johnson, committed in the 2027 class. Five-star guard Jalen Davis, a Bremerton High School standout, is also scheduled to take an official visit to the Kennel on Nov. 7 for GU’s nonconference game against New Mexico State.

Gonzaga.title: Denver Nuggets sign former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard to two-way contract
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga point guard Ryan Nembhard is on the move for the third time this offseason.

Nembhard, who was traded from the Dallas Mavericks to the Atlanta Hawks on July 19 before being shipped to the Charlotte Hornets last week, has seemingly found a permanent landing spot for the 2026-27 season after signing a two-way contract with the Denver Nuggets.

The second-year pro will team up with former Gonzaga wing Julian Strawther in Denver and split time between the NBA’s Nuggets and G League Grand Rapids Gold in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Denver waived guard KJ Simpson to open up a two-way spot for Nembhard.

It becomes the fourth team for Nembhard since a two-game stint with the Mavericks this July at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas. Days after his second Summer League game, Nembhard was involved in a three-team trade that sent the former Zag to Atlanta in exchange for Zaccharie Risacher. The Hawks also acquired Oklahoma City guard Lu Dort as part of the deal.

Nembhard’s time with Atlanta lasted just two months before the Hawks traded the point guard, Buddy Hield and cash considerations to Charlotte for forward Dorian Finney-Smith. Within days of that move, reports indicated that Charlotte intended to waive Nembhard before training camp, making him an unrestricted free agent.

The Mavericks signed Nembhard to an undrafted two-way deal last summer and leaned on the point guard throughout the regular season. Nembhard’s two-way contract was converted to a standard deal late in the season and the rookie made 60 appearances for Dallas, including 27 starts.

Nembhard, who broke Gonzaga’s single-season assists record in each of his two seasons with the program, averaged 6.6 points, 5.3 assists and 2.2 rebounds for the Mavericks while shooting 41.5% from the field, 35.6% from the 3-point line and 80.6% from the free throw line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga unveils full 2026-27 schedule, will open Pac-12 season with rivalry matchup at WSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s inaugural Pac-12 season is right around the corner and might feel even closer now that the Bulldogs have a full regular-season schedule to parse through.

The Pac-12 Conference revealed its men’s basketball schedule on Wednesday, allowing Gonzaga to formally announce its complete 31-game regular-season slate featuring at least 15 nonconference games and 16 more as part of the Pac-12’s double round-robin format.

There weren’t any new developments with Gonzaga’s nonleague slate, which has been pieced together over the last handful of months and includes at least 10 games against high-major opponents. The Zags could potentially play an 11th power-conference foe, and 16th nonconference game, if they qualify for the championship game at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

Gonzaga will have to get through a new batch of opponents to win its first Pac-12 championship, but Mark Few’s team will open conference play against a familiar foe when it travels to Pullman on Jan. 6 for the 155th all-time meeting with Washington State.

The conference home opener is scheduled for Jan. 9 against Colorado State, followed by a Jan. 13 road test at Fresno State.

Gonzaga returns home on Jan. 16 for one of its most-anticipated matchups in the new Pac-12, pitting Few against Boise State and longtime Zags assistant Leon Rice. The game also doubles as a reunion for the Few family with AJ Few, the oldest son of Gonzaga’s Hall of Fame coach, entering his second season on Boise State’s staff as a director of player personnel.

After the Boise State matchup, Gonzaga will be back on the road for a two-game swing against Utah State (Jan. 21) and Oregon State (Jan. 24). The Aggies are targeting a fifth straight NCAA Tournament appearance under their fourth different coach and announced a sellout for the Gonzaga game two weeks before the schedule was released.

Three days later, the Zags will face another first-year coach, Oregon State’s Justin Joyner, in Corvallis, Oregon. Joyner was an assistant coach for Michigan’s national title-winning team last season and had the scouting report when the Wolverines thumped Gonzaga 101-61 in the Players Era championship.

Gonzaga won’t leave the state of Washington for its next three games, hosting Fresno State on Jan. 27 before traveling to Seattle on Jan. 30 for a nonleague matchup with Oregon at Climate Pledge Arena. The Zags return home on Feb. 4 for their first-ever meeting with Texas State, which left the Sun Belt Conference to join the revamped Pac-12.

Two more intriguing road games follow for Gonzaga, which travels to play San Diego State at Viejas Arena before a return game with Boise State on Feb. 10 at ExtraMile Arena.

The Zags travel back to Spokane for a single game against Washington State on Feb. 17 before leaving for another nonconference game on Feb. 20 against Duke at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

Gonzaga will stay on the road to play Texas State in San Marcos on Feb. 25 before returning to the Inland Northwest for a two-game home swing against San Diego State (Feb. 27) and Oregon State (March 3). The team’s Pac-12 regular-season finale will take place on March 6 at Colorado State.

The Pac-12 Tournament opens just three days later at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, but Gonzaga could avoid playing on March 9, 10 or 11 if the Zags are able to secure a No. 1 or 2 seed and earn a bye to the Pac-12 semifinals on March 12. The conference championship game will take place on March 13 and air on CBS/Paramount+.

Tipoff times and television broadcast details for the majority of Gonzaga’s nonconference games, and all 16 conference games, will be announced in the coming weeks.

Under the new Pac-12 schedule, all nine teams are playing 16 games, with home and road matchups against each of the other eight schools. No team is playing three consecutive road games or four of five games on the road and every team is opening and closing its conference schedule with one home and road game across its first and final two contests.

Zags add exhibition

Gonzaga’s preseason exhibition schedule will start on Oct. 24 against Arkansas and resume four days later with a home matchup against NAIA opponent Lewis-Clark State.

A tipoff time and television details for the Oct. 28 exhibition have yet to be announced.

The Lewiston-based school has been a common exhibition opponent for Gonzaga, with the Zags and Warriors meeting as recently as 2023-24, when Graham Ike scored 24 points and Braden Huff added 21 to help Few’s team pull away for a 96-58 win.

Ferris High School product Dylan Skaife returns to LCSC’s roster after starting in all 32 games for the Warriors as a sophomore.

Gonzaga.title: Wait continues for Gonzaga's Xaivian Lee, Ines Bettencourt after California injunction hearing
Gonzaga.summary:
A preliminary injunction hearing held Tuesday afternoon in Santa Clara County came with some good news, some bad news and, in many ways, no news at all for a pair of Gonzaga players seeking a fifth year of college eligibility.

The Glancey v. NCAA lawsuit including Xaivian Lee, a Florida transfer looking to extend his career with Mark Few and the Gonzaga men, and Ines Bettencourt, a returning starter hoping to return for one final season with Lisa Fortier and the Zag women, continued Tuesday afternoon in Northern California, where a Santa Clara County judge heard statements from player plaintiffs and coaches, along with arguments from attorneys representing the NCAA.

Lee, Bettencourt and more than 70 other player plaintiffs involved in the case are seeking a preliminary injunction that would grant them a fifth year of eligibility, extending their clocks months after the NCAA passed its new 5-in-5 eligibility model.

No ruling was made Tuesday and another hearing was scheduled for Oct. 20, according to Ryan Downton, one of the attorneys representing the player plaintiffs.

“There was not enough time for all of the players and coaches to testify today, so the hearing will resume on October 20,” Downton wrote in an email to The Spokesman-Review. “The TRO (temporary restraining order) remains in place pending the next hearing.”

Tuesday’s no-decision could be interpreted as either a negative or positive development.

Although players now have to wait at least three weeks for clarity, the TRO issued by the Superior Court of Santa Clara on Aug. 7 gives them eligibility until a judge makes a final ruling. Specifically, it allows Lee and Bettencourt to practice with their respective teams and participate in the upcoming Kraziness in the Kennel and Numerica Fan Fest events scheduled the next two weekends.

The second injunction hearing will take place four days before the Gonzaga men travel to Fayetteville, Arkansas, for a preseason exhibition against Arkansas and seven days before the Zag women host Westmont College for their only preseason exhibition on Oct. 27.

A preliminary injunction would signify an important step for Lee and Bettencourt, but the NCAA is expected to counter with an appeal and push for a stay motion, which would reverse both players’ eligibility until the case is heard by a Court of Appeals.

Two other incoming Gonzaga men’s basketball transfers seeking a fifth year of eligibility, Javon Bennett (Dayton) and Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State), initially secured eligibility through similar injunctions in Ohio and Georgia, but judges in both cases granted the NCAA’s request for a stay, making both players ineligible for the time being.

Downton is representing player plaintiffs in a handful of other 5-in-5 cases across the country, including the Ohio lawsuit involving Bennett and Georgia lawsuit involving Wiggins. It’s possible final verdicts on one or multiple cases won’t arrive before Gonzaga opens the season on Nov. 2 against Purdue in Las Vegas.

A handful of fifth-year hopefuls including BYU’s Jaxon Kohler, a Michigan State transfer, testified in person Tuesday afternoon. St. John’s coach Rick Pitino also attended the injunction hearing in Santa Clara to testify. Reed Bailey, a fifth-year forward who transferred from Indiana to St. John’s this offseason, is one of the player plaintiffs named in the lawsuit.

“The NCAA should give up on all of these lawsuits and let everyone in the Class of 2022 play this year,” Pitino said during the hearing, according to a post on X from Downton’s firm, the Texas Trial Group.

Other notable players named in the California suit include former UCLA guards Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark, both of whom transferred to play for LSU and first-year coach Will Wade. If granted an injunction, all three of Lee, Dent and Clark could be on the floor when the Tigers travel to Spokane for a Nov. 14 matchup with Gonzaga at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Former Saint Mary’s, UConn and UC Santa Barbara guard Aidan Mahaney is also part of the lawsuit, as is fifth-year point guard Moe Odum, who faced the Zags at each of his three college stops: Pacific, Pepperdine and Arizona State.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga announces jersey patch sponsorship with AI network Altana
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga will be debuting not one but two new patches on its men’s basketball jerseys in 2026-27.

Along with the Pac-12 Conference logo, Gonzaga players will wear a patch to represent the school’s newly announced partnership with Altana, an artificial intelligence network for supply chain management and trade commerce.

Gonzaga and other college programs around the country are taking advantage of jersey sponsorships as new revenue streams after receiving approval from the NCAA in January. As of Aug. 1, Division I teams can use up to two patches of no more than 4 square inches for regular-season games.

“Altana is an exceptional organization that represents innovation and forward thinking, and we are excited to welcome them as a partner of Gonzaga Athletics and Gonzaga Basketball,” Gonzaga Athletic Director Chris Standiford said in a school news release. “As we enter a new era for Gonzaga Athletics and begin competition in the Pac-12, we are grateful for Altana’s support and belief in our student-athletes and our program. We look forward to building a strong partnership together.”

Altana, founded in 2018 by Evan Smith, Peter Swartz and Raphael Tehranian and based in New York City, claims to be the world’s first AI network for global trade. The company uses AI to suggest efficient trade routes when considering factors like tariffs and regulations on forced labor, for example, according to its website.

The fast-growing company contracts with retailers shipping product across the globe. It uses AI models fed with public and private data to track each step a product takes in the global supply chain, sometimes down to its raw materials.

The company has notable partnerships with government agencies such as the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, as well as retailers.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection has contracted with Altana since 2023, using their global supply chain map, or “Atlas,” to help prevent products made with forced labor from entering the United States, according to a news release from Altana at the time of their contract.

“We’re excited to have Altana represented on our jerseys this season,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said in the Gonzaga news release. “They’re an incredibly innovative and successful company, and we appreciate their support of Gonzaga Basketball and our student-athletes. It’s an exciting time for our program, and we’re looking forward to representing Altana on the court.”

Gonzaga becomes the second local Division I school to reach a jersey patch sponsorship in recent months. In June, Washington State announced a five-year, $8.43 million agreement with Colville Tribes to wear the company’s patch on all of its athletic uniforms.

Gonzaga.title: Experienced Gonzaga women return Ines Bettencourt after court ruling: 'It's a new energy'
Gonzaga.summary:
Expectations are going to be high for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team in 2026-27.

A late addition to the roster now may blow those expectations through the roof of McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags were set to essentially return their entire team from 2025-26 with the exception of guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring.

The NCAA’s new five-years-to-play-five-seasons eligibility model announced this summer opened the door for the Portugal native to fight for an additional year of eligibility. She joined a California class action lawsuit, gaining a temporary restraining order and immediate eligibility.

Bettencourt returned to Spokane on Sept. 5.

Now the band is back together for Gonzaga, which will have one of the deepest rosters in the nation with 10 returners, including five starters to go with two transfers and one freshman.

Bettencourt and GU coach Lisa Fortier were cautious in calling it a done deal when the Zags took the court for their first preseason practice last week. A preliminary hearing on Tuesday in Santa Clara County appeared to push a final decision to October 20, at the earliest. 

The Zags are proceeding as if they’ll have Bettencourt.

“It’s been a long summer ever since I graduated,” said Bettencourt, who went back to Portugal and practiced frequently with her national team. “I kind of knew that this would be a possibility. So I was just working behind the scenes and talking with Lisa (Fortier), not really telling anyone else because it wasn’t for sure.”

As soon as the NCAA adopted the new eligibility format, Bettencourt began talking to Fortier and Gonzaga compliance officials “to figure out what exactly I have to do to come back because as an international it’s harder to come back than an American.”

There Bettencourt was going through drills and running up and down the court with her teammates like she had never left.

“Like McKynnlie (Dalan, senior forward) said, ‘we set you off, (had) all these goodbyes and now you’re back.’ ”

Fortier said Gonzaga will proceed as if Bettencourt will be eligible the whole season.

“She had asked us pretty early on in April or May (about coming back) and she was kind of joking at first,” Fortier said. “No one actually thought that any of this was gonna happen. The answer was like sure (you can come back).”

Bettencourt is stoked to have another year with her coaches and what she calls her “best friends.”

“Just having one more shot at this, making the (NCAA) Tournament. Just being more prepared for whatever’s next for me,” Bettencourt said. “So it’s just awesome. Everyone was happy for me.”

Fortier is overjoyed to have Bettencourt back – something the Zags never thought would be an option four months ago.

“She’s one of ours so we would love to have her back,” Fortier said. “She shows up every day around the program and she takes care of business like a professional. She’s a pro in all ways.”

The familiarity will be a team strength no doubt.

“We know each other,” Bettencourt said. “So it was just super nice for them to receive me well again.”

Bettencourt spent most of the summer playing 3-on-3 in Portugal. It was different preparation for returning to Gonzaga.

“I have to run more now,” Bettencourt said, smiling.

Bettencourt took over a leadership role last year as the team’s lone senior. Now as a graduate, she wants to continue to lean into leadership.

“Just building on the leadership,” she said.

She expects to be a better player, too.

“Stay composed and stay consistent at everything,” she said about her personal expectations. “I’m just taking it day by day because I get to come back and be with my teammates, with my coaches, and practice with them again.”

Junior point guard Allie Turner started alongside Bettencourt in the backcourt last year. Turner, Bettencourt and sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker all lived together last year.

The trio can’t run that arrangement back as living assignments had already been passed out. But Turner is glad to have Bettencourt along for one more year.

“We’re super happy to have her back,” Turner said. “It’s a new energy.”

Whittaker agreed.

“For a long time we didn’t really think it was an option. And then kind of a quick turnaround within a couple of weeks we heard (she) was coming back,” Whittaker said. “She’s a player that I think is really seamless to bring back to the team. She has a lot of experience and was a great leader last year and obviously a great player. So it was kind of just an easy transition for her and everyone has been really supportive of it. It’s kind of like she’s never left.”

Bettencourt is looking forward to returning to McCarthey Athletic Center and seeing the fans for FanFest on Oct. 10.

“Super excited,” Bettencourt said. “I’m sure they (the fans) are going to be like ‘what? What are you doing here again?’ But I’m super excited to be back in front of all the fans with my team and showing them again what we can bring this year.”

Gonzaga.title: Who is 2027 Gonzaga commit Dooney Johnson?
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – It wouldn’t have been apparent that Dooney Johnson was dealing with any kind of physical stress last spring when the five-star Gonzaga commit carried Milwaukee Juneau to the school’s first state championship.

Not when he exploded for 40 points, accounting for 61% of his team’s overall scoring production during a third-round victory against Living Word Lutheran.

Not a week later when he popped Howard Grove High School for 36 points, 12 rebounds and five assists in the state quarterfinals.

Certainly not during a championship matchup against Cambridge, when Johnson rattled off 14 consecutive first-half points – and 23 in the game, with seven rebounds – to help Milwaukee Juneau rally back from a first-quarter deficit, win 62-54 and complete a 28-1 season.

There were no obvious signs of discomfort, just dominance from someone who averaged 27.8 points, 8.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 3.4 steals for a Milwaukee Juneau team that won 27 straight games to finish No. 8 in MaxPreps’ postseason national Top 25 rankings.

Only a few people in Johnson’s close circle knew about the underlying issue he was facing as he guided the Pioneers to a historic season.

“We never really put it out there, he won a state title on basically a fractured ankle,” said Johnson’s father Torre, also the head coach at Milwaukee Juneau last season. “Once the state tournament was over, we sat out for a whole month.”

It’s a window into the competitive drive and winning mindset Gonzaga’s first high school commit in the class of 2027 commit plans to bring to Spokane next fall, after one more prep season at East River High in Orlando, Florida – the school Johnson announced he’d be transferring to last month.

“I never really sit out during injuries, especially I can still go out there and somewhat play, especially to my full potential,” Dooney told The Spokesman-Review in July while competing for AAU Team Herro at a Nike EYBL (Elite Youth Basketball League) event in Las Vegas. “I always want to be out there for myself, not even just myself but for my team because I know I can push through it and continue to be there and compete at the highest level.”

• • • 

Thirteen years ago, Torre Johnson coached the Wisconsin-based Playground Elite AAU program to a 10-and-under national championship in Cocoa Beach, Florida.

It’s nearly impossible to identify Division I talent at a phase when players are still trying to grasp the game’s fundamentals, but one of Johnson’s fifth-graders was athletically advanced for his age and already a step or two ahead of his peers.

A basketball-obsessed toddler, Dooney took advantage of every opportunity to tag along to his father’s AAU games and practices. Although Dooney can’t remember his actual introduction to Jalen Suggs, the Gonzaga commit maintained a close relationship to the former Gonzaga guard and father Larry through basketball, and Jalen eventually became a key mentor to the now five-star prospect.

“Literally just a young fella running around the gym,” Suggs said, looking back at his first memories of Dooney. “Always at all the games, always had a rock in his hands and his dad was amazing. Always showed me the utmost love and really helped me on the mental side of everything as far as handling games, handling pressure, staying locked in and making sure I’m attacking every weekend we have.

“It’s gone right into Dooney. You see he applies that every game he plays. Super competitor. So for me, it’s just dope seeing him grow from that little kid to now he’s doing his thing and even coming into the Zags, it’s such a full journey. Very full circle.”

Now in his sixth season with the Orlando Magic, Suggs offered support to Johnson through the college recruiting process and not surprisingly, gave a strong endorsement for the Zags, who went to the national championship in 2021 after the guard’s iconic Final Four buzzer-beater against UCLA.

“They’re my guys,” Dooney said of Jalen and Larry Suggs. “But it was overall just the school and the coaches, how they treated me.”

Gonzaga’s playing style and culture were two of the main factors that prompted an early commitment from the Milwaukee native, who collected 11 other high-major offers before his junior high school season.

“It was a real nice time going there, everyone was nice, brotherhood, the campus was great,” Johnson said. “It was just an all-around brotherhood, it felt good. … Fast-paced system, really can just be who you are on the floor. Not too many sets, just be who you are and go get a bucket.”

Suggs and Johnson, the two highest-rated guard commits in Gonzaga history according to 247Sports.com, reconnected this summer. Suggs pulled double duty in Las Vegas, following Orlando’s NBA Summer League team at the Thomas & Mack Center while making time to watch Johnson and Team Herro at Nike EYBL a few miles away at the Vegas Convention Center.

Gonzaga assistants Brian Michaelson and Zach Norvell Jr. also traded days in Vegas, catching each of Johnson’s four games at the EYBL tournament.

“We were always pushing the Zags,” Suggs said. “It’s a beautiful place to be, you’re going to play great basketball, they’re going to really win and really treat you like family. That was just another piece. They really want you for the human you are and that’s really what we were trying to preach to him and understanding he can go anywhere and all these schools around the country, all the money, all the names and everything, notoriety, but there’s no place like Gonzaga, there’s no place like Spokane in the country in my opinion.

“I’m glad he kind of took that. B-Mike and Few did their job showing him the love. I can’t wait to see him in Spokane.”

• • • 

Johnson sat idle for a month after celebrating with teammates and lifting the state title on his fractured ankle at the University of Wisconsin’s Kohl Center. With highly-competitive Nike EYBL games approaching, Torre urged his son to take a few more weeks off, fearing the risk of re-injury.

Those efforts proved unsuccessful.

“When I asked him to sit out that first EYBL session until he gets his rhythm back, he looked me in my eyes and said, ‘What , Dad, you don’t think I’m going to be able to compete?’ ” Torre recalled. “So at the end of the day like I tell him, he’s the engine, I’m just the driver.”

Even in a slightly limited capacity, Johnson made his impact on the EYBL circuit, leading Team Herro – the AAU program sponsored by Milwaukee Bucks guard Tyler Herro – to an 18-4 record and semifinal run at the prestigious Peach Jam event based in Augusta, Georgia. The 6-foot-5 Johnson paced Team Herro at 14.9 ppg during the AAU circuit to go with 4.4 rpg, 3.0 apg and 1.1 spg.

Entering the AAU season, Johnson was mostly concentrated on making defensive strides, vowing to hold the opponent’s “star players or second star players” below their scoring averages and “continue to be a defensive anchor for my team.”

Chris Herro, Tyler’s father and the coach of Johnson’s 17U Team Herro squad, noticed growth there and in other areas.

“He’s really become a leader more,” Herro said. “He hit some big shots there for us and you’re getting a dog at the end of the day. He’s going to push them to the next level of competitiveness, which I don’t think Gonzaga’s had in a while. They haven’t had that in a while, that competitive edge. It’s good, I think he’s going to learn from coach Few.”

Johnson’s distribution and willingness to get teammates involved were other bright spots, particularly coming off a high school season where the guard often needed to score at a high clip for his team to have success.

The No. 27 prospect in the country, Johnson wasn’t the highest-rated player on his AAU squad, playing alongside Duke commit Kager Knueppel, the 17th-rated player in the country and younger brother of Charlotte Hornets guard Kon Knueppel. Team Herro’s roster also consisted of Iowa State commits Donovan Davis and Jack Konen, Nebraska commit Ty Schlagel and top-100 prospect Deuce McDuffie.

“He’s grown a lot in the realm of being able to play with other really good players, because that’s part of it,” Chris Herro said. “When you go out of high school, you’ve got to be able to play with other guys and that’s where he’s grown. He’s sharing the ball more, he understands that part of it, so yeah he’s doing well.”

The Zags are still a year away from deciding how they’ll deploy Johnson, who should be a candidate to get rotation minutes as a freshman, or potentially vie for a starting role for a program that could lose three point guards from the 2026-27 roster.

The consensus from AAU teammates and coaches is that Johnson is a hybrid point guard – someone who can create for himself and hunt shots as needed or fill more of a pass-first role when the situation calls for it.

“I’d say about 50/50,” said Davis, a four-star power forward who had recruiting conversations with Gonzaga before committing to Iowa State. “He’s really good at scoring. That’s the thing he’s really known for.”

Johnson’s big frame, skill level, athleticism and versatility will probably evoke one or two comparisons to the former Gonzaga guard he’s leaned on for advice and mentorship.

“So versatile, man,” Suggs said of Johnson. “Few’s going to love him in that sense because he can come out here and do everything. He can defend the best player, he’s coming out getting guys involved, he’s a force going downhill; the rim and his jumper and his skill are going to continue to evolve so I think he’s in a great space right now.”

• • • 

As a rising prospect who climbed to No. 21 in On3.com’s national rankings this summer, Johnson’s managing a busy schedule as he prepares for his final go-round with high school basketball.

Just consider his summer calendar. In addition to Nike EYBL stops in Atlanta, Memphis, Kansas City, Las Vegas and Augusta, Johnson traveled to the Pangos All-American Camp in Vegas, the NBPA Top 100 Camp in Rock Hill, South Carolina, the Chris Paul Elite Guard Camp in Vegas, the Nike Academy in Thousand Oaks, California, and the Nike NYvsNY game in New York City.

Shortly after his move to Florida, Johnson was invited to take part in the USA Basketball Junior National Minicamp from Oct. 9-11 in Colorado Springs, Colorado. A full high school schedule and All-American games in the spring are likely to follow.

Johnson has plenty on his plate and even more on his calendar before he can pack his things, move to the Inland Northwest and don a Gonzaga uniform for the first time, but judging by conversations with the guard and volume of Zag-centric posts on his Instagram account, that day also can’t arrive soon enough.

“Just got to be patient, but I’m always ready to go be at Gonzaga,” he said. “Great program, great coaches. Especially coach Few, he was really great when I went there. B-Mike, that’s my guy. So yeah it’s going to be good.”

Gonzaga.title: Women’s Basketball Announces 2026-27 Non-Conference Schedule
Gonzaga women release nonconference schedule, including games at Stanford, Arizona State and Michigan State
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga released its women’s basketball nonconference schedule Monday for the 2026-27 season, and it shapes up as possibly the most challenging out-of-conference slate the Zags have had under coach Lisa Fortier.

Fortier begins her 13th season with a nonconference schedule that features six teams that finished in the top 100 of the NET last season with four teams earning NCAA Tournament berths.

Gonzaga’s three most attractive nonconference dates are road games – at Stanford (Nov. 15), at Arizona State (Dec. 6) and a men’s/women’s multi-event doubleheader vs. Michigan State (Dec. 19), the Acrisure Challenge, in Palm Desert, California.

Eight of 15 nonconference games are at McCarthey Athletic Center. Gonzaga was going to have a 16th nonconference game – the maximum allowed with 16 conference games – but a third opponent in the North Shore Classic in Hawaii – Gonzaga’s holiday tournament this year – pulled out last minute.

Whether Gonzaga lands a one-off additional nonconference game remains to be seen.

Gonzaga starts the season Oct. 27 with an exhibition game against Westmont College from Santa Barbara, California.

The Zags’ first three games are at home against North Dakota State (Nov. 2), a return game from last year’s season opener, Idaho (Nov. 6) and UC Riverside (Nov. 8), a return game from a year ago.

Gonzaga follows with two road games at Grand Canyon (Nov. 13) and Stanford.

After taking a year off from its traditional nonconference series with Montana, the Grizzlies visit Gonzaga on Nov. 18. The Zags have won 12 straight in the series.

Then the Zags are off for Hawaii where they will take on the host Rainbows (Nov. 21) and California (Nov. 23).

Gonzaga then makes the short trip to Cheney to face Eastern Washington (Nov. 29), concluding the November portion of the schedule. The Zags have won 20 straight against EWU.

An Ivy League school visits when Yale (Dec. 4) comes to town.

Two days later Gonzaga visits Arizona State to complete a two-year deal.

Gonzaga has just one former West Coast Conference opponent on its schedule, but it’s a good one when Loyola Marymount, which won the regular-season championship last year. LMU visits Dec. 10.

Following the neutral-court game against Michigan State, Gonzaga concludes nonconference play with two home games – against South Dakota State (Dec. 30), which is always a test, and St. Thomas (Jan. 2) from the Summit League.

Gonzaga was 5-4 last year against teams it was scheduled to play the first two months of the season.

Fortier is four wins shy of becoming the all-time winningest women’s basketball coach at Gonzaga (313-84), eclipsing Kelly Graves (316-136), whom Fortier succeeded.

Times and television information for the nonconference games will be released at a later date.

Pac-12 Conference play begins in early January.

The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Looks To Sustain Momentum Against San Diego State
Oregon State.summary:
To start their first conference schedule in the relaunched Pac-12, the Oregon State Beavers picked up a blowout win over Colorado State this past weekend. Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree continued their impressive run of form and the tight ends also got heavily involved en route to the 56-26 result. Time to review that result and what else worked for JaMarcus Shephard to get his team to a 3-2 record on the year.

This Saturday, the Beavers host a 2-3 San Diego State squad, who are coming off of a dramatic 31-29 win over the Texas State Bobcats. What challenges does Sean Lewis' team present to the Beavers as the Aztecs deal with a mumps outbreak? In addition to our thoughts, you'll hear clips from Shephard's media availability, as well as offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen and defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre.

All that, plus a look at the five college football games that Matt Bagley thinks you should watch this weekend. 

Thank you for your support of the show, and as always, Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Returns to a Pac-12 Schedule
Oregon State.summary:
After a win over the UTEP Miners in El Paso, the Oregon State Beavers are 2-2 under the direction of JaMarcus Shephard. While many Power Conference programs around the nation likely wouldn't be satisfied with that type of start, it's important to keep perspective on the progress made in Shephard's first several months leading the team. 

As your host Matt Bagley looks at that, you'll also hear audio from JaMarcus Shephard's Monday press conference. Oregon State travels to Fort Collins this week for their Pac-12 opener against the Colorado State Rams. 

In between all the football talk, we also take some time to discuss the No. 21 Oregon State men's soccer team with our own John Severs, as they get into the home stretch of the 2026 season.

All that, and a look at the five games that you should watch during your college football weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Beaver Football Looks To Sustain Momentum After First Win of Shephard Era
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State football have their first win under JaMarcus Shephard's direction after defeating the Montana Grizzlies this past Saturday by a score of 52-17. 

After that contest, Shephard praised his team's efforts to get their first victory on the board and take heed of the message he has been trying to send since he arrived in Corvallis: that this is only the beginning. This week, you'll hear part of the audio from Shephard's Monday presser and his thoughts on this week's return trip to Texas to face the UTEP Miners in El Paso.

On this week's State of the Beavs, your host Matt Bagley also dives into what we, as a fanbase, learned about this Beaver team from the Montana game and what the next steps should be in order to sustain that momentum moving forward.

All that, plus Bagley's five games to watch in college football this weekend as conference play begins in most of the country. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football is 0-2, But The Culture is Changing
Oregon State.summary:
Two weeks into the new college football season, JaMarcus Shephard's Oregon State Beavers are 0-2. Hanging tough with two ranked power conference teams is certainly better than being blown out, it has become clear in the days since the Texas Tech loss that moral victories are not what the program is chasing. 

This week on State of the Beavs, your host Matt Bagley reacts to the signs of progress that the Beavers showed in their home opener loss to Texas Tech. Also hear comments from Shephard himself and linebacker Dylan Layne, both of whom noted they intend to change the larger perception of the program.

It's also time to prepare for the non-conference finale against Montana at Reser Stadium this week, and look ahead to the Pac-12 schedule that begins next weekend. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: WSU football’s loss to Boise State made offensive-line problem clear
Washington State.summary: There are lots of ways to dissect the reasons why WSU’s margin for victory has been so thin this season, but the main ones center around the team’s offensive line.
Washington State.author: Greg Woods

Washington State.title: WSU's Darrius Clemons, Jeremiah Bernard day-to-day with injuries as Cougars play starters heavy snaps
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State may have to go another week without two starters on each side of the ball.

That’s according to head coach Kirby Moore, who said Monday that wide receiver Darrius Clemons (ankle) and safety Jeremiah Bernard (shoulder) are considered day-to-day ahead of a road matchup with San Diego State this Saturday. Both missed the Cougars’ home loss to Boise State last weekend, but both are set to return to practice this week, Moore added.

Their absences are wearing on a WSU team still looking for its first FBS win of the season, falling to 1-7 overall and 0-4 in Pac-12 play after a 31-10 home loss to BSU. Without Clemons, who suffered an ankle injury against Oregon State on Oct. 17, the Cougars didn’t expand their receiver rotation to include West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees or walk-on Caleb Northcroft, as Moore indicated could take place ahead of the game.

Instead, they played their top three receivers all heavy snaps: Branden Ganashamoorthy and Daniel Blood each played all 76 snaps of offense, while Tank Hawkins played 65 snaps. Those are the only three wideouts who played for Washington State in that game.

This season, Ganashamoorthy has played 503 snaps, the most among Pac-12 wide receivers. Four Cougars have played at least 500 snaps, making them one of only two Pac-12 teams to play four players that many snaps.

“We talk about deliberate practice,” Moore said. “That really starts with bringing great energy, having verbal combat, doing your assignment, making sure you’re not thinking out there, that you’re just reacting. I think we’ve had too many errors from a practice standpoint, with guys knowing their assignments, whether it’s motions, details within the position. We’ve got lot of trust in the guys who are out there on the field. If other guys improve and they’re to the standard, they’ll be out there.”

Bernard suffered his shoulder injury during WSU’s loss at Oregon State earlier this month, Moore said, describing it as “a little bit of a stinger.” In his absence, WSU coaches trusted Arizona State transfer Jackquintin Bal with 56 snaps, his second most of the season and his most in four games. Against Boise State, Bal wasn’t targeted in the secondary, but he missed four tackles, most on the team.

That contributed to the Cougars’ inability to prevent big plays on defense, like BSU star running back Dylan Riley’s touchdown rushes of 33 yards and 72 yards, both of which came during the Broncos’ 21-0 fourth quarter that they used to seal the win. As a team, WSU missed 16 tackles, bringing its season total to 93 – second most in the Pac-12, behind only Colorado State, which ranks last in the country in total defense.

Changes to O-line?

Moore said the team is “going to explore” shuffling personnel on its offensive line, which permitted 16 pressures and two sacks on QB Owen Eshelman against Boise State. The Cougars’ front five often allowed the Broncos to get home using stunts. Other times, that group was pushed back at the line of scrimmage, a big reason why running backs Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi managed only 20 yards on 10 carries.

As currently constructed, WSU’s starting offensive line includes right tackle Jaylin Caldwell, right guard Nick Bakken, center Noah Dunham, left guard Jonny Lester and left tackle Ashton Tripp, the last of whom returned to action last weekend after missing the Oregon State game with an ankle injury he sustained against Utah State on Oct. 9. All are returners, including Tripp and Lester, who started last season. Caldwell started two games before suffering an injury.

The possibilities seem numerous for the Cougars, who won’t be able to reach the six wins required for bowl eligibility, which the program has earned in 9 of the last 10 full seasons. Theoretically, WSU could still reach a bowl game by finishing the regular season 5-7, which would open up the possibility of being selected for a bowl if there aren’t enough 6-6 teams.

But the Cougs wouldn’t just end their five-game losing streak and win out. They would also need to achieve at least a 930 multiyear Academic Progress Rate.

“We’re gonna explore that this week with, obviously, practice,” Moore said of making changes on the offensive line. “We wanna give guys opportunities. At the same time, right now in the season, we gotta understand where we’re at, the communication with who’s been on the right side, with who’s been on the left side. Naturally, we wanna give some reps to some other guys as well, and then we gotta make a call there by the time we get to Thursday.”

Washington State.title: Still looking for first FBS win of season, WSU hits the road to take on San Diego State | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against San Diego State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

Looking to end a five-game slide and secure its first FBS win of the season, WSU heads to the Golden State to take on San Diego State, which has lost two of its last three games. The Cougars are coming off a 31-10 loss to Boise State, which marked quarterback Owen Eshelman’s second start.

It’s the first Pac-12 matchup between the Cougars and Aztecs, who have met each of the last two seasons, both wins for WSU. The Cougs, whose bye week comes next week, are also playing their third road game in the last four weeks.

Where is it?

Snapdragon Stadium in San Diego, California.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 4 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

CBS Sports Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

WSU opened as a 2.5-point underdog.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 31-10 loss to Boise State, WSU played the first-place Broncos to a 10-10 tie through three quarters, but that’s when things went south for the hosts. Boise State followed with a 21-0 fourth quarter, turning a costly Eshelman interception into a touchdown, then adding two more on each of its next two drives.

In Eshelman’s second start, it was another slow offensive outing for the Cougars, who tied the game shortly before halftime on a long touchdown drive and again on a field goal from kicker Jack Stevens, who has now connected on eight in a row. But that’s all the scoring WSU did, punting on four of its first five drives of the game.

The Cougars weren’t at full strength on offense. Wide receiver Darrius Clemons missed the game after going down the previous week with an ankle injury, a tough blow to a WSU receiver corps that has been thin since star wideout Tony Freeman tore his ACL in Week 1. But the Cougs didn’t exactly expand their rotation at that spot, instead opting to play receivers Branden Ganashamoorthy and Tank Hawkins heavy snaps and leaving Jordan Dees and Caleb Northcroft – both of whom WSU coach Kirby Moore said would get increased snaps – on the bench entirely.

Plus, the Cougars didn’t get much of anything from their rushing game, which produced only 53 yards on 33 carries. Running backs Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi accounted for only 20 yards on 10 carries, while fellow back Maxwell Woods played only 11 snaps and did not get any carries. In seven games against FBS competition, WSU running backs are averaging 15 carries for 48 yards.

That helped spotlight the problems facing WSU’s offensive line, which allowed 16 pressures and two sacks on Eshelman, who took four total. On several occasions, the Cougs were beaten on stunts. On others, they weren’t able to generate any push on running plays, a key reason why their running backs haven’t gotten anything consistent going. A group of five returners – left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell – have shared a good dosage of the blame for a paltry offense.

“Offensively, we weren’t good enough, especially up front,” Moore said, “protecting the quarterback, running the football, and it led to 17 third downs. We want to limit the number of third downs. We gotta be more efficient on first and second down and create more explosive plays.”

On defense, the Cougs allowed several more big plays, including two long touchdown rushes from Boise State star running back Dylan Riley, who piled up 128 yards and two touchdowns, both in the fourth quarter. WSU, which whiffed on 16 tackles, has had some issues preventing explosive plays all season.

Perhaps just as important: Washington State couldn’t generate any real pass rush. The Cougars finished with only eight pressures on QB Maddux Madsen, according to Pro Football Focus, which gave him ample time in the pocket to complete passes. Madsen completed several key third-down conversions, including a 17-yard scramble in the third quarter, which later led to a touchdown.

Scouting San Diego State …

In head coach Sean Lewis’ third season, the Aztecs are 3-5 overall and 2-2 in Pac-12 play, coming off a 56-49 road loss to Colorado State. In that one, backup QB Stone Saunders made his starting debut and threw two touchdowns against two interceptions, totaling 369 yards through the air.

But the Aztecs’ defense couldn’t make it count, as has been the case all season. After eight games, SDSU ranks No. 135 of 138 FBS teams in total defense (462 yards per game), No. 133 in scoring defense (36 points per game), No. 109 in rush defense (178 ypg) and No. 134 in pass defense (284 ypg). That group is also allowing opponents to convert third downs at a 47% clip, which is No. 129 nationally.

It hasn’t been pretty for SDSU’s defense, which had to replace several key pieces on last year’s unit, including cornerback Chris Johnson, a first-round NFL draft pick in the spring, as well as edge rusher Trey White and three others who transferred to Power Four schools.

The Aztecs are dealing with an injury to quarterback Jayden Denegal, the team’s starter for the first seven games. The Aztecs opened the season with a home romp over FCS Portland State, only to drop three straight games, including road matchups with UCLA and Toledo and a home contest against James Madison. Since then, SDSU has dispatched Texas State at home, lost to Oregon State on the road, bounced back with a home win over Fresno State then fell in a road tilt with CSU.

In the Aztecs’ win over the Bulldogs, Saunders came on for the injured Denegal, leading fourth-quarter two scoring drives to secure the win. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 222 pounds, Saunders profiles as a pure pocket-passer, and he does it well. In his first start last weekend, Saunders completed 23 of 33 passes for 369 yards, two touchdowns and two picks. He isn’t much of a mobile threat, posting only four carries for minus-9 yards, an indication of the two total sacks he’s taken.

“They’re doing a nice job of playing complementary football,” Moore said. “They got in a shootout last week. They’re 3-1 at home. For us, it’s gonna be a challenge, third out of four games being on the road.”

What happened last time?

WSU and San Diego State’s last meeting came last fall in Pullman, where former Cougar quarterback Jaxon Potter led his team to a 36-13 win, scoring 22 unanswered points to pull away. Potter would go on to make one more start, in a loss to North Texas, before being benched for veteran Zevi Eckhaus for the rest of the season.
