Washington State and Washington have agreed to move next year’s rivalry game from Sept. 18 to Aug. 28, according to a Monday release, moving the longstanding series to August for the first time in its 118-year history.

The 2027 game, set for Gesa Field in Pullman, will be the fourth game of a five-year series extension the sides agreed to in 2023, not long after the traditional Pac-12’s collapse. The 2028 game, scheduled for Seattle, is the last one under contract.

The Huskies won this year’s game, a 24-10 decision in Seattle, and they own an all-time advantage of 78-34-6.

With this move, WSU now has a bye for its fourth week of action. Here is the Cougars’ 2027 schedule so far.

Aug. 28: vs. Washington

Sept. 4: vs. Idaho

Sept. 11: vs. Kansas

Sept. 18: Idle

Sept. 25: at Arizona

Washington State.title: As chaos reigns and CFP rankings loom, Boise State and Oregon State remain on track | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

The Pac-12 dodged the mayhem that walloped conferences across the country the past two weekends.

As undefeated teams tumbled and title favorites flopped, Boise State and Oregon State held their positions as the frontrunners for the Pac-12 championship and a potential berth in the College Football Playoff.

One Saturday remains before the first CFP rankings are released Nov. 3. If the Broncos handle Texas State at home and the Beavers win at Fresno State – it’s their toughest assignment since conference play began – at least one, if not both, will receive consideration for a spot in the selection committee’s top 25.

For the moment, UT-San Antonio, from the American, is the highest-ranked team in ESPN’s strength-of-record (SOR), an important data point that mirrors the private version used by the selection committee.

SOR measures how a given team performs against its schedule compared to how an average Top 25 team would fare against the same schedule. It offers the committee a means of comparing teams with similar records but no head-to-head results.

UTSA is ranked 23rd in the SOR metric, one spot ahead of Boise State. The Roadrunners have one loss: by 24 points at Texas, while the Broncos’ lone defeat was by seven points at Oregon. The teams’ strength-of-schedule rankings are comparable.

(Notably, UTSA’s toughest remaining game, against North Texas, is the same day, Nov. 14, as the Boise State-Oregon State showdown.)

Only No. 34 New Mexico, the Mountain West frontrunner, and No. 39 James Madison, from the Sun Belt, are close to UTSA and Boise State in the SOR rankings.

Then comes No. 45 Louisiana Tech (Sun Belt), No. 47 North Texas (American) and No. 49 Liberty (Conference USA).

The Beavers are 50th, which reflects their weak collection of victories. Of course, that will change if they defeat Fresno State, Texas State and Boise State in the upcoming triple whammy.

Which scenario would best position the Pac-12 for the berth in the CFP reserved for the top team in the Group of Six?

It’s possible the conference would be well served by Oregon State winning out and Boise State losing only to the Beavers.

That would result in a matchup of 10-2 teams for the conference title, placing the winner, whether it’s the Broncos or Beavers, in prime position for the playoff bid.

Granted, the results in the American and Mountain West in coming weeks will shape the Group of Six landscape.

But given the lunacy across the country – not to mention the plot twist currently unfolding 45 miles south of Corvallis – the Pac-12 should consider itself fortunate.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (6-1/3-0)

Result: won at Washington State 31-10

Next up: vs. Texas State (7 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: Remember back in September, when we described the result at Oregon as a quality loss that would strengthen the Broncos’ resume in much the same fashion as the narrow defeat in Eugene in 2024? Never mind. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (5-2/3-0)

Result: did not play

Next up: at Fresno State (8 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Texas Tech and Houston did Oregon State no favors Saturday with their losses. If the Beavers end up in a resume showdown for a playoff berth with the best team in the American or Mountain West, they would benefit from claiming a close defeat to a Big 12 playoff-bound team. That scenario is less likely than it was a few days ago. (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (4-3/1-2)

Result: did not play

Next up: vs. Oregon State (8 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: The Bulldogs’ pass defense is statistically average compared to the other 137 FBS teams. There is nothing average about Oregon State’s aerial attack. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (3-4/1-2)

Result: beat San Diego State 56-49

Next up: at Utah State (12:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: As insane as it sounds, holding their opponent to 49 points constitutes an improvement for the Rams, who have allowed at least 56 points in each of the previous three games. (Last week: 6)

5. San Diego State (3-5/2-2)

Result: lost at Colorado State 56-49

Next up: vs. Washington State (4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: That was a bad loss for SDSU’s bowl math. A very bad loss. Now, the Aztecs must handle Washington State and Utah State at home and either beat Boise State or win their Flex Saturday matchup, which will be on the road. (Last week: 4)

6. Texas State (4-3/2-1)

Result: beat Utah State 20-17

Next up: at Boise State (7 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: With Boise State and Oregon State on the road on consecutive Saturdays, the Bobcats should stay in Bend for the week rather than schlepping home and back. They will be far better prepared for whatever weather awaits them in Corvallis. (We’re joking, mostly.) (Last week: 5)

7. Utah State (2-5/1-2)

Result: lost at Texas State 20-17

Next up: vs. Colorado State (12:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: There goes Bronco Mendenhall, nearly pulling off a Bronco Mendenhall? Oh well, there will be more opportunities for the Aggies to rise up and disrupt the race in November. (Last week: 7)

8. Washington State (1-7/0-4)

Result: lost to Boise State 31-10

Next up: at San Diego State (4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: Given the level of competition in the new Pac-12, which is substantially worse than in the old Pac-12, this qualifies as one of the most disappointing seasons in the modern history of WSU football. There are problems galore, and coach Kirby Moore seemingly has no answers. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: An uncertain future for an Apple Cup hoops rivalry that only one side wants to preserve
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – The hoops version of the Apple Cup is unrecognizable these days.

Washington and Washington State have been playing against each other since 1910 and have matched up in 301 games, which is one of the oldest and most played series in men’s college basketball.

In front of 7,011 fans at Alaska Airlines Arena, the two teams met once again Sunday afternoon, and the Huskies lost 84-80 in an exhibition in a rivalry that used to mean something.

“Rivalries in college basketball, it’s tough,” said former UW star Isaiah Thomas who watched from stands below his No. 2 jersey, which hangs in the rafters. “It’s a different time, day and age.”

The 37-year-old Thomas talked to the Huskies before the game and tried to explain the importance of the UW-WSU rivalry to a team comprised of 12 newcomers born outside of the state, including five international players.

“It’s just human nature if you’re not from here to be a little clueless about the Apple Cup and what that really means,” Thomas said. “All these games probably feel the same, but just reminding them that it’s not about you the individual. It’s about the program, the city and the state rivalry.

“You just understand it more and more the longer you’re here. My job is to show them that it does mean something no matter if it’s a game that counts or not.”

Did they receive the message?

“If we win, they did,” Thomas said smiling at halftime. “If we lose, they didn’t.”

None of the current Cougars played in last year’s 81-69 loss while Wesley Yates III, Lathan Sommerville and Jasir Rencher suited up for the Huskies.

“I’ve coached two of their guys more than either of us have coached an entire team,” WSU coach David Riley said referring to UW’s Steele Venters and LeJuan Watts. “It’s a weird deal.”

Riley coached Venters at Eastern Washington and led Watts at EWU and at WSU.

“This is always a fun game, but I’ve never won so maybe it’s me,” Watts said smiling, referring to his 0-2 Apple Cup record, including an 89-73 WSU loss on Dec. 18, 2024, when he tallied 15 point, eight rebounds and three assists. “There’s no little brother thing (at Washington). That’s kind of what it was on the other side, just being the underdog.

“It’s a lot more drive and motivation if you’re Wazzu. I mean, you don’t have anything to lose.”

Despite a game-high 28 points on 7-for-12 shooting from the field from Watts, Lathan Sommerville scoring 19 points and Nikola Dzepina adding 16 points and 12 rebounds, Washington lost control midway in the second half.

The Huskies led 50-43 when the Cougars took control for good with a 13-2 run to go up 56-52 following an alley-oop dunk from Ronnie Harrison, who finished with a team-high 23 points.

Washington State went up 79-71 with 46 seconds left when Washington made one last push and cut its deficit to 81-78 following Venters’ 3-pointer with 15 seconds left.

After WSU guard Casey Jones missed a couple of free throws, the Huskies had a chance to tie but Watts’ 3-point attempt was deflected and fell short.

When it was over, Riley admitted he’s not sure if the series will continue.

“I hope we can get them on the schedule for a real game next year,” he said. “We’re taking this thing day by day. There’s a lot going on. There’s a lot of changes in college basketball, so hopefully we can make it happen next year.”

The Cougars have ceded the fate of the Apple Cup to the Huskies because they’re struggling to remain financially viable even in the Pac-12.

Among its 16 nonconference matchups on the 2026-27 schedule, Washington State plays just five in Pullman and nine on the road against High Point, Duquesne, Hawaii, Duke, Murray State, Southern Illinois, Weber State, UNLV, Seattle U, Eastern Washington and LSU.

“Home games against lesser teams usually cost a lot of money, and we’re in a spot now where it’s like we’d rather spend some of that on our roster,” Riley said. “We’re in a tough spot. It’s hard to find home-and-home (deals), especially in Pullman. So, we’re going on the road a lot and that’s part of the deal where we’re just, we’re going to play anyone anywhere at any time. We have a hard schedule, and we’ll be hardened by the time conference play hits.”

UW coach Danny Sprinkle, who begins his third season with the Huskies, knows canceling series with traditional rivals Gonzaga, Seattle U and potentially Washington State, is unpopular with UW fans.

However, he has his reasons.

“I know I’ll get killed for not playing (the Cougars) this year, but with our schedule, I have to do what’s best for Washington basketball,” Sprinkle said. “Fitting them in at a certain time, it was hard with us going to the Maui and playing BYU and two other terrific teams. Already having Baylor coming here, going to Utah, and then a lot of people around here forget you’re playing 20 Big Ten games … and probably 18 of them are Quad 1 games against the hardest teams in the country. So, that takes a toll on you.”

Riley, who is close friends with Sprinkle, understands.

“I’ve known Danny a long time,” he said. “There’s only a couple friends I’ve got in this business and he’s one of them. … He’s a good coach, great guy and he has to do what’s best for his team.”

Still, he wants the Apple Cup to continue.

“Whatever they tell us, we’ll go play the game,” Riley said. “We’ll find a way to make it work because it’s important to me. It’s important to our fans. It’s a great game, and it’s worth preserving.”

Washington State.title: Washington State beats rival Washington in men's basketball exhibition
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – For the first time since 1917, the men’s basketball teams from Washington State and Washington won’t meet in the regular season. But the Cougars still got a shot at their bitter rivals in a preseason matchup, and made the most of it.

WSU topped UW 84-80 in an exhibition on Sunday at Alaska Airlines Arena – a preseason boost for a Cougars team that was coming off a 28-point exhibition loss at New Mexico on Oct. 18.

The 7,011 in attendance were treated to a free-throw shootout. The teams combined for 87 foul shots. WSU went 31 of 46 from the line and the Huskies shot 30 of 41 from the stripe. The teams both shot 22 of 56 from the field. WSU’s 9-for-26 mark from 3-point range – compared to UW’s 6-for-23 – gave the visitors the edge.

The Cougars trailed by 10 points midway through the first half, but used an 8-2 run to get back in it and took a 38-37 lead into halftime. The Huskies opened a seven-point lead about seven minutes into the second period before a Casey Jones 3 keyed a 13-2 WSU run that put the Cougars up by four.

WSU’s Ronnie Harrison scored back-to-back buckets on a tip-in and a dunk with just over five minutes left to break a tie. The Cougars led by as many as eight points with under a minute left before a UW rally, but WSU got a game-winning block from Harrison on LeJuan Watts’ game-tying 3-point attempt with six seconds left.

Harrison, a senior transfer forward from East Texas A&M, led the Cougs with 23 points and 11 rebounds, shooting 8 of 9 from the floor. Guard Lazerek Houston, a Central Missouri transfer, added 15 points. Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips chipped in 12 points. Providence transfer guard Jaylen Harrell scored 11 points and Jones, a former Eastern Washington standout, had 10 for the new-look Cougars, who had to entirely rebuild their roster this offseason.

Watts, a former WSU and EWU star who spent last season at Texas Tech, led the Huskies with 28 points, shooting 7 of 12 from the field and 12 of 13 from the foul line. Gonzaga transfer Steele Venters had three points for UW.

The Cougs open their regular season Nov. 2 at home against Davidson.

In loss to No. 21 Boise State, WSU defense undone by big plays, a theme this season
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The collective shock from the crowd, a giant combination of screams and gasps and screeches, sounded like it came from a recording and blasted across Gesa Field.

It happened when Boise State running back Dylan Riley broke free for a 72-yard touchdown rush, the final dagger in his group’s 31-10 win over Washington State on Saturday night. The blue-clad fans shouted their ecstasy, but the crimson-clad ones followed with their disapproval, watching their Cougars wobble to their fifth straight loss.

If there’s anything these WSU fans can’t say, though, it’s that they haven’t seen something similar happen this season. Across this fall, a 1-7 disaster without an FBS win, the Cougars’ defense has had one weakness shine through most: The group is giving up too many big plays.

That was a theme on Saturday, when Boise State pulled away in the fourth quarter with two long rushes, a 33-yard scoring jaunt from Riley and the 72-yarder he followed up with, reminding the country why he’s one of college football’s best tailbacks. Earlier in the game, BSU quarterback Maddux Madsen also unleashed a 33-yard strike to receiver Raesean Jones, who hauled it in to convert a key third down.

And that’s to say nothing of perhaps the game’s biggest plays, which came late in the third quarter, with the Broncos facing third-and-6 near midfield. The game was tied at 10-10, underscoring how evenly the Cougars (1-7, 0-4 Pac-12) played the first-place Broncos (6-1, 3-0) through three quarters, and the hosts could have swung the game by getting off the field and getting the ball back to their offense.

Instead, Madsen dropped back, sensed pressure and escaped. He darted up the middle, made WSU linebacker Isaiah Hung miss and jetted 17 yards upfield. To cap off a long drive, the Broncos scored on a pass from Madsen to receiver Cam Bates, the first salvo in their 21-0 fourth quarter.

“I remember the ball skirted out to me, and I have to make that play,” Hung said. “That’s a play I gotta make, and gonna watch it on film, and figure out what I could do better. I’m gonna make that play next time it comes to me.”

Those are the kinds of plays that this WSU defense, which has played generally solid football all season, cannot seem to stop permitting. Last weekend in Corvallis, the Cougars gave up two scoring plays of 80-plus yards, a 90-yard completion to star wideout Jesse Legree and an 88-yarder to wideout AJ Newberry, who eluded WSU tacklers all the way to the end zone.

That’s been a thorn in the side of Cougar defensive coordinator Trent Bray, no matter how often his group has kept the team in close games, a remarkable achievement considering the way quarterback Caden Pinnick dragged down the entire operation in his six games at the controls. Even when this defense has acquitted itself well, the unit has been undone by a series of big plays that drag their team’s chances down like an anchor.

What have been the issues? In Saturday’s game, most had to do with WSU defenders’ bad pursuit angles. On Riley’s 72-yarder, the honors went to backup cornerback Kai Rapolla, who took an outside path to Riley, who darted inside and broke free. It harkened back to last weekend, when Legree sprung free for his long scoring reception. In coverage was Rapolla, who has had a forgettable season in his first year with a meaningful role.

Then, earlier in the game, Riley found himself sprinting 33 yards into the end zone. He had that opportunity in large part because WSU cornerback Khamari Terrell came charging in too fast. He couldn’t slow down in time to wrangle Riley, who took advantage and burst upfield, all the way to six points.

“I think that we’ve played a lot of tough backs this year and had success in tackling them,” Hung said. “I mean, obviously we respect our opponents, but we know that we can tackle anybody. It’s just something that’s gotta improve. We had him to limited yards, and we had to hold him to limited yards, and we just didn’t get it done.”

That’s the interesting part about WSU’s defense on Riley. Outside of his two longer gashes, he totaled only 23 yards, which would have been his season-low by a wide margin. All things considered, the Cougs defended well against one of the country’s single best running backs.

But as has been the case this season, WSU hasn’t been able to play a complete game. The Cougars can turn that around next weekend at San Diego State. But they’ll have to tackle better.

Washington State.title: With WSU out of bowl contention, coach Kirby Moore’s motivational tools will be tested | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Only seconds after Owen Eshelman threw a back-breaking interception, the exact kind of turnover that Washington State needed to avoid to upset No. 21 Boise State on Saturday night, his head coach sat him down on a nearby bench.

On the sideline, Eshelman talked with coach Kirby Moore, going over the play and what went wrong. Eshelman was looking for running back Kirby Vorhees, who ran to the right. Eshelman threw it left. It turned into a turnover, which sank WSU’s chances in this 31-10 loss to Boise State, the class of the rebuilt Pac-12.

Turns out, that was a play that the Cougars had installed early in the year, sometime in spring ball or fall camp. After the game, it seemed to frustrate Moore, who has placed his trust in a redshirt freshman making only his second career start.

“We weren’t on the same page there,” Moore said. “Obviously, it starts with me, and we gotta do a better job from that standpoint.”

The Cougars only have five more opportunities to do a better job, and at 1-7, their bowl hopes are gone. It’s their first time being eliminated from bowl eligibility before November since 2010. They have nothing left to play for except pride and for the 14 seniors who are playing their final year of college football.

Moore has missed chances to avoid letting things get to this point, and many of them center on his reluctance to bench quarterback Caden Pinnick for Eshelman, a decision that took so long it likely cost the Cougars multiple wins. But things are where they are, and with four games left to play, Moore can no longer rely on motivating his players with a bowl game, with the kind of national relevance they likely envisioned for themselves back in August.

Instead, Moore will have to find other ways to motivate these Cougars. He will have to find a way to get something out of a lost season: a win at San Diego State next week or a home win over Colorado State after the bye week.

The Cougars’ chances at a successful season may be gone, but they can still eke out something resembling success with the four games they have left, which is why Moore’s motivational skills will be put under the microscope across these last five weeks of his debut season.

Moore needs to get more from his offensive line, whose lack of physicality is creating exponentially more problems for the Cougars’ offense. He needs to corral his defense, which is yielding long scoring plays , and he needs to use his offensive acumen to point Eshelman in the right direction and make sure that in his last four starts, he learns the lessons he needs to so that if/when he returns for the 2027 season, he’s ready to lead an explosive offense.

“I think our players are pretty motivated on a daily basis,” Moore said. “Naturally, there’s different parts that go into every game, and things that we’ve drawn from from the offseason, things throughout fall camp, week-to-week with the opportunities we have. But I think our leadership group does a really good job as well, and I’ve got no reservations about our guys showing up with the right mindset tomorrow.”

It’s a tricky spot for Moore, who is naturally an even-keeled guy, at least publicly. In his last two postgame news conferences, after losses to Oregon State and Boise State, he has seemed more fired up – but the bar is low because he’s usually quieter.

The topic is still a bit difficult to wrangle because of some of the physical limitations that seem to be behind losses like these. The top ones belong to Washington State’s offensive line, which gave up four sacks against Boise State’s defense. That group – left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell – also couldn’t clear space for their running backs, who finished with 20 yards on 10 carries.

For WSU, that has been a problem all season. Check out how the Cougars’ tailback trio of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi has fared in their seven FBS games:

• vs. Washington: 16 carries, 38 yards

• vs. Kansas State: 17 carries, 72 yards

• vs. Arizona: 17 carries, 59 yards

• vs. Fresno State: 12 carries, 45 yards

• vs. Utah State: 19 carries, 77 yards

• vs. Oregon State: 13 carries, 26 yards

• vs. Boise State: 10 carries, 20 yards

That comes out to an average of 15 carries for 48 yards.

Could those three be doing more to break free? Maybe, but the bigger problem involves their offensive line, which has struggled in short-yardage situations.

Against Boise State, the group couldn’t clear enough space on a third-and-1 and Pulalasi was stuffed. To their credit, they helped convert a fourth-and-1 QB keeper, which led to the Cougars’ one touchdown.

Still, WSU’s offensive line has been a glaring issue all season, even when Caden Pinnick was playing QB and running himself into all manner of unforced sacks. It’s worth keeping in mind that three of the Cougs’ five linemen – Tripp, Lester and Dunham – were recruited to play in an Air Raid-adjacent system, which doesn’t lend itself to gritty physicality on third-and-1. But that’s what they’re being asked to do now, and it isn’t working out so well.

Beyond that, Moore will have to draw on his offensive mind and mentor Eshelman, find a way to steer him away from the kind of interception that dashed the Cougs’ chances here on Saturday evening. Moore has always fashioned himself an offensive guy. He was Missouri’s offensive coordinator for three years. Previously, he worked the same job at Fresno State, including as QBs coach.

With that type of experience, Moore hasn’t just gotten adept at the X’s and O’s. He’s had a chance to work with all kinds of quarterbacks with all types of skillsets. To get something out of the rest of this season, he’ll have to draw on that with Eshelman, who has a compelling skillset.

Can he play well enough to get a couple more wins out of this season? Neither Eshelman nor any of his teammates will be motivated by a bowl game, so now it falls to Moore and his coaching. For WSU, this season may be lost, but not every game has to feel that way.

“I think it comes down to who you are, and there’s a lot more that’s revealed about who you are when things aren’t going your way,” Eshelman said. “That’s what I’ve loved to see with guys in our locker room the last few weeks – they respond and they go back to work, and so that’s something that I’m really proud of with our guys.

“Just trying to continue to push the envelope, continue to press and see where we can get better, continue to press and grow. As a believer, that’s where I want to be in my life, whether it’s me as a husband, whether it’s me as a father, whether it’s me in whatever future career I’m in. There has to be a standard for my life and the way I do things, and I want to continue to push that standard.”

Washington State.title: Until a fourth-quarter error, Washington State played close with No. 21 Boise State | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
A fourth-quarter turnover turned a close game into a lopsided loss for Washington State, which kept pace with a heavily favored opponent for three quarters before crumbling.

The Cougars defense played admirably for much of the game. WSU’s offense was stuck in the mud for most of the day, and a communication error between the Cougs quarterback and running back resulted in a costly interception that spelled another defeat for WSU.

In the end, No. 21 Boise State pulled away for a 31-10 Pac-12 win on Saturday at Gesa Field.

WSU fell to 1-7 overall and 0-4 in conference play under first-year coach Kirby Moore. The Broncos (6-1, 3-0) captured their first-ever win in Pullman and remained the front-runners in the Pac-12 with their sixth straight win.

Game spirals on crucial mistake

The Cougars were very much alive until a game-changing blunder early in the fourth quarter.

Quarterback Owen Eshelman, making his second start for WSU, wasn’t playing great, but he had mostly avoided big mistakes and was playing just well enough to keep it close. But the redshirt freshman made his first truly costly mistake of his young career with 12 minutes, 23 seconds left in the game and his team down by a touchdown.

Eshelman looked to pass over the middle on a second-and-10, expecting running back Kirby Vorhees to cut left on his route. But Vorhees went right, and Eshelman had already released the throw. His pass went right to Boise State linebacker Boen Phelps, a Freeman High grad, who returned the pick to the WSU 33 to set up a touchdown that suppressed the Cougs’ hopes of earning a signature win.

That turnover was the turning point. WSU’s offense had labored all game to move downfield, and a 14-point deficit in the fourth quarter was pretty much insurmountable. WSU reached midfield on its next drive, but a third-down sack stalled the possession – WSU’s offensive line had a game to forget, surrendering four sacks and eight QB hits.

Eshelman finished 21 of 40 for 191 yards with no TDs. He had a handful of nice moments, improvising to convert third downs (WSU went 6 of 17 on third downs) and using his legs effectively – excluding yards lost from sacks, Eshelman gained 70 yards on 19 carries. But the downfield passing game left much to be desired, and the Cougars tailbacks were a nonfactor yet again against a stout Boise State front. Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi gained 20 yards on 10 carries.

Offense remains this team’s weak spot. The unit showed some promise during a long TD drive late in the first half and a possession that ended with a field goal midway through the third quarter. But there’s just not any sustained fluidity and a glaring lack of big plays – WSU only had one play of 20-plus yards.

Despite stats, WSU defense earned props

The Cougars defensive front had a respectable outing against one of the nation’s best rushing teams – until the fourth quarter.

Boise State finished with 258 rushing yards and three TDs on the ground, averaging 7 yards per carry. Broncos running back Dylan Riley, who entered the game ranked No. 6 nationally in rushing yards, produced 128 yards and two touchdowns.

But 133 of the Broncos’ rushing yards came during the fourth quarter, and two Riley runs accounted for 105 of those. Before the superstar junior tailback broke off scoring runs of 33 and 72 yards in the fourth quarter against a deflated WSU defense, the Boise State ground game hadn’t overpowered the Cougars like it had so many other teams this year.

BSU running backs only had one carry of 20 yards before the fourth. WSU’s linebackers and defensive line did well to swarm to the ball and meet the Broncos ball-carriers near the line of scrimmage.

And the Cougars secondary deserves some credit for limiting Boise State’s downfield passing attack. WSU’s pass defense slipped on the Broncos’ first scoring drive, allowing a chunk gain on fourth down and a 33-yarder, and the Cougs defensive backs gave up four straight completions during a BSU drive that ended in a field goal at the end of the first half. Aside from those slips, it was a commendable effort for the WSU DBs. Boise State’s veteran quarterback, Maddux Madsen, was held to 14 of 23 for a season-low 149 passing yards, with two completions of 15 yards or more.

Could’ve been worse

The Cougars are officially eliminated from postseason contention. It’s a lost season that began with so much hope, a thoroughly disappointing debut for Moore in the new Pac-12. Having said that, the Cougars aren’t as bad as they were a few weeks ago.

To be sure, a 1-7 team doesn’t deserve optimism, but WSU has at least been more fun to watch over the past two weeks, showing some competitiveness against the Pac-12’s top two teams. On Saturday, the Cougars had the score tied against a ranked team heading into the fourth quarter. A month ago, that would’ve seemed impossible.

The Cougars should have a chance to win back a smidge of faith in the coming weeks. They have what appear to be three very winnable games on the horizon against fellow Pac-12 underachievers in San Diego State, Colorado State and Texas State. That first FBS win has to be in there somewhere.

Washington State.title: Freeman grad Boen Phelps makes game-changing play, Dylan Riley adds another big day for Broncos | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
BSU LB Boen Phelps

The junior Freeman High graduate made a game-changing play early in the fourth quarter, picking off a pass to set up a touchdown that allowed Boise State to all but put the Cougars away. On second-and-10 with just over 12 minutes remaining, WSU quarterback Owen Eshelman expected running back Kirby Vorhees to cut left on a short route over the middle. But Vorhees went the opposite direction, and Eshelman’s pass went directly into the hands of Phelps, who returned the pick 13 yards to the WSU 33. BSU scored a touchdown two plays later to go up by 14 points. Phelps, a former walk-on who has developed into a key BSU defender, finished tied for the team high with six tackles.

BSU RB Dylan Riley

The Broncos’ superstar running back struggled to break off big gains for three quarters against a WSU defense that was keying in on the ground game. But Riley produced two explosive touchdown runs in the fourth quarter, turning a close game into a runaway win for Boise State. After Phelps’ interception, Riley cut outside and raced 33 yards for a TD to put BSU ahead by 14. On the fourth play of the Broncos’ next possession, Riley bounced outside, made two defenders miss and jetted downfield for a 72-yard score. The junior finished with 128 yards and those two TDs on 13 carries. Riley entered the game ranked No. 6 nationally in rushing yards, and boosted his total to 963 yards on the year.

Washington State.title: Cougars show promise but remain behind elite of Pac-12 | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
Perhaps there was a time when Washington State’s season could have been salvaged, but it wasn’t Saturday against No. 21 Boise State.

It wasn’t last week against a surging Oregon State team that is averaging 51 points during its current five-game winning streak.

But in those two games – the first two starts for Owen Eshelman after coach Kirby Moore made a switch at quarterback – the Cougars showed some … spirit? Vitality, maybe?

It would strain credulity to say the offense played well in Saturday’s 31-10 loss to the Broncos. Scoring points, after all, is the only goal for an offense that really matters.

Yet in a 1-7 season that has long gone stale, the Cougars at least threatened success with Eshelman at the helm, even if they couldn’t quite get there.

Consider, Boise State entered the game ranked No. 1 nationally in time of possession, bludgeoning opponents with long, methodical drives. WSU, however, actually managed to hold the ball for a minute longer than the disciplined Broncos.

How did they do it? Because Eshelman showed some capacity for playmaking, both with his arm and his feet. Within that 10-point offensive output were third-and-long passes thrown moments before a defender took his head off with a well-timed safety blitz. We also saw a 10-yard scramble on third-and-nine, and WSU’s offense converted four of five fourth-down attempts.

Was it perfect? No. It was chaotic. Eshelman threw no touchdowns, one interception, and somehow gave back 37 yards on four sacks. Yeesh. But the chaos created the possibility of big plays.

Ultimately, the Broncos were too good, and WSU once again failed to take advantage of a superb performance by the defense. The game was tied at 10 entering the fourth quarter. Then Eshelman threw a costly interception following a Broncos touchdown drive, and Boise State needed just two plays to get back into the end zone.

And that was it. The Cougars weren’t coming back from two scores down because their issues on offense run far deeper than quarterback, even if Eshelman provides a breath of fresh air.

The longer a person watches football, the more they come to understand that highlight catches and long runs are little more than window dressing. A football game is won and lost on the line of scrimmage, and a viewer can get a pretty good sense of which team is winning by watching the linemen–and no one else.

Well, the WSU offensive linemen are getting their butts whooped – to the degree that I’m not sure it matters how good the quarterback, running backs, or wide receivers may be. Despite Eshelman’s patience in the pocket and ability to look downfield at second and third reads, he completed only 21 of 40 pass attempts while under constant duress.

Despite having a mobile quarterback who ran the ball 19 times, no Cougar had a run longer than Eshelman’s 10-yard third-down scamper. Leo Pulalasi, whose speed was evidenced by a 54-yard run against Utah State earlier this season, managed just 12 yards on five rushes.

Kirby Vorhees got five attempts as well, netting eight yards for his troubles.

With four games left, WSU is in a precarious position. Most fans are staying home these days, and with no chance of qualifying for a bowl game, the Cougars will need to win them back by showing improvement and momentum heading into next season.

Eshelman’s first two starts came against the Pac-12’s best. Maybe he can do more against the rest.

Moore began his postgame press conference by telling reporters, “Nobody’s quitting. We’re pissed off and disappointed. We need to play better. We can be a better football team.”

Washington State.title: No. 21 Boise State pulls away in fourth quarter to beat WSU | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — Owen Eshelman got up slowly, his head tilted up at the sky, regretting the costliest play of his young career. As he headed toward the sideline, his Washington State teammates all patted him on the helmet, trying to cushion the blow, doing their best to turn his attention away from the party Boise State was enjoying a few feet away.

The damage was done, though, and the Broncos were making the Cougars’ quarterback hear about the interception he had just thrown in Saturday’s game. It was early in the fourth quarter, and down by only one touchdown, WSU had a chance to tie the game.

Instead, Eshelman wasn’t on the same page with running back Kirby Vorhees. Eshelman threw it left. Vorhees went right. The ball sailed into the hands of BSU defender Boen Phelps, whose team needed only two plays to parlay that into another score, one of the final daggers in the No. 21 Broncos’ 31-10 win at Gesa Field.

With this loss, WSU officially falls out of bowl eligibility for just the second time in the last 11 full seasons.

It’s the fifth straight loss for the Cougars, who are still looking for their first FBS win of head coach Kirby Moore’s tenure, falling at the hands of the first-place Broncos, who scored 21 unanswered in the fourth quarter. In his second start, Eshelman completed 21 of 40 passes for 191 yards and the one pick, the first truly disastrous play of his career.

Until that point, Eshelman and the Cougs were in the game just about the entire way, tying the game once with a second-quarter touchdown rush from running back Kirby Vorhees and again with a 47-yard field goal from kicker Jack Stevens in the third, but it was all Broncos in the fourth quarter.

In the Cougars and Broncos’ first clash in Pullman since 2017, Boise State pulled away with three touchdowns in the fourth frame: First on a short passing touchdown from quarterback Maddux Madsen to receiver Cam Bates, then on a 33-yard rushing score from star running back Dylan Riley, who followed up with an even more explosive play, a 72-yard touchdown rush on his team’s next series. All told, Riley totaled 128 yards and two touchdowns, clearing the century mark for the fifth time in seven games.

Going back to WSU’s loss at Oregon State last weekend, that was the third scoring play of 70-plus yards the Cougs have given up recently, exposing one of that group’s central weaknesses: Giving up big plays. Last weekend, WSU cornerback Kai Rapolla couldn’t contain star wideout Jesse Legree on a 90-yard touchdown. This Saturday, Rapolla took a bad pursuit angle, springing Riley free.

The Cougars had chances to keep pace, but those were scuttled by the time Eshelman had in the pocket, or lack thereof. Eshelman was sacked X times for a total loss of 37 yards, highlighting the way Boise State torched WSU’s offensive line, both on dropbacks and on running plays.

In this one, the Cougars posted only 53 rushing yards on 33 attempts, an average rush of 1.6 yards. Eshelman picked up 33 of those yards, so narrowing that down to the Cougars’ running backs, you get these numbers: 20 yards on 10 carries and one touchdown, the short dive from Vorhees. In seven games against FBS competition, WSU has not been able to generate any meaningful rushing attack from its tailback trio of Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi.

The Cougars also played this game without two key pieces, one on each side of the ball: Wide receiver Darrius Clemons missed the game with an ankle injury, while safety Jeremiah Bernard was out for undisclosed reasons. Clemons’ absence further hampered the Cougs’ receiver depth, which was already thin to begin with, while their defense missed Bernard’s physicality in the secondary.

WSU tied the game late in the second quarter, taking a page out of Boise State’s book with a long drive that took nearly seven minutes off the clock. Inside the 10 yard line, Eshelman lasered a pass toward receiver Daniel Blood, who hauled it in just shy of the goal line. One play later, Vorhees plunged into the end zone, and replay review showed he was in for a touchdown.

That happened with 46 seconds left in the first half. It was enough time for the Broncos, who benefited from a kickoff-out-of-bounds penalty from kicker Jack Stevens, setting the visitors up at their own 35. They needed just seven plays to drive into the Cougar red zone, aided by a holding call on safety Jackquintin Ball, and then kicker Oscar Doyle connected on a short field goal.

WSU headed into the halftime intermission looking at a 10-7 deficit.

The Cougars return to action next week at San Diego State.

Pregame

Washington State will have to play its most complete game of the season so far to earn its first FBS and Pac-12 Conference win of the season.

No. 21 Boise State arrives in Pullman as the presumptive favorite to win the league. The Broncos are on a five-game winning streak after losing the season opener to Oregon.

For first-year WSU head coach Kirby Moore, the game will be a reunion of sorts. Moore starred as a wide receiver for the Broncos along with his brother Kellen.

The Cougars are on the cusp of losing bowl eligibility with a 1-6 record, adding more stakes to Saturday’s game. WSU has qualified for a bowl game in 10 of the last 11 seasons.

Redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman will get another start at QB for the Cougars after compiling over 400 yards of offense against Oregon State.

The game is scheduled to kick off at 3 p.m. on USA Network.

Series history

Washington State holds a 5-2 advantage in its history against Boise State. However, the Broncos have won two out of the last three matchups, the last being a 45-24 win in Boise during the 2024 season.

Washington State.title: Why No. 21 Boise State will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – All season, Washington State’s defense has been a little tricky to parse.

On one hand, the Cougars have excelled in tough spots, given short field after short field, jumping into action in pinch after pinch thanks to offensive turnovers. Their pass rush has been above average. So has their tackling.

But when you’re playing No. 21 Boise State, above average won’t fly, which is why we’re picking WSU to fall to the Broncos Saturday afternoon in Pullman.

The Cougars are tasked with doing something that only Oregon has done this season, which is slow down BSU tailbacks Dylan Riley and Sire Gaines, one of the country’s best running back tandems. Riley ranks second in the country with 139 rushing yards per game, and Gaines has cleared the century mark in each of his last two games.

Complicating matters for WSU is Boise State’s average time of possession: 36 minutes. That leads the entire country. That will put some serious strain on the Cougars’ defense, especially if their offense commits a turnover, which new quarterback Owen Eshelman did well to avoid in meaningful settings last weekend in his first start.

Overall, it’s a lot to ask out of this WSU team, and there’s no shame in losing to this Boise State team. But the Cougars will have to look elsewhere for their first FBS win of the season.

Final score: No. 21 Boise State 30, WSU 20

Washington State.title: Washington State's keys to victory against No. 21 Boise State | Two-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State vs. No. 21 Boise State

Saturday, 3 p.m.

Line: Boise State favored by 13½

TV: USA Network Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU secondary against Boise State running backs: Earlier this week, WSU cornerback Khamari Terrell made a fairly strong claim: “I’m gonna make it noticed that you’re not gonna be able to just run to my side and just think that you’re gonna get a big gain or anything,” he said. It bears examining because it indicates that Terrell understands that to pull an upset on the Broncos, the Cougars’ defensive backs will have to wrap up running backs Dylan Riley and Sire Gaines.

It’s a paramount theme for WSU, which missed 18 tackles last weekend in a loss to Oregon State. The Cougars can’t afford many whiffs against Riley, who has forced 28 missed tackles, according to Pro Football Focus. WSU has done well this season to bottle up runs up the middle, and it’s fair to expect that trend to continue on Saturday. That shifts the spotlight to players like Terrell and other Cougar secondary players, including cornerback Jalil Tucker and safeties Jaylen Thomas and Jeremiah Bernard.

Thomas leads the team with 12 missed tackles, while Bernard is second with eight. Some of those are to be expected, as that duo has played some of the most snaps on their defense. But if Riley and Gaines have to bounce it to the outside, where they’re averaging a combined 4.9 yards per carry, watch how well the Cougars tackle. That may end up telling the story of Saturday’s game.

How the Cougs win …

Outside of limiting Boise State’s potent rushing attack, which no team besides Oregon has been able to do, WSU can win by generating more of its own offense. In quarterback Owen Eshelman’s second game at the controls, he’ll have to follow up on an encouraging performance, and he’ll have to avoid turnovers. Besides a late, meaningless interception last weekend, he did well in his first showing.

With receiver Darrius Clemons doubtful to play with an ankle injury, Eshelman will likely have to show a similarly sharp connection with wideout Branden Ganashamoorthy, who set career highs last weekend with 11 catches for 147 yards and one touchdown. And because the Cougars’ rushing game from their tailbacks has been all but invisible this fall, they will also need Eshelman to produce more on the ground, which he did last weekend to the tune of 136 yards and one score.

Here’s another way WSU could pull the upset: Generate a turnover or two. The only problem is that the Broncos have only lost two offensive turnovers this fall.

How the Broncos win …

Boise State can win this game with the same recipe it has in five straight wins: let tailbacks Dylan Riley and Sire Gaines run wild, avoid turnovers and grind out long drives that keep the opposing offense off the field, capitalizing on their average time of possession of 36 minutes – which ranks No. 1 in the country.

The Broncos will want to stay on the field for long stretches, which could wear out a Cougar defense that has already played heavy snaps due to their turnover issues, many caused by previous QB Caden Pinnick. WSU, which missed 18 tackles last weekend against Oregon State, will have to tackle well against BSU.

Key stat: 220

That’s how many minutes BSU QB Maddux Madsen and the Broncos’ offense has been on the field this season, which ranks tops in the entire country, highlighting their ability to stretch out long drives with Riley and Gaines’ steady contributions. That has also generated key rest for the Broncos’ defense, which has been active less than 40% of total snaps, keeping playmakers like edge rushers Max Stege and Jayden Virgin-Morgan fresh.

Quotable

“Definitely take pride in stopping the run,” WSU defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele said. “Someone of my size, my build, is not really a pass rusher build, but if I’m going to do anything, I’m going to stop the run as much as I can, and with my ability, I take pride in that. I think our defense takes pride in stopping the run. Our D-line takes pride in stopping the run because that’s what it starts with. Just being a defensive lineman, that mentality has to be there. I don’t think you can be a D-lineman without that mentality.”

Washington State.title: To pull upset on No. 21 Boise State, WSU will have to play its best all-around game of the season
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When people look at the word Boise, the capital city of Idaho, most feel compelled to pronounce it with a Z. Boi-zee.

Not Washington State coach Kirby Moore. He knows better.

“We had quite a few guys on the team from Idaho,” Moore said earlier this week, “and they would correct you if you use the Z.”

That’s because Moore’s playing days came at Boise State, the very team his Washington State team is hosting this weekend for homecoming, set for a 3 p.m. Saturday kickoff on USA Network. It’s a full-circle moment of sorts for Moore, who didn’t just play for the Broncos. Many of the connections he used to build his WSU staff came courtesy of his days in Boise.

It’s an intriguing matchup for WSU, which is hosting Boise State for the first time since 2017, when the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead a wild triple-overtime comeback. It’s also the first Pac-12 matchup between the Cougars and No. 21 Broncos, who find themselves on opposite ends of the conference standings headed into this one.

WSU (1-6, 0-3 Pac-12), which last week pivoted from Caden Pinnick to Owen Eshelman at quarterback to try and snap out of an offensive lull, is looking to end a four-game losing streak. Boise State (5-1, 2-0), which was idle last weekend, has followed a season-opening loss to Oregon with five straight victories.

Still looking for their first FBS win of Moore’s tenure, the Cougars’ offense looked far sharper in a loss to Oregon State last weekend than it ever did in Pinnick’s six games at the helm. Meanwhile, the Broncos’ offense ranks among the best in the country, much of it generated by their rushing attack, No. 8 nationally with 235 yards per game.

What’s on the line for WSU in this one? Mathematically, the Cougars can still earn bowl eligibility, which they have done in 10 of the past 11 full seasons. But to get there, they will have to end the regular season with five straight wins, and that would require them to buck just about every pattern they’ve shown in their first seven games. WSU is about a 13-point underdog in Saturday’s game, according to most sportsbooks.

“At the end of the day, ultimately, it’s about winning, though,” Moore said, “and we gotta do a better job on what it takes to win. This week, we’ll challenge our guys with (their) attitude when they hit the building. What’s their attitude? That’s their choice on a daily basis, and to make sure we’re being as prepared and detailed as we can for the Boise State game.”

Can the Cougars turn things around in such a big way? If there’s a glimmer of possibility, it stems from the change they made at quarterback, which paid off to the tune of nearly 300 passing yards from Eshelman last week. He passed for two touchdowns and added one more on the ground, where he tallied 136 yards against OSU, turning heads and making people wonder: Where was this guy all along?

If Eshelman can turn in similar results Saturday afternoon, his team might have a chance to pull the upset on Boise State, whose defense ranks No. 130 of 138 FBS teams in Pro Football Focus’ tackling grades. The Broncos have only missed a combined 17 tackles in their past two games, though, indicating that coach Spencer Danielson’s team may have cleaned up that issue.

The other issue facing Eshelman and WSU’s offense this weekend: Who will step up at receiver? The Cougars have spent all but 10 snaps this season without star wideout Tony Freeman, who has a torn ACL. Then last weekend in Corvallis, fellow receiver Darrius Clemons went down with an ankle injury, and he’s listed as doubtful for Saturday’s game. That is putting a serious strain on the Cougars’ wide receiver corps, which was already thin to begin with.

That puts three WSU wideouts in the spotlight: Branden Ganashamoorthy, who set career-highs last weekend with 11 catches for 147 yards and one touchdown, plus Daniel Blood and Tank Hawkins. Those are just about the only receivers WSU has left who have generated any production this season. Depth is a serious concern for the Cougars.

Can the Cougs survive with only those three? Last week, Blood hauled in his first career touchdown pass, finishing with six receptions for 59 yards. He’s been fairly consistent this season. Then there’s Hawkins, whose playing time has come and gone this fall. He played 50 snaps of offense against Oregon State, though, and he will likely be in line for even more against Boise State.

But there could be two other candidates to get more snaps at wide receiver, Moore indicated: West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees and walk-on Caleb Northcroft, who have combined for just 17 snaps of offense. Those two have been low on the depth chart all season. It might be asking a lot for them to jump into action and produce against a ranked team, but that’s the kind of spot the Cougars are in at the moment. At the very least, those two wideouts could give their top three counterparts a breather.

“They’ll get a bunch of reps this week, and then we’ll evaluate where they’re at,” Moore said, “whether that’s 11 personnel, 12 personnel. What gives us the best opportunity to win? And then we’ll play that way.”

Still, perhaps a bigger theme in this one involves Boise State’s running back tandem of Dylan Riley and Sire Gaines, who have carved up just about every defense they’ve faced. Riley is averaging 139 yards per game, which ranks second in the country, while Gaines is going for about 89 yards per game in four outings. Those two have made things easy on quarterback Maddux Madsen, who has 13 touchdowns and no interceptions, taking care of the ball exceptionally well.

The Cougs, whose defense ranks fifth in the Pac-12, will have to tackle those two to give themselves a chance to spring the upset. Their coach may know how to pronounce Boise, but he’ll hope that the next time he says the city’s name in a public setting, he’ll be talking about a win.

Washington State.title: What Washingon State, UW need to do to make bowl games | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
The stretch run is looming, the first College Football Playoff rankings are two weeks away and the hierarchy has been deliciously flipped on its head across the region.

UCLA and Utah are undefeated.

Oregon has two losses.

Arizona has one loss.

Washington has three.

Also, Oregon State is a juggernaut.

How should we make sense of it all? With a deep dive into the bowl math.

Five Pac-12 legacy schools have either clinched postseason bids or are one victory away with a slew of winnable games remaining: Arizona, Oregon State, UCLA, USC and Utah.

They are playing for spots in conference championship games and the College Football Playoff. (Yes, even the Beavers have a path to the CFP).

The math is trickier for the other seven: Arizona State, Cal, Colorado, Oregon, Stanford, Washington and Washington State.

Let’s focus on their equations (in alphabetical order).

Arizona State

Wins needed: 3

Games remaining: 6

The math: Calculus. The lineup includes a trip to second-ranked BYU, which essentially means the Sun Devils must win three of the other five. That group includes home dates with Oklahoma State (4-2) and Kansas State (4-2) and the finale at No. 25 Arizona. Clearly, the Devils must beat Colorado next month.

Cal

Wins needed: 3

Games remaining: 5

The math: Trigonometry. The Bears don’t play at home until Nov. 21, when they host Stanford. If they lose at SMU, NC State and Virginia (combined record: 12-7), then elimination is assured. The Big Game and the finale against Pittsburgh won’t matter. We suspect they will steal a win in Raleigh or Charlottesville to make things interesting.

Colorado

Wins needed: 4

Games remaining: 6

The math: Differential equations. The Buffaloes have lost four in a row (three by double digits). All six remaining opponents have winning or .500 records.

Oregon

Wins needed: 2

Games remaining: 6

The math: Long division. We have included the Ducks due to the ineptitude of their offense without injured quarterback Dante Moore (concussion). If Moore returns sooner rather than later, they could run the table – remember, Ohio State quarterback Julian Sayin is also hurt. Without Moore, the defense should be good enough to support three or four wins. But there are no guarantees.

Stanford

Wins needed: 3

Games remaining: 5

The math: Algebraic geometry. The Cardinal is abysmal on the road (outscored 150-17) and has trips to Louisville, Virginia Tech and Cal remaining. But even one road win won’t be enough for a bowl berth unless Stanford beats NC State and No. 23 SMU at home.

Washington

Wins needed: 2

Games remaining: 5

The math: Probability. The Huskies host Penn State (3-4) and visit Michigan State (2-5). Win both, and they are fine. Lose one, and they must beat either Nebraska, Indiana or Oregon (combined record: 15-5). Lose both, and it’s trouble. Big trouble.

Washington State

Wins needed: 5

Games remaining: 5

The math: Quantum physics. At some point, the Cougars should turn their attention to 2027.

There’s one more component to consider: Teams with 5-7 records can participate in Bowl Season if there aren’t enough teams with .500-or-better records to fill all the spots.

However, the early signing window for high school recruits (early December) and the transfer portal window (early January) are such that five-win schools could decline invitations to fully focus on rebuilding their rosters.

That is, if they aren’t immersed in hiring new coaches.

To the projections …

Pac-12 legacy bowls

Alamo Bowl: Utah

Comment: Given the impressive showings last weekend by Texas Tech and BYU – and considering the Utes (6-0) have not looked sharp the past two weeks – we now expect them to finish with two losses and no Big 12 title. That won’t be enough for a playoff bid.

Las Vegas Bowl: UCLA

Comment: The Bruins (6-0) could land in the CFP or Alamo Bowl but don’t have much margin for error with the weak schedule, which will impact their resume, and the season-ending injury to quarterback Nico Iamaleava. The finale could mean more to UCLA than USC.

Holiday Bowl: Oregon State

Comment: All roads are open for the Beavers (5-2), including a berth in the College Football Playoff. But to reach the highest heights, they need help – specifically, Texas Tech and Houston must keep winning, and one of them needs to reach the Big 12 championship game. Any polish that can be applied to those early-season losses will strengthen OSU’s case.

Sun Bowl: Arizona

Comment: The Wildcats (5-1) are very much alive in the race for a berth in the Big 12 championship but have the toughest road of the contenders. Our current forecast calls for a 9-3 finish, but let’s be real: For a program that hasn’t made back-to-back postseason appearances in more than a decade, any bowl bid would constitute an important milestone.

Poinsettia Bowl: USC

Comment: Imagine the reaction if UCLA qualifies for the playoff in Bob Chesney’s first season and the Trojans (6-1), who have never participated, do not. There would be no greater humiliation.

Independence Bowl: Oregon

Comment: Imagine the reaction across the college football world, but especially in Corvallis and Seattle, if a $40 million roster ends up in Shreveport. With quarterback Dante Moore’s return uncertain, we foresee two more losses for the Ducks (4-2). That could drop them down the bowl lineup behind a handful of nine- and 10-win teams.

At-large/ESPN bowl pool: Arizona State

Comment: At this point, we should note the implications for every Pac-12 legacy team if nobody jumps into the CFP. In that scenario, there would be more bowl-eligible teams than bowl bids available. Like a few others, the Sun Devils (3-3) could be at ESPN’s mercy.

At-large/ESPN bowl pool: Washington

Comment: The Huskies (4-3) would seem vulnerable to a barrage of opt-outs, with players who had CFP dreams skipping the bowl game to prepare for the NFL draft. Except how many draft-caliber players are on the roster?

Non-qualifier: Cal

Comment: It feels like the Hotline has entered an alternate universe, where quarterback Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele is required to compete for the starting job despite clearly being the best option for the Bears (3-4), who are headed nowhere with blazing speed.

Non-qualifier: Colorado

Comment: The Buffaloes (2-4) must win four of their last six and seemingly will be underdogs in five. At least their fans can look forward to basketball season.

Non-qualifier: Stanford

Comment: With one more victory, rookie coach Tavita Pritchard and the Cardinal (3-4) will equal the total attained last year by interim coach Frank Reich. Not going backwards isn’t much, but it’s better than going backwards.

Non-qualifier: Washington State

Comment: The Cougars (1-6) have changed offensive play-callers and starting quarterbacks. There aren’t any cords left to pull. Well, there’s one, but it’s incredibly costly and probably a tad extreme at this point. Six weeks from now? Who knows.

Pac-12 new bowls

College Football Playoff: Boise State

Comment: We aren’t suggesting the Broncos (5-1) are facing a two-game season, with those being the showdown with Oregon State next month and the Pac-12 championship game. But obviously, it’s a two-game season.

Poinsettia Bowl: Fresno State

Comment: If both Boise State and Oregon State fail to reach the CFP, the new Pac-12 lineup would become much more cramped. The Bulldogs (4-3) could end up in Hawaii or the ESPN bowl pool.

Hawaii Bowl: San Diego State

Comment: The Aztecs (3-4) host Washington State and Utah State in coming weeks, which makes a victory in Fort Collins on Saturday the key to securing a spot in the postseason: It would allow them to avoid must-win games at Boise State and on the Flex Saturday.

ESPN bowl pool: Texas State

Comment: The Bobcats (3-3) have a heavily back-loaded schedule with Boise State, Oregon State and Fresno State upcoming, plus the Flex Saturday matchup. We suspect they will play the role of disruptor at least once.

Non-qualifier: Colorado State

Comment: The Rams (2-4) are last in major college football – that’s 138 teams – in scoring defense, total defense and yards-per-play allowed. Too bad their head coach doesn’t have expertise on that side of the ball. Err ….

Non-qualifier: Utah State

Comment: To be clear: The Aggies (2-4) have a non-zero chance of becoming bowl-eligible. It’s just that the likelihood is 0.01 percent and we are rounding up.

Editor’s note: Jon Wilner’s Pac-12 bowl selection process in 2026 treats the former conference as if it never imploded, grouping the 12 legacy schools together just as it did the previous two years. Meanwhile, the new Pac-12 teams have separate postseason arrangements. To simplify the situation, we have split them into two groups: Pac-12 legacy bowls and Pac-12 new bowls. Washington State and Oregon State are part of the legacy bowl process with the exception of the Poinsettia Bowl.

Washington State.title: Ahead of WSU and Boise State's first Pac-12 clash, a look back at the first seven matchups
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Washington State takes the field this weekend against No. 21 Boise State, the Cougars will be in for a lot of firsts.

It’ll be WSU’s first time hosting Boise State since 2017, when the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead a wild comeback. It’ll be the first time that Cougar coach Kirby Moore has faced the Broncos, for whom he played in the early 2010s. It will also be quarterback Owen Eshelman’s first home start after taking over the reins last weekend.

But what about the previous matchups between the Cougs and Broncos, who will be meeting for the first time as Pac-12 foes? The teams have only clashed seven times before. WSU owns a 5-2 record in the matchup.

Here is a look back at all seven games, in chronological order.

1997: WSU wins a blowout in Pullman, 58-0

In WSU quarterback Ryan Leaf’s senior season, the Cougars started 7-0 and wound up in the Rose Bowl. They laid the foundation for that magical season in late September, when they handed the Broncos a 58-0 loss, to this day Boise State’s largest loss in program history and still the last time the program has been shut out .

All told, Leaf completed 17 of 30 passes for 289 yards and three touchdowns, and the Cougars churned out 209 more yards and two touchdowns on the ground. Michael Black piled up 17 carries for 141 yards and two total touchdowns, while receiver Kevin McKenzie caught six passes for 101 yards and two touchdowns.

Also notable from that game: WSU kicker Rian Lindell connected on a 57-yard field goal. That put the Cougars up 17-0 in the second quarter.

The game also featured this interesting twist: Boise State kicker Todd Belcastro, a product of Mead High in Spokane, was not recruited by WSU and coach Mike Price. Ahead of the game, he gave this quote to the Idaho Statesman: “I hate the Cougars. I really do. I’m going to wear my Washington hat on the sideline Saturday after we win. I’m going to sign a football, put the score on it, and hand it to Price.”

1998: WSU follows up with a close win in Boise

In the following year, the Cougars traveled to the blue turf in Boise, where they emerged with a 33-21 win. The visitors were down 7-6 at halftime, but thanks to a 27-point second half, they won by a relatively comfortable margin.

In the fourth quarter, WSU went up by two scores on a touchdown pass from Steve Birnbaum to Leaford Hackett. Moments later, the Broncos drew within one score on a fumble recovery for a touchdown, only for the Cougars to put the game away with an explosive 79-yard touchdown rush from DeJuan Gillmore.

“They were blitzing us on just about every play in the first quarter,” said WSU coach Mike Price, whose team moved to 2-0 with that win. “That was keeping the quarterback off balance. He wasn’t able to get his feet set and make the plays we had to make.”

2000: Cougars eke out close win at Martin Stadium

In the final minute of a 35-35 game, WSU’s offense found itself at the Boise State 1-yard line.

“There was no doubt that we were going to go for it,” Price said.

The Cougars made their coach look wise, scoring on a short rush by Adam Hawkins, putting the hosts up by the final margin of 42-35. They could have kicked a field goal, but decided against it, giving their defense some extra wiggle room for the Broncos’ final drive.

In that one, WSU quarterback Jason Gesser completed 21 of 30 passes for 290 yards and two touchdowns, playing through concussion symptoms from the third quarter on.

2001: WSU spoils BSU coach Dan Hawkins’ debut with 41-20 victory

In this one, the visiting Cougars at one point ran off 28 points to secure what turned into a blowout 41-20 win, handing the Broncos a loss in new coach Dan Hawkins’ first home game at the helm of the program.

Some highlights from this game: Linebacker Raonall Smith returned an interception 54 yards for a touchdown, Gesser found James Price for a 55-yard touchdown and, in the third quarter, Collin Henderson took a lateral from Gesser in the backfield, then threw it to Nakoa McElrath, who scored on a 71-yard play to give the Cougs a 41-13 lead.

2016: Cougars’ late rally not enough in 31-28 loss

WSU and Boise State didn’t meet again for another 15 years, but the game was worth the wait. In the third quarter, the Broncos went up 24-7, only for the Cougars to come roaring back, scoring three touchdowns to pull within three in the final moments.

But it wasn’t enough for WSU, which fell in a 31-28 defeat, quarterback Luke Falk’s final desperation heave going incomplete. For the game, Falk completed 55 of 71 passes for 480 yards, four touchdowns and one interception, which turned into a long pick-six by BSU cornerback Tyler Horton.

With under a minute to go in the fourth frame, BSU inexplicably kept throwing. The Cougars made former Shadle Park High star quarterback Brett Rypien pay, getting an interception from Charleston White in the end zone.

That gave the Cougs new life in the final minute, but with a few seconds to play, Falk had to launch one deep. It hit the blue turf, sealing the Broncos’ win.

“It’s like a boxer if he’s really good at hitting the bag, and then all of a sudden he fights a boxing match and he won’t throw any blows. That’s who we are,” the late WSU coach Mike Leach said. “We have to be a tougher football team and right now we’re not. Right now we’ve got a bunch of good, nice, jolly guys who will work their asses off, at times, but as soon as anybody hits them or there’s any adversity, we fold.”

2017: Hilinski comes off the bench to lead wild triple-overtime comeback

Where to start with WSU’s 47-44 triple-overtime win in 2017? The Cougars found themselves trailing 31-10 with a shade under 11 minutes to go, only to come back to tie it and send the game to overtime, doing so on a crazy series of scoring plays.

Early in the fourth frame, BSU lineman Curtis Weaver recovered a Luke Falk fumble and returned it for a touchdown. Falk was injured on the play and did not return to the game, paving the way for the late backup Tyler Hilinski to come off the bench and lead the rest of the comeback.

The Cougars drew within two scores on a 17-yard pass from Hilinski to Jamire Calvin. That’s about when things got weird. Later, Rypien stumbled and tried a shovel pass, which was promptly picked off by WSU linebacker Peyton Pelluer, who returned it for a touchdown. That trimmed the Broncos’ lead to 31-24.

Things got even crazier from there. With about three minutes left, WSU punted, but the ball caromed off a Boise State player and was recovered by the Cougs. A few plays later, Hilinski found running back Jamal Morrow for the game-tying touchdown.

Then, after the teams played to a draw after two overtimes, the Cougars forced the Broncos into a field goal in the third. They won on their possession, thanks to a 22-yard pass from Hilinski to Morrow, who jetted to the end zone and dove across the pylon for the winning score.

A few months later, Hilinski died by suicide, making this win extra special for his family and WSU.

2024: Ashton Jeanty boosts Heisman case in BSU’s 45-24 win over WSU

In the teams’ most recent clash, things were interesting in the fourth quarter, when quarterback John Mateer unleashed a deep touchdown pass to receiver Kyle Williams, helping the visiting Cougars claw within 24-17.

But thanks to Boise State’s runaway fourth frame, that’s as close as they got, good for a 45-24 BSU win.

In this one, Bronco running back Ashton Jeanty torched the Cougar defense for 259 yards rushing for four touchdowns, helping his case for the Heisman Trophy, finishing second in that race.

Washington State.title: How does WSU's defense match up with No. 21 Boise State's rushing attack? Look no further than tackling
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Khamari Terrell makes a tackle in space, for a brief moment, he enters a world all by himself. Washington State’s veteran cornerback will usually lower his head, staring down into the turf, maybe closing his eyes, closing himself off to the chaos unfolding around him.

Then he usually takes his hands and slaps himself on the helmet. Once. Twice. Lets his energy seep off him like condensation off a glass of ice water.

Then he rejoins the action, ready to make another play for the Cougars, for whom he’s playing his fifth and final season of college football.

“I think it’s big, especially in college, just knowing that the corners have to tackle every game,” Terrell said earlier this week. “Especially this week, I’m gonna make it noticed that you’re not gonna be able to just run to my side and just think that you’re gonna get a big gain or anything.”

Terrell and the WSU defense will get a chance to prove it this weekend, when No. 21 Boise State comes to town for a showdown, the teams’ first clash in Pullman since 2017, the night the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead the Cougars to a triple-overtime comeback.

Here’s the short version of why Terrell and his fellow defensive backs, like cornerback Jalil Tucker and safety Jaylen Thomas, will have to come up big for their team: The Broncos own one of the country’s best rushing attacks, spearheaded by junior tailback Dylan Riley, who ranks second nationwide with 139 rushing yards per game. As a team, the Broncos’ 234 rushing yards per contest ranks ninth in the country.

That figures to put quite the strain on this WSU defense, which was gashed last weekend, giving up 48 points to Oregon State’s prolific offense in a three-score loss. But for the Cougars, as they prepare for their next outing, it’s not all about preventing scoring. It’s about one of Terrell’s favorite parts of the game: tackling.

All things considered, WSU (1-6, 0-3 Pac-12) has done a fine job of that this season. The Cougars have earned a Pro Football Focus tackling grade of 61.4, which ranks No. 93 nationwide, fifth in the Pac-12. They’ve turned in some gems of tackling outings, including in their loss to Fresno State earlier this season, when they missed just three total tackles.

In fact, some of the WSU defenders who have logged the most snaps are also the ones who have tackled the best. Veteran linebacker Keith Brown, who leads the team with 418 snaps, has missed only six tackles. Terrell, who has played 339 snaps, has whiffed only three times. And redshirt freshman nickelback Jamarey Smith, who has 313 snaps, has missed only one tackle all season.

So from a 30,000-foot view, the Cougars have done well to tackle, and their coaches deserve credit for that: defensive coordinator Trent Bray, cornerbacks coach Brandyn Thompson and defensive line coach Eti Ena, among others. Past Cougar teams have not tackled particularly well – Jake Dickert’s 2024 team finished the season ranked fifth-to-last in PFF’s tackling grades, while Jimmy Rogers’ 2025 club finished dead last – so for the program, this represents a key step in the right direction.

“Game to game, you gotta be prepared to tackle,” Terrell said, “especially going against a team that runs a lot. So just be physical and just shut down the side of the field and just stop the run, so they won’t try to keep running to that side.”

The only problem at hand: Boise State’s playmakers have excelled at forcing missed tackles. In six games, Riley has forced 28 whiffs, which ranks second in the Pac-12. Riley has forced 18. They have excelled in space, and while the Cougars have usually done well to tackle in those types of settings, they aren’t coming off a particularly encouraging outing on that front.

In WSU’s loss to Oregon State last weekend, the Cougs missed 18 tackles, one off their most of the season, which came in a season-opening loss to Washington back in early September. In Corvallis, safety Jeremiah Bernard led the way with five whiffs, while fellow safety Jaylen Thomas followed with three and two players missed two tackles apiece: linebacker Isaiah Hung and cornerback Kai Rapolla.

How will those two realities clash on Saturday afternoon on the Palouse? If the Cougars can’t make tackles in space, they might be in for a long day, and as 14-point underdogs, they’re expected to meet that fate anyway. But it’s an interesting conversation because of one key development: Bray’s unit has done a stellar job of stacking up runs up the middle.

That’s where some of the Cougars’ best defenders play, from defensive tackles like Jirah Leaupepetele and Kaden Beatty to defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, which is why opponents haven’t enjoyed much success running up the middle this season. Even Brown, a linebacker, has graded out as the Cougars’ best run defender, with a mark of 79.9.

It’s on the outsides where the Cougs have had less luck, at least in their most recent showing. To turn that fortune around – to reverse the fortune of this entire season – WSU defenders will have to clean that up. Maybe that’s where Terrell, a veteran cornerback, could come in handy.
