Washington State.title: How did WSU QB Owen Eshelman engineer such a strong showing in his first start? Three things stood out most
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – In the aftermath of quarterback Owen Eshelman’s first start, an electric showing in his Washington State group’s fourth straight loss over the weekend, the reactions came showering in like a typhoon.

He’s actually airing it out!

He looks poised in the pocket!

Look how sharp the Cougs’ offense looks!

Indeed, Eshelman guided WSU to 30 offensive points, the team’s most all season. That wasn’t enough to prevent the Cougs from falling short again, this time to the tune of a 48-30 final margin, but Eshelman looked accurate. He was willing to look for the deep ball. He executed a couple really well.

For the Cougars, that represented a firm step in the right direction, an indication that head coach Kirby Moore made the right call pivoting away from Caden Pinnick and swapping in Eshelman. Should coaches have made that move sooner in the season? Probably, and that conversation has been fleshed out in all kinds of ways.

“We’re not looking in the rearview mirror,” Moore said after Saturday’s game on that topic. “We gotta keep building on where we’re at right now.”

What isn’t as immediately obvious at first blush is how different the Cougs’ passing attack was with Eshelman at the controls. He aired it out, sure, but how much of a change did that represent for WSU? How did his accuracy bolster the offense? And how did he navigate the pocket?

As Washington State prepares for its homecoming game, a home showdown with first-place Boise State this weekend, those questions are worth exploring. Do the Cougs have a shot at pulling the upset? They might be 12.5-point underdogs, but Eshelman and the life he brings to his offense could be reason to believe the answer might be yes.

1. Eshelman looked to push the ball downfield

Perhaps the most striking part of Eshelman’s performance, the development that might have made you say “wow” right away, came in his readiness to stretch the field vertically. Pinnick wasn’t just shaky at this in his six starts; he wasn’t even willing to do it.

Think about this: In WSU’s loss to Utah State earlier this month, Pinnick attempted only six passes 10 yards or further downfield, according to PFF. That included zero passes 20 yards or deeper. It was clear that he wasn’t comfortable in the pocket. He didn’t trust his eyes, didn’t trust his arm.

Think about it this way: In the country, 61 QBs have dropped back at least 200 times. Among that group, Pinnick is the only one to attempt fewer than 20 passes of at least 20 yards downfield. His official numbers on those types of throws: 2-for-16 for 78 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions.

On Saturday, Eshelman tried 16 passes at least 10 yards downfield, connecting on six of them. That isn’t a great completion rate – just 38% – but his willingness to try those opened up a lot for the Cougars’ offense. On one play in the first half, Eshelman lofted one downfield for receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who hauled it in for a 40-yard touchdown pass.

“It was a great look,” Eshelman said after the game about the touchdown pass. “Had a couple different options there, and he ended up popping and was really excited for him on that touchdown, and just the offense was clicking well.”

Outside of Pinnick’s one FBS touchdown toss, a 46-yard completion to Ganashamoorthy on which an Arizona defender fell down in coverage, that was the Cougars’ longest passing scoring play all season. Eshelman showed great touch on that pass, as well as a layered 24-yard throw, also to Ganashamoorthy. It was obvious he felt confident letting throws like that fly.

On another play in Saturday’s game, a first-and-10 near the redzone, Eshelman showed the same willingness. He dropped back and spotted an open receiver in Daniel Blood, so Eshelman reared back and put the same kind of nice touch on this pass, finding Blood for a 23-yard gain. Four plays later, QB Julian Dugger came in for a short touchdown plunge.

2. Eshelman’s pocket presence stood out in a big way

One of the central problems facing Pinnick, especially in his last handful of starts, was his pocket presence. He often ran himself into sacks. He held onto the ball too long. He didn’t throw it away when he had the opportunity, leading to even more sacks. Sometimes he was too indecisive to avoid a rusher headed right for him.

Even with one fewer game under his belt, Pinnick is still tied for the nationwide lead in QB-fault sacks with 11, according to PFF.

Contrast that with the one game of Eshelman, who took just one sack of that variety, according to PFF. He was sacked on two other occasions, which were the fault of the Cougars’ offensive line, which played without injured left tackle Ashton Tripp.

In fact, some of Eshelman’s best plays came on the ground, when he identified pressure and bailed at the right times. He recorded three rushes of 20-plus yards: a 22-yard scramble, a 41-yard burst and a 19-yard read option, which he took 20 yards into the end zone for his first career rushing touchdown at the college level.

“Obviously there’s a lot of situational stuff with that, and knowing when it’s OK to punt, knowing when you might need to take a shot,” Eshelman said. “There were definitely some missed opportunities tonight, some times that I thought I did a good job, and we’ll keep working on that and growing in it.”

3. He didn’t let a slow start bog him down

How many times did we see this kind of situation unfold with Pinnick at the controls? He’d slog through something of a slow start, which is normal for any quarterback, and that kind of uneven beginning would follow him around the rest of the game.

At least from an outsider’s perspective, it seemed easy for Pinnick to let slow starts color the rest of his outing, never letting him find a rhythm later in the game.

Eshelman was hardly perfect in Saturday’s game. He missed on each of his first three passes, costing his team early chances, which was one of the ways Oregon State mounted an early 17-0 lead. He targeted Ganashamoorthy on each of his first three throws, all of which sailed wide of the mark, including a third-down throw that led to a punt.

But Eshelman didn’t let that throw him off for the rest of the game. He went on to complete 8 of his next 10 passes, including the aforementioned 24-yarder to Ganashamoorthy and a 14-yard toss to tight end Jack Pedersen.

Also in that stretch, he showed nice patience in the pocket, taking the shorter throws when they were there. That was another part of Eshleman’s game that stood out, to which he even alluded after the game: He seemed to understand when it’s OK to throw checkdowns and shorter passes.

That kept the Cougars’ offense moving.

Washington State.title: Two rookie coaches, two wildly different starts | Pac-12 football midseason awards
Washington State.summary:
The midpoint of the inaugural football season for the new Pac-12 does not exist, at least not in a clean, easily identifiable fashion.

Half the teams have played seven games; half have played six.

Half have played three conference matchups; half have played two.

But against the full sweep of a competition calendar that runs from Labor Day weekend (for everyone) through Thanksgiving weekend (for all but two teams), the end of Week 7 marks a reasonable middle.

With that, the Hotline presents our Pac-12 midseason report, in which we highlight the best and worst, key themes and standout performers.

Top storyline: CFP relevance. Two teams, Boise State and Oregon State, remain in pursuit of a berth in the College Football Playoff. The Broncos (5-1) have a quality loss at Oregon and key wins over Memphis and Western Michigan. If they win out, a bid should follow. The Beavers (5-2) have a trickier path but will be in play if they finish with two losses. The conference could not have realistically asked for more at this point.

Best coach: Oregon State’s JaMarcus Shephard. The rookie coach has made a series of master-class moves with his staff and roster and could land on the short list for national Coach of the Year if the Beavers keep winning. Also considered: Boise State’s Spencer Danielson

Hottest seat: Washington State’s Kirby Moore. The rookie coach has made a series of deeply flawed decisions with his staff and roster. We don’t expect Moore to get fired after the season, although if the current trajectory continues, you could make the case for dismissal. Also considered: San Diego State’s Sean Lewis

Best offensive player: Oregon State WR Jesse Legree. The freshman has been a revelation and is generating second-tier Heisman Trophy support. He leads the country in receiving yards and touchdowns – not bad for a three-star prospect. Also considered: Oregon State QB Braden Atkinson, Boise State TB Dylan Riley and Texas State TB Torrance Burgess

Best defensive player: San Diego State LB Sione Hala. The senior leads the Pac-12 and is fifth in the country in tackles (68) and recorded sacks against James Madison and Oregon State. He also forced a fumble against Fresno State that led to an Aztecs field goal in what became a three-point win. Also considered: Oregon State edge Takari Hickle and Fresno State lineman Dylan Hampsten.

Top transfer: Oregon State QB Braden Atkinson. The Mercer transfer threw 34 touchdown passes last year for an FCS team that won nine games, so he’s not exactly a rookie. But Atkinson’s field vision and downfield accuracy mesh perfectly with Legree’s skills. Also considered: Nobody

Best game: San Diego State 31, Texas State 29. The Oct. 3 affair in Snapdragon Stadium featured a series of momentum shifts, 40 points in the second half, just two turnovers and a stellar individual effort from Texas State quarterback Brad Jackson. Also considered: Boise State 38, Fresno State 31

Best win: Boise State 38, Memphis 20. If the Pac-12’s best team is drawn into a resume showdown with the American’s best team for a playoff berth, the Broncos’ Week 2 head-to-head win over a top American team could loom large. Also considered: Boise State over Western Michigan and Texas State over North Texas

Worst loss: Idaho State 29, Utah State 17. Double-digit home losses to FCS opponents are always ugly. Add 11 penalties and four turnovers, and this was an all-systems failure for the Aggies. Also considered: None. (We didn’t have the stomach to continue the research.)

Best performance: Oregon State WR Jesse Legree. The freshman’s breakout game came in Week 2, when he sliced and diced Texas Tech’s secondary for 240 yards receiving and two touchdowns. Also considered: Boise State TB Dylan Riley (Memphis), Texas State TB Torrance Burgess (North Texas) and San Diego State TB Javion Kinnard (James Madison)

Worst luck: San Diego State. Misfortune during the football season typically takes the form of injuries, officiating blunders or players short-circuiting in some fashion. When was the last time a team was derailed by the mumps? Probably the 1950s. Goodness, gracious.

Washington State.title: WSU WR Darrius Clemons, OT Ashton Tripp questionable with injuries, plus other notes
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State’s offense is looking better, but that group may not be at full strength this weekend when No. 21 Boise State comes to town.

Left tackle Ashton Tripp is day-to-day with an ankle injury, WSU coach Kirby Moore said Monday, while wide receiver Darrius Clemons is dealing with his own ankle injury. Medical staff is “determining the extent of that injury here early this week,” Moore said.

Tripp missed WSU’s road loss to Oregon State on Saturday, which prompted Washington transfer Maximus McCree to take his place, marking the first time someone other than Tripp has played left tackle for WSU since 2023. Tripp is a key cog on the Cougars’ offensive line.

Clemons’ injury could also be costly for the Cougs, who were already running low on depth at the wide receiver spot thanks to a season-ending ACL tear to Tony Freeman in the Sept. 6 Apple Cup. Clemons played just 12 snaps in Saturday’s game before coming out with his injury, getting carted to the locker room and returning to the bench with crutches by his side.

Listed at 6-foot-3 and 217 pounds, Clemons had played a big role in the pass-catching department, hauling in 20 receptions for 218 yards, starting in all seven games. If Clemons can’t play this weekend against Boise State, the Cougars will ask more from receivers Daniel Blood, Tank Hawkins and Branden Ganashamoorthy, the latter of whom posted 11 catches for 147 yards last weekend – both career highs.

A couple other receivers could get more reps, Moore added , West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees and walk-on Caleb Northcroft. A year after reeling in 35 receptions for 508 yards and three touchdowns at the FCS level, Dees has played just four snaps this season, all of which came against FCS Duquesne in Week 3.

Asked what’s preventing Dees from seeing a bigger role, Moore said , “There’s guys ahead of him right now on the depth chart. He’s gotta work to continue to be consistent, just like his teammates, and that’s the big focus for him is just focusing on doing his job, alignment, assignment, obviously playing catch with the quarterbacks and being on the same page.”

• In other injury news, defensive ends Malachi Wrice and Michael Hughes are expected to play “full speed” this weekend, Moore said. After missing five straight games, Hughes returned against Oregon State, posting one pressure in 30 snaps. Wrice, who has been out since Week 2, suited up but didn’t play.

That’s a meaningful development for WSU, which needs some depth behind starting pass rushers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, who combined for five pressures against Oregon State.

• On Monday, Moore also said name, image and likeness earnings have no bearing on playing time: “No, the best players are gonna play. We’ve had those evaluations at a number of positions, whether that’s quarterback, receiver, D-tackle. It’s really about who gives us the best opportunity to win.”

That has been something of a discussion lately in the wake of the coaches’ decision to bench QB Caden Pinnick, a transfer from UC Davis, in favor of redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman. Did NIL play a factor in Pinnick remaining the starter for six games? Moore said no.

So what separated those two in fall camp, and how much of what Eshelman put on display in Saturday’s game – completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one garbage-time interception, plus 15 carries for 136 yards and one score – did he seem capable of earlier in the year?

“He definitely showed flashes,” Moore said. “I think the one thing, and he would say it as well, in fall camp there, there was probably some (issues) in terms of taking care of the football. Probably had a few more than we wanted, and he’s definitely grown from that. Obviously, it starts in practice and preparing like you’re the starter, and he continued to do that throughout the season.”

In fall camp, Eshelman did commit an interception or two, including coming inches away from another at the hands of safety Jaylen Thomas. But Pinnick also had his share of turnover problems, including a three-interception (two tipped) outing in the team’s second and final scrimmage.

Washington State.title: WSU set to host Boise State for first time since 2017 | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against No. 21 Boise State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

Still looking for its first FBS win of the season, WSU (1-6, 0-3) returns home for the first time in three weeks to host No. 21 Boise State (5-1, 2-0), which was idle last week. It’s the Cougars’ and Broncos’ first time meeting in Pullman since 2017, when the late Tyler Hilinski came off the bench to lead WSU to a triple-overtime win.

It’s a full-circle moment for WSU coach Kirby Moore, who played for the Broncos from 2009-13, which is also when he met quarterbacks coach Matt Miller and formed many of the connections that he uses today.

Where is it? Gesa Field in Pullman.

When is it? Kickoff is set for 3 p.m.

Where can I watch it? USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored? WSU opened as a 14-point underdog.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 48-30 loss to Oregon State, WSU redshirt freshman quarterback Owen Eshelman got his first start, completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one late interception in garbage time. He also racked up 136 rushing yards on 15 carries, sparking the Cougs’ offense to its most points against an FBS opponent all season.

The Cougars’ offense looked much improved, at least in the passing game, but it wasn’t enough to upset the Beavers and their prolific offense. OSU QB Braden Atkinson piled up 347 passing yards and three touchdowns, including a 90-yard strike to freshman Jesse Legree and an 88-yard completion to receiver AJ Newberry, both of which came after the Cougars elected to punt on fourth-and-short near midfield – making Moore pay for his conservative approach.

After those plays, WSU couldn’t climb out of an early hole, trailing 17-0 before the visitors got on the scoreboard with a short field goal from kicker Jack Stevens. The Cougars pulled to within three scores on a 40-yard touchdown pass from Eshelman to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who finished with career highs in both receptions and receiving yards, but it was too little too late for Washington State.

“I would just say we lost there,” WSU cornerback Khamari Terrell said. “It wasn’t really we got beaten there. Just a little technical, little details. The look that we got and that they scored on, we’ve got multiple times in practice, just doing the little details. And the technique part, just staying on top and just executing there.”

Eshelman may have looked sharp on the ground, but it was another slow day for the WSU running back trio of Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi, who combined for just 26 rushing yards on 13 carries. Against FBS opponents this year, they are averaging only 52 yards per game, a far cry from the elite trio they were projected to be headed into the season.

“The tailbacks need to be able to run the ball better, but that starts up front,” Moore said on Monday. “We gotta block better, and we gotta have our hands inside. We gotta win our one-on-one matchups. We gotta put the ball in the corner in the safeties, and then from a running back standpoint, we gotta make people miss as well. So it’s a combination of things there, but we gotta do a much better job.”

Scouting Boise State…

Under head coach Spencer Danielson and veteran quarterback Maddux Madsen, the Broncos have followed a season-opening loss to Oregon with five straight wins, most recently a 38-31 win over Fresno State on Oct. 10. That has landed Boise State squarely in the discussion for the College Football Playoff.

The strength of the Broncos’ team is their rushing attack, which is averaging 235 yards per game, ninth nationally and second in the Pac-12. Running back Dylan Riley ranks second in the country with 139 yards per game, totaling six touchdowns on the ground, and fellow tailback Sire Gaines has provided an additional three scores and 354 yards. Those two have spearheaded the Broncos’ offense all season.

In his third season as BSU’s full-time starting QB, Madsen has taken phenomenal care of the ball, throwing zero interceptions and 13 touchdowns. He’s completed 110 of 166 passes (66%) for 1,296 yards. He’s also only taken five sacks, an impressive feat from the Broncos’ offensive line, which has only been responsible for three sacks according to Pro Football Focus.

The Broncos’ ground game has become so dangerous in part because their running backs are hard to bring down. Riley has forced 28 missed tackles, according to PFF, which is second in the Pac-12. Gaines isn’t far behind, with 18. Combined with Madsen’s ability to avoid turnovers – BSU has lost only three turnovers, tied for second-fewest nationally – and you get a machine of an offense.

“They’ve got a really good front,” Moore said. “They have a good scheme. They’ve got good backs. They put the ball in the corner, and a lot of times the back makes the corner miss, whether it’s a move or he breaks a tackle, and both those guys, Sire Gaines as well. They both do a really good job with the ball in their hand.”

What happened last time?

In a 2024 matchup in Boise, former Bronco running back Ashton Jeanty ran ragged over the Cougars, piling up 259 yards and four touchdowns, boosting his Heisman Trophy case. The Cougars were within one score early in the fourth quarter, but the Broncos ran away with three straight touchdowns.

Washington State.title: Washington State hoops rolled by New Mexico in exhibition; Andrew Cook shines in EWU's win over CSU Bakersfield
Washington State.summary:
Mountain West Freshman of the Year and sophomore guard Jake Hall scored 22 points on 8 of 10 shooting and the University of New Mexico Lobos Men’s basketball team beat the Washington State Cougars 92-64 in an exhibition game at The Pit in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Sunday. 

The Cougars never really stood a chance after the Lobos went on an 8-2 run to start the game, and pulled away with a 16-0 run with just under 14 minutes left in the first half.

Midway through the second half, the Cougs trailed by 42 points 80-38, their largest deficit of the game. 

Uriah Tennette hit a 3-pointer on the Lobos’ first possession but East Texas A&M senior transfer guard Ronnie Harrison replied with a layup to make it 3-2. 

But the Lobos separated themselves with a 16-point surge in a four-minute span in the first period started by redshirt freshman Imran Suljanovic’s 3-pointer at 13 minutes, 47 seconds. 

The Cougars stopped the bleeding when Dembele stole the ball from Hall, and connected with Houston on a fastbreak to make it 30-16. But WSU couldn’t recover and found themselves in a 25-point deficit entering halftime. 

Houston led WSU with 14 points and two assists, and Harrison added 12 points, four rebounds, and four assists for the Cougs. 

Andrew Cook leads Eagles to close win over CSU Bakersfield 

After missing all of last season with an ankle injury, and uncertainty surrounding his college eligibility this year, Andrew Cook shined in his 2026 season debut with the Eastern Washington Eagles, leading all players with 24 points in a 71-65 exhibition victory against CSU Bakersfield Roadrunners at Reese Court in Cheney on Sunday. 

Cook also added five rebounds to go with three assists. He was also a defensive force with a block early in the first half and two steals, including a critical one late in the second half that helped the Eagles retake the lead with just over three minutes remaining. 

Down 58-56 with 4 minutes, 7 seconds remaining, Cook stole the ball and was fouled by Tom Koppens on the fastbreak. Cook made his first free throw, but missed the second. But returning redshirt junior forward Emmett Marquardt got the offensive rebound, and Cook converted the layup to make it 59-58. EWU never trailed again. 

After a close first five minutes, the Eagles scored six straight thanks to a 3-pointer from Isak Homelius and found themselves up by eight 15-7 midway through the first half – their largest lead of the game. 

But the Roadrunners marched back, regaining the lead with 5 minutes, 25 seconds left in the first period after Malachi Richardson missed his 3-pointer, and Jaden Alexander converted his shot to make it 23-21. 

EWU and CSU Bakersfield exchanged leads, and the Eagles entered halftime down three.

Washington State.title: QB Owen Eshelman, WR Branden Ganashamoorthy spark Cougs' offense in loss to Oregon State
Washington State.summary:
CORVALLIS, Ore. – Branden Ganashamoorthy insisted the sunlight was no problem. When he strode open toward the Oregon State end zone, he said, all he saw was the ball. He tracked it in the air, on its descent, into his hands as he fell onto the black turf for six.

“When you’re in those moments,” Ganashamoorthy said, “it’s almost like tunnel vision. Everything kinda slows down. The amount of tennis balls, the amount of footballs I’ve caught. I feel like I can catch those balls almost blind.”

In his Washington State group’s 48-30 loss to Oregon State, the Cougars’ fourth straight loss, Ganashamoorthy enjoyed the best outing of his career: He logged 11 catches for 147 yards and the one score, which came on a 40-yard pass in the second quarter, pulling the Cougs to within 27-10.

It amounted to a huge day for Ganashamoorthy, an indicator of what he’s capable of. It also went a long way in illustrating how he accomplished it, finding a sharp rapport with quarterback Owen Eshelman, who made his first start. By his number, you would never have known it: He completed 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one meaningless interception in garbage time. He also totaled 11 carries for 147 yards and another touchdown, racking up the second-most yards in one game by a WSU QB in program history.

A redshirt freshman from Oklahoma, Eshelman shattered expectations for his first real game action. He looked willing to air it out deep, which the Cougars didn’t get from Caden Pinnick, who started each of the first six games of the season. He made the right reads in the pocket, bailing at the right times to scramble for yards on the ground. And he made a fantastic decision on his rushing touchdown, pulling the ball and jetting straight into the end zone, cruising in for a 20-yard score.

“We just had a much better rhythm,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said of Eshelman’s outing and what it provided to the team. “That takes all 11 being on the same page, whether it’s communication, whether it’s in the run game, the RPOs, obviously the pass game. It’s about landmarks and alignments there with the receivers and guys winning versus man and the quarterback trusting them. Today it was much better on first and second down. Third down, obviously did a better job in the second half than the first half.”

“It was definitely excitement,” Eshelman said of his emotions headed into his first start. “Obviously Oregon State’s been playing really good football, and to have the opportunity to come here and showcase what our offense is capable of … There’s that Cougar mentality that we’re just gonna keep swinging, and I thought that showed up tonight, even with some missed opportunities. I was just really proud of all of our guys. We kept swinging, kept swinging, kept swinging, and making the most out of opportunities.”

In this one, Eshelman and the Cougars’ offense was hardly perfect. They converted just 7 of 17 third downs, and through three quarters, the number was 0-for-9. They still are getting almost nothing from the running back trio of Maxwell Woods, Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi, who combined for only 26 yards on 13 carries. Under a coach like Moore, who unlocked Missouri’s rushing game to incredible results in his three years as the Tigers’ offensive coordinator, that will raise eyebrows for all the wrong reasons.

The Cougars also slogged through four three-and-outs, but their biggest problems didn’t center on things they did. They were about things they didn’t. On two spots in the first half, fourth-and-1 from the Beaver 48 and fourth-and-3 from the Cougar 49, Moore chose to punt. In both scenarios, Oregon State turned those into long touchdowns, both on the very next play. Chalk those up to misses for Moore and his game management.

“No, I’ve got a ton of confidence in our defense,” Moore said about whether he regretted punting on those plays. “Obviously, when you punt the ball and they have the ball inside their 15-yard line, you get a stop, you’ve got great field position. That didn’t happen. Give them credit. They’ve got good players. They executed and made plays.”

But overall, WSU’s offense looked far more capable than it ever has this season. The Cougars’ 30 points are their most against FBS competition all season. Outside of Eshelman’s late interception, a truly meaningless development, they avoided turnovers for the first time all season. It’s clear that Eshelman is the right quarterback for this team.

With Eshelman at the controls, and with Ganashamoorthy playing one of his favorite targets, a few more wins could be on the docket for this group.

“With the new change at quarterback, obviously, I would say just meshing together,” Ganashamoorthy said. “Now that we have that set, Owen at quarterback, I’d say meetings and everything can start to flow a little bit easier. Practices and everything, with his leadership, I think everything will come together when it does.”

Washington State.title: WSU may have lost to Oregon State, but in QB Owen Eshelman’s first start, the Cougars grew up | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
CORVALLIS, Ore. – After each of his Washington State team’s first five games of the season, Kirby Moore strode up to the postgame microphone and sounded neutral. He sounded the same after his group’s loss to Utah State and after its win over FCS Duquesne. He talked like a coach whose team had just played to a tie.

After WSU’s 48-30 loss to Oregon State here on Saturday night, the Cougars’ fourth straight loss, he talked like a coach who was furious. He was far more animated, much more visibly frustrated with the way things had unfolded. He had never shown so much emotion, low as the bar is for the usually vanilla Moore.

Here’s a sampling.

What did you think of Owen Eshelman’s play in his first start?

“We had a much better rhythm,” Moore said. “I thought the first couple drives we had some chances there didn’t execute, and then finding completions, obviously extending plays. Thought there was some tempo elements to the offense, and we gotta keep building on that.”

Do you wish you would have pivoted to him sooner in the season?

“We’re not looking in the rearview mirror,” Moore said. “We gotta keep building on where we’re at right now.”

Regardless of what you think of those answers , understand this: Moore had never looked so fired up after a game. He looked comfortable expressing both his likes and dislikes, looked confident in explaining his decisions, questionable as some were. He looked more like a head coach.

Pair that with his decision to bench Pinnick and roll with Eshelman and you wind up with this conclusion from Saturday’s game: WSU grew up. The Cougars entered their next chapter with this game. They started the right quarterback. Their coach is beginning to look and sound more like a guy who believes in his system.

It’s a significant development for WSU, even if it’s true that these things took too long to happen. Did coaches wait too long to start Eshelman? Probably. Did Moore take too long to sound so convicted? Also likely. But Moore is a first-time head coach, and these are lessons he had to learn at some point. Give him credit for being open enough to apply them midseason.

Moore almost certainly knows that he stuck with Pinnick for too long, same as he knows that it was a mistake to punt it away on two fourth-and-short situations around midfield, both of which immediately led to long Oregon State touchdowns. He didn’t acknowledge either after the game – it’s not fair to expect him to, given the way that would affect cohesion in the locker room – but you can see him learning the right lessons. That matters for the Cougs, even in what is turning into a lost season, now at 1-6 overall and 0-3 in Pac-12 play.

Here is his response to whether he regretted punting it on fourth-and-1 from the OSU 48, then punting again on fourth-and-3, both of which turned into OSU touchdowns on the very next play: “No, I’ve got a ton of confidence in our defense. Obviously, when you punt the ball and they have the ball inside their 15-yard line, you get a stop, you’ve got great field position. That didn’t happen. Give them credit. They’ve got good players. They executed and made plays.”

Two things can be true. One: Moore understands he should not have punted in those spots, and if a similar situation arises next weekend against Boise State, expect him to go for it. Two: He expressed confidence in his defense, which is key to keeping this season from going completely off the rails. Sometimes you just have to back your guys, even if it sounds silly to the rest of the world.

Now let’s get to Eshelman, who looked electric in his first career start, completing 32 of 49 passes for 289 yards, two touchdowns and one meaningless interception in the final seconds with the game out of reach. He also carried 15 times for 136 yards and one more score, earning the second-most rushing yards by a WSU QB in program history. If you didn’t know this was Eshelman’s first start, and your friend told you mid-game, you’d call them a liar.

As he made play after play, as he connected with Branden Ganashamoorthy for a 40-yard touchdown pass and as he glided 20 yards into the end zone in the second half, you might have had this thought: Why didn’t they go with Eshelman sooner? Why did they stick with Pinnick so long?

All of those thoughts are normal to feel, and heck, there’s probably some level of truth in them. Eshelman looked tremendous in this game. He aired it out for a long touchdown. He made a great read to score with his legs. He oozes talent and potential. The Cougars probably have one or two more wins with Eshelman at the controls.

Still, keep this in mind: Eshelman was not clearly WSU’s best quarterback coming out of fall camp. At that time, he looked less like a guy who could have pulled this off and more like a second-year freshman still learning the ropes of playing QB at the FBS level. Which was totally fine. Tons of quarterbacks aren’t ready to play at this stage of their careers.

During fall camp, Pinnick was pretty obviously the team’s best quarterback. He had some turnover problems, but because Eshelman didn’t look ready and because Julian Dugger didn’t pose enough threat with his arm, Pinnick felt like the right choice. That’s why it was no surprise when he was announced as such.

You can also squint and see the logic in rolling with him as long as Moore did. Pinnick looked static and turnover-prone in all six games he played, but as the struggles became clear and Moore took over playcalling duties ahead of the Utah State game, maybe coaches wanted to see how he looked with Moore calling plays. If he didn’t look any better, the thinking might have gone, pivot away from him then. That’s what coaches did.

Now, about that logic. Against FBS competition, Pinnick never really looked sharp. After he lost two turnovers in a 26-6 loss to Fresno State, it was probably time to bench him. At that point, it was clear that the opponent wasn’t the one causing Pinnick to play so poorly. It was his decision-making, his inability to stretch the field, his lack of willingness to even look at passes downfield, and all of that had a downstream effect on the Cougs’ offense. It hearkened back to the Paul Wulff days, which is not a conversation Moore wants to be in.

Besides, Moore isn’t paid to learn lessons. He’s paid to win games. He made a mistake riding with Pinnick for so long. Based on the results, Moore probably made a mistake pursuing Pinnick in the first place.

But these are things Moore was always going to have to take time to learn. As a first-time head coach, he was going to need to learn how to identify the right quarterback. He was going to need to learn when to pivot away from that guy. He was going to need to learn that, when you’re 1-5 and 18.5-point underdogs, you don’t punt it from midfield and take opportunities away from your new – and very capable – quarterback.

In hiring a first-time head coach, WSU brass implicitly acknowledged all of that, too.

With Eshelman at the controls, the complexion of the rest of this season changes a bit for the Cougars. They don’t look like a team that can beat Boise State next weekend, but they do look like one that can beat San Diego State, Colorado State, even Texas State on the road. Maybe they would be gunning for bowl eligibility in those games if they had gone to Eshelman sooner. But Eshelman is here now, and that’s the right call from Moore.

Washington State.title: Oregon State quarterback Braden Atkinson's stellar season continues | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
OSU QB Braden Atkinson

The sophomore transfer continued his remarkable debut season at the FBS level, completing 23 of 38 passes for 347 yards with three touchdowns and no turnovers. Atkinson, who won the Jerry Rice Award (FCS freshman of the year) at Mercer last season, entered the game leading the FBS in passing yards and TD throws, and he boosted his numbers on the season to 2,604 yards and 24 TDs with only two interceptions. Atkinson connected on seven completions of 15 yards or more, including a 90-yard scoring bomb in the first half to star freshman receiver Jesse Legree. Atkinson completed eight straight passes during one stretch in the second half, two for TDs, as the Beavers put the game away.

OSU RB AJ Newberry

A senior Vanderbilt transfer, Newberry had the most productive game of his collegiate career, producing 225 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown. The 6-foot-1, 200-pound Texas native was a problem for Cougar tacklers, averaging 9.5 yards on 11 carries for 105 yards on the ground, with long rushes of 30, 26 and 19 yards. He was also a threat in the passing game, recording five receptions for 120 yards. On a screen pass late in the second quarter, Newberry outraced everyone and hurdled the last WSU tackler on his way to an 88-yard touchdown, which extended Oregon State’s lead to 27-3, an insurmountable deficit for a Cougars team that found some offensive success with a new quarterback, but is still searching for consistency.

Washington State.title: WSU men's hoops releases full 2026-27 schedule
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State’s first men’s basketball schedule in the rebuilt Pac-12 has arrived.

In coach David Riley’s third season, the Cougars have five home nonconference games in Pullman, and their Pac-12 opener is set for Jan. 3 at Fresno State. WSU will also play 11 nonconference games away from Pullman, the program’s most since 1973-74, underscoring the ways coaches have to keep budgets in mind when building schedules in this new athletics ecosystem.

WSU has a home game on Nov. 14 against Kirkland, of the NAIA ranks, marking the Cougars’ first time hosting a non-Division-I opponent since 2015.

WSU and Gonzaga will meet in Pullman on Jan. 6, which is a Wednesday during the Cougars’ winter break, and in Spokane on Feb. 17.

In the new Pac-12, it’s become clear that teams will play primarily on Wednesdays and Saturdays, which is the case for the majority of the Cougars’ games. They have a few games set for Sunday, particularly early in the conference slate, but those will be the most prevalent game days.

It’s also now official that for the first time since 1917, WSU and rival Washington will not play a regular-season game against each other. Instead, the clubs will meet for an exhibition matchup Oct. 25 in Seattle.

The beginning of the new Pac-12 schedule won’t be easy for WSU, which faces a stretch of three of four road games: at Boise State, at home against San Diego State, then on the road to face Colorado State and Utah State, the last of which figures to be a new conference power.

The Cougars also have what figures to be a brutal two-game stretch Feb. 17 and Feb. 20, which include road games against Gonzaga and San Diego State, respectively.

The new Pac-12 Tournament is set for March 9–13 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas.
